This model is created by a new transformation relating the joint probabilities of attributes in the database to the weights (Gibbs potentials) of the distributed network model. The theory of this transformation is presented together with experimental re(cid:173) sults. One advantage of this approach is the network weights are prescribed without iterative gradient descent. paragraphs: The paper presents a way to construct a neural network whose outputs are accurate probability estimates. The network represents the training database through a Gibbs probability distribution. This gives the model an explicit probabilistic foundation, with its weights connected to the statistical relationships among attributes observed in the database.

The main contribution is a transformation from joint attribute probabilities to network weights, described as Gibbs potentials. The paper develops the theory of this transformation and presents experiments. Because the transformation prescribes the weights, constructing the model does not require iterative gradient descent to discover those weights through repeated error-based adjustments.

When used for classification, the resulting network matches or exceeds published results across a variety of databases. This supports the practical usefulness of the probability-based construction as well as its role in estimating probabilities. The approach connects database statistics, a distributed network representation, and classification through a single mapping from observed joint probabilities to model parameters.
summary.tldr: A transformation from database joint probabilities to Gibbs potentials constructs neural probability estimators without iterative gradient descent.

title: Probability Estimation from a Database Using a Gibbs Energy Model

paragraphs: The paper connects two simple accounts of neuronal firing. A Poisson neuron generates random spikes according to a rate determined by the current stimulus. An integrate-and-fire neuron instead filters and accumulates its input until a threshold is reached, emits a spike, and resets. For a specified input, the latter model behaves deterministically.

The authors show how a slightly modified Poisson model can be derived from an integrate-and-fire neuron receiving a signal plus noise. The resulting relationship between stimulus and firing rate has a sigmoid shape described by an error function. Its shape depends on the variance of the input noise.

This result explains how stochastic firing can emerge from threshold-based dynamics when the inputs themselves fluctuate. It connects the rate-based description used in studies of neurons in living animals with a dynamical description used to conceptualize single-cell behavior. The equivalence concerns the modified Poisson model derived under noisy input, making noise part of the explanation for the relationship between the two descriptions.
summary.tldr: Noisy inputs allow an integrate-and-fire neuron to yield a modified Poisson description with a noise-dependent sigmoid firing-rate function.

title: When is an Integrate-and-fire Neuron like a Poisson Neuron?

abstract: The full Bayesian method for applying neural networks to a pre(cid:173) diction problem is to set up the prior/hyperprior structure for the net and then perform the necessary integrals. However, these inte(cid:173) grals are not tractable analytically, and Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods are slow, especially if the parameter space is high-dimensional. Using Gaussian processes we can approximate the weight space integral analytically, so that only a small number of hyperparameters need be integrated over by MCMC methods. We have applied this idea to classification problems, obtaining ex(cid:173) cellent results on the real-world problems investigated so far .

paragraphs: A fully Bayesian neural-network prediction requires averaging over uncertain parameters according to a prior and hyperprior structure. The obstacle is computational: the necessary integrals cannot generally be evaluated analytically, and sampling becomes slow when there are many parameters. This paper uses Gaussian processes to reduce the amount of sampling required.

The key step is to approximate the integral over network weights analytically. After that step, Monte Carlo methods need to handle only a small collection of hyperparameters. The approach therefore changes where the computational effort is spent, replacing a large weight-space sampling problem with analytical work plus sampling in a much smaller space.

The authors apply the idea to classification and report excellent results on the real-world problems investigated. These findings support Gaussian processes as a practical route to Bayesian classification when direct integration over neural-network weights is burdensome. The reported success concerns those investigated problems, while the broader methodological contribution is the reduction of the high-dimensional integration burden.
summary.tldr: Gaussian processes approximate Bayesian weight integration analytically, leaving only a few hyperparameters for Monte Carlo sampling.

title: Gaussian Processes for Bayesian Classification via Hybrid Monte Carlo

abstract: We introduce an algorithm for estimating the values of a function at a set of test points Xe+!, ... , xl+m given a set of training points (XI,YI), ... ,(xe,Ye) without estimating (as an intermediate step) the regression function . We demonstrate that this direct (transduc(cid:173) ti ve) way for estimating values of the regression (or classification in pattern recognition) can be more accurate than the tradition(cid:173) alone based on two steps, first estimating the function and then calculating the values of this function at the points of interest.

We demonstrate that this direct (transduc(cid:173) ti ve) way for estimating values of the regression (or classification in pattern recognition) can be more accurate than the tradition(cid:173) alone based on two steps, first estimating the function and then calculating the values of this function at the points of interest.

paragraphs: A conventional prediction pipeline first estimates a function from training examples, then evaluates that function at test inputs. This paper considers a more targeted problem: estimating the values at a particular collection of test points directly. The available evidence consists of training inputs paired with their known outputs.

The proposed algorithm uses transductive inference, meaning that the requested test values are the immediate objects of estimation. It avoids estimating an entire regression function as an intermediate step. This changes the scope of the learning task, concentrating it on the points for which answers are actually requested.

The authors demonstrate that this direct approach can be more accurate than the conventional two-stage procedure. They describe its relevance to both regression values and classification in pattern recognition. The claim is a possibility established by their demonstration, not a guarantee that transduction always improves prediction. Its significance is that learning a general function need not be the most accurate route when the objective is to answer a specified set of prediction queries.
summary.tldr: Directly estimating outputs at specified test points can be more accurate than first learning a general prediction function.

title: Transductive Inference for Estimating Values of Functions

abstract: Vapnik's result that the expectation of the generalisation error ofthe opti(cid:173) mal hyperplane is bounded by the expectation of the ratio of the number of support vectors to the number of training examples is extended to a broad class of kernel machines. The class includes Support Vector Ma(cid:173) chines for soft margin classification and regression, and Regularization Networks with a variety of kernels and cost functions. We show that key inequalities in Vapnik's result become equalities once "the classification error" is replaced by "the margin error", with the latter defined as an in(cid:173) stance with positive cost. In particular we show that expectations of the true margin error and the empirical margin error are equal, and that the sparse solutions for kernel machines are possible only if the cost function is "partially" insensitive.

The class includes Support Vector Ma(cid:173) chines for soft margin classification and regression, and Regularization Networks with a variety of kernels and cost functions. We show that key inequalities in Vapnik's result become equalities once "the classification error" is replaced by "the margin error", with the latter defined as an in(cid:173) stance with positive cost. paragraphs: The paper extends a theoretical link between the number of support vectors and expected generalization error. The original result bounds expected error by the expected fraction of training examples that are support vectors. The extension covers a broad class of kernel machines, including soft-margin support vector classification, regression, and regularization networks.

The authors then replace classification error with margin error, defined here as an example receiving positive cost. Under that change, key inequalities become equalities. In particular, the expected true margin error equals the expected empirical margin error. These statements concern expectations, so they do not assert that the corresponding errors coincide for every individual training sample.

A further result gives a necessary condition for sparse solutions: the cost function must be partially insensitive. The claim does not say that this property alone guarantees sparsity. Together, the results connect the way a learning objective assigns cost with the possibility of a compact data representation and with theoretical error relationships.
summary.tldr: The paper extends support-vector error results to broader kernel machines and shows partial cost insensitivity is necessary for sparse solutions.

title: Sparsity of Data Representation of Optimal Kernel Machine and Leave-one-out Estimator

abstract: This paper explores a framework for recognition of image sequences using partially observable stochastic differential equation (SDE) models. Monte-Carlo importance sampling techniques are used for efficient estimation of sequence likelihoods and sequence likelihood gradients. Once the network dynamics are learned, we apply the SDE models to sequence recognition tasks in a manner similar to the way Hidden Markov models (HMMs) are commonly applied. The potential advantage of SDEs over HMMS is the use of contin(cid:173) uous state dynamics. We present encouraging results for a video sequence recognition task in which SDE models provided excellent performance when compared to hidden Markov models.

The potential advantage of SDEs over HMMS is the use of contin(cid:173) uous state dynamics. We present encouraging results for a video sequence recognition task in which SDE models provided excellent performance when compared to hidden Markov models.

paragraphs: This paper explores image-sequence recognition with partially observable stochastic differential equation models. The models describe evolving dynamics whose state is not fully observed through the images. Their proposed attraction for sequence recognition is the use of continuous state dynamics, which the authors identify as a potential advantage over hidden Markov models.

To learn and evaluate these models, the authors use Monte Carlo importance sampling to estimate sequence likelihoods and their gradients efficiently. The likelihood measures how well a model accounts for a sequence, while its gradient supplies information for learning the network dynamics. These estimates make the dynamical formulation usable within the proposed recognition framework.

After learning the dynamics, the SDE models are applied to recognition in a manner similar to the common use of hidden Markov models. The authors report encouraging results on a video-sequence recognition task, describing excellent performance in comparison with HMMs. The reported experiment supports the framework's promise, while continuous dynamics remain the stated potential reason for preferring this model family.
summary.tldr: Partially observable SDE models use importance sampling for learning and show encouraging video-recognition performance compared with HMMs.

title: Partially Observable SDE Models for Image Sequence Recognition Tasks

abstract: Hebbian learning rules are generally formulated as static rules. Un(cid:173) der changing condition (e.g. neuromodulation, input statistics) most rules are sensitive to parameters. In particular, recent work has focused on two different formulations of spike-timing-dependent plasticity rules. Additive STDP [1] is remarkably versatile but also very fragile, whereas multiplicative STDP [2, 3] is more ro(cid:173) bust but lacks attractive features such as synaptic competition and rate stabilization. Here we address the problem of robustness in the additive STDP rule. We derive an adaptive control scheme, where the learning function is under fast dynamic control by post(cid:173) synaptic activity to stabilize learning under a variety of conditions. Such a control scheme can be implemented using known biophysical mechanisms of synapses. We show that this adaptive rule makes the addit ive STDP more robust. Finally, we give an example how meta plasticity of the adaptive rule can be used to guide STDP into different type of learning regimes.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the fragility of additive spike-timing-dependent plasticity, a rule for changing synapses based on spike timing. The authors describe additive STDP as versatile but sensitive to changing conditions. Multiplicative STDP is more robust, but lacks attractive properties such as synaptic competition and rate stabilization.

They derive an adaptive control scheme in which postsynaptic activity rapidly regulates the learning function. Learning is therefore influenced by the current dynamics of the receiving neuron. The aim is to stabilize the additive rule across a variety of conditions, including changes that can make fixed learning rules sensitive to their parameters. The authors state that known synaptic biophysical mechanisms could implement this control.

The resulting adaptive rule makes additive STDP more robust. The authors also provide an example in which metaplasticity—changes to the regulation of plasticity itself—guides the rule into different learning regimes. The contribution is a mechanism connecting neuronal activity to the control of synaptic learning, with demonstrated robustness improvements and a possible biophysical implementation.
summary.tldr: Fast control by postsynaptic activity makes additive STDP more robust and can help direct it into different learning regimes.

title: Why Neuronal Dynamics Should Control Synaptic Learning Rules

abstract: We rigorously establish a close relationship between message passing algorithms and models of neurodynamics by showing that the equations of a continuous Hop- (cid:2)eld network can be derived from the equations of belief propagation on a binary Markov random (cid:2)eld. As Hop(cid:2)eld networks are equipped with a Lyapunov func- tion, convergence is guaranteed. As a consequence, in the limit of many weak con- nections per neuron, Hop(cid:2)eld networks exactly implement a continuous-time vari- ant of belief propagation starting from message initialisations that prevent from running into convergence problems. Our results lead to a better understanding of the role of message passing algorithms in real biological neural networks.

paragraphs: This paper establishes a mathematical connection between probabilistic message passing and neural network dynamics. The authors derive the equations of a continuous Hopfield network from belief propagation on a binary Markov random field. The connection provides a precise relationship between two descriptions of computation: messages exchanged in a probabilistic model and evolving activity in a neural network.

A key part of the argument concerns convergence. Hopfield networks have a Lyapunov function that supports a convergence guarantee. The authors use this property to identify a connection with belief propagation that avoids convergence problems for the relevant message initializations.

The exact implementation statement applies in the limit where each neuron has many weak connections. In that limit, Hopfield networks implement a continuous-time form of belief propagation with the specified initialization behavior. These conditions are central to the result. The contribution gives a rigorous way to understand how neural dynamics can correspond to probabilistic inference and informs the interpretation of message passing in biological neural networks.
summary.tldr: In the many-weak-connections limit, continuous Hopfield networks exactly implement a convergent continuous-time form of belief propagation with suitable initializations.

title: The Neurodynamics of Belief Propagation on Binary Markov Random Fields

abstract: A discriminative method is proposed for learning monotonic transforma- tions of the training data while jointly estimating a large-margin classi(cid:12)er. In many domains such as document classi(cid:12)cation, image histogram classi(cid:12)- cation and gene microarray experiments, (cid:12)xed monotonic transformations can be useful as a preprocessing step. However, most classi(cid:12)ers only explore these transformations through manual trial and error or via prior domain knowledge. The proposed method learns monotonic transformations auto- matically while training a large-margin classi(cid:12)er without any prior knowl- edge of the domain. A monotonic piecewise linear function is learned which transforms data for subsequent processing by a linear hyperplane classi(cid:12)er. Two algorithmic implementations of the method are formalized. The (cid:12)rst solves a convergent alternating sequence of quadratic and linear programs until it obtains a locally optimal solution. An improved algorithm is then derived using a convex semide(cid:12)nite relaxation that overcomes initializa- tion issues in the greedy optimization problem. The e(cid:11)ectiveness of these learned transformations on synthetic problems, text data and image data is demonstrated.

paragraphs: Monotonic transformations change the scale of data while preserving order. They can be useful before classification, but choosing them often involves manual experimentation or domain knowledge. This paper learns such transformations automatically together with a large-margin classifier, making the preprocessing choice part of the supervised learning problem.

The learned transformation is a monotonic piecewise linear function, followed by a linear hyperplane classifier. The authors develop two implementations. The first alternates between quadratic and linear programs and converges to a locally optimal solution. The second uses a convex semidefinite relaxation to overcome initialization difficulties in the greedy optimization procedure.

Experiments demonstrate the usefulness of learned transformations on synthetic problems, text data, and image data. The approach matters because the representation and classifier are fitted together, so the transformation can be chosen for the classification objective. Its optimization claims remain specific: the alternating procedure reaches a local optimum, while the improved formulation addresses initialization through a relaxation.
summary.tldr: Jointly learning monotonic data transformations and a large-margin classifier automates useful preprocessing, with two optimization formulations and empirical demonstrations.

title: Learning Monotonic Transformations for Classification

abstract: Point-based algorithms have been surprisingly successful in computing approx- imately optimal solutions for partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) in high dimensional belief spaces. In this work, we seek to understand the belief-space properties that allow some POMDP problems to be approximated efﬁciently and thus help to explain the point-based algorithms’ success often ob- served in the experiments. We show that an approximately optimal POMDP so- lution can be computed in time polynomial in the covering number of a reachable belief space, which is the subset of the belief space reachable from a given belief point. We also show that under the weaker condition of having a small covering number for an optimal reachable space, which is the subset of the belief space reachable under an optimal policy, computing an approximately optimal solution is NP-hard. However, given a suitable set of points that “cover” an optimal reach- able space well, an approximate solution can be computed in polynomial time. The covering number highlights several interesting properties that reduce the com- plexity of POMDP planning in practice, e.g., fully observed state variables, beliefs with sparse support, smooth beliefs, and circulant state-transition matrices.

paragraphs: Planning with partial observability involves beliefs about the state, and those belief spaces can be high-dimensional. Yet point-based POMDP algorithms often approximate good solutions successfully. This paper investigates why, focusing on a covering number: a measure of how many points are needed to represent the relevant belief space at the required resolution.

The authors show that an approximately optimal solution can be computed in time polynomial in the covering number of the space reachable from a given initial belief. A small covering number only for beliefs reachable under an optimal policy is a weaker condition, and planning remains NP-hard under that condition. The distinction concerns which reachable space is small.

However, if a suitable set of points covering the optimal reachable space is supplied, an approximate solution can be computed in polynomial time. This separates a useful compact representation from the difficulty of obtaining it. The analysis also highlights helpful structures, including fully observed variables, sparsely supported or smooth beliefs, and circulant transition matrices, offering explanations for practical approximation success.
summary.tldr: POMDP approximation depends on how compactly reachable beliefs can be covered, with a crucial distinction between all reachable beliefs and those under an optimal policy.

title: What makes some POMDP problems easy to approximate?

abstract: We consider continuous state, continuous action batch reinforcement learning where the goal is to learn a good policy from a sufficiently rich trajectory generated by another policy. We study a variant of fitted Q-iteration, where the greedy action selection is replaced by searching for a policy in a restricted set of candidate policies by maximizing the average action values. We provide a rigorous theoretical analysis of this algorithm, proving what we believe is the first finite-time bounds for value-function based algorithms for continuous state- and action-space problems.
originalAbstract: We consider continuous state, continuous action batch reinforcement learning where the goal is to learn a good policy from a sufficiently rich trajectory generated by another policy. We study a variant of fitted Q-iteration, where the greedy action selection is replaced by searching for a policy in a restricted set of candidate policies by maximizing the average action values. We provide a rigorous theoretical analysis of this algorithm, proving what we believe is the first finite-time bounds for value-function based algorithms for continuous state- and action-space problems.

paragraphs: The paper studies batch reinforcement learning when both states and actions are continuous. The learner must construct a good policy from a trajectory previously generated by another policy. A stated requirement is that this trajectory be sufficiently rich, so the learning problem depends on the information already available in the collected experience.

The authors modify fitted Q-iteration, a value-function-based learning approach. They replace greedy action selection with a search over a restricted collection of candidate policies. The search selects a policy by maximizing average action values, shifting the improvement step toward choosing among whole candidate policies using the estimated values.

The main contribution is a rigorous theoretical analysis of this variant, including finite-time bounds. Such bounds characterize the algorithm's behavior after a finite amount of learning rather than describing only an eventual limit. The authors believe these are the first bounds of this kind for value-function methods with continuous states and actions. The result concerns the analyzed algorithm and its setting, including the restricted policy collection and sufficiently rich trajectory.
summary.tldr: A fitted Q-iteration variant searches a restricted policy class and receives finite-time theoretical bounds for continuous-state, continuous-action batch learning.

title: Fitted Q-iteration in continuous action-space MDPs

abstract: Policy gradient Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms have received much attention in seeking stochastic policies that maximize the average rewards. In addition, extensions based on the concept of the Natural Gradient (NG) show promising learning efficiency because these regard metrics for the task. Though there are two candidate metrics, Kakades Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) and Morimuras FIM, all RL algorithms with NG have followed the Kakades approach. In this paper, we describe a generalized Natural Gradient (gNG) by linearly interpolating the two FIMs and propose an efficient implementation for the gNG learning based on a theory of the estimating function, generalized Natural Actor-Critic (gNAC). The gNAC algorithm involves a near optimal auxiliary function to reduce the variance of the gNG estimates. Interestingly, the gNAC can be regarded as a natural extension of the current state-of-the-art NAC algorithm, as long as the interpolating parameter is appropriately selected. Numerical experiments showed that the proposed gNAC algorithm can estimate gNG efficiently and outperformed the NAC algorithm.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning methods that adjust a probabilistic action policy to increase average reward. Natural-gradient methods make these adjustments using a mathematical description of the policy's geometry. The authors focus on two proposed descriptions, both expressed as Fisher information matrices, and note that existing natural-gradient algorithms had used only one of them.

Their generalized natural gradient interpolates linearly between the two matrices. This makes the choice of geometry adjustable rather than fixed. They then develop generalized Natural Actor-Critic, or gNAC, to estimate this gradient efficiently using estimating-function theory. A near-optimal auxiliary function reduces the variability of the gradient estimates, addressing the practical problem of learning from noisy information.

With an appropriate interpolation parameter, gNAC can be understood as an extension of the existing Natural Actor-Critic algorithm. Numerical experiments report efficient estimation of the generalized gradient and better performance than NAC. These findings support the proposed combination of flexible geometry and variance reduction in the tested settings.
summary.tldr: An adjustable natural-gradient geometry and variance-reduction method extend Natural Actor-Critic and outperform it in reported experiments.

title: A Generalized Natural Actor-Critic Algorithm

abstract: We investigate the representational power of sum-product networks (computation networks analogous to neural networks, but whose individual units compute either products or weighted sums), through a theoretical analysis that compares deep (multiple hidden layers) vs. shallow (one hidden layer) architectures. We prove there exist families of functions that can be represented much more efficiently with a deep network than with a shallow one, i.e. with substantially fewer hidden units. Such results were not available until now, and contribute to motivate recent research involving learning of deep sum-product networks, and more generally motivate research in Deep Learning.

paragraphs: The paper investigates the representational value of depth in sum-product networks. These are computation networks whose units calculate either products or weighted sums. The authors compare architectures with multiple hidden layers against shallow architectures with one hidden layer, asking how many hidden units are needed to represent the same functions.

Their theoretical result identifies families of functions that deep sum-product networks can represent with substantially fewer hidden units than shallow ones. This establishes an efficiency advantage for depth within those families. The relevant resource is representation size: adding layers can reduce the number of units required to express particular computations.

The finding supplies a mathematical motivation for studying and learning deep sum-product networks, and the authors connect it more broadly to interest in deep learning. Its claim is existential: there are function families for which depth provides a strong advantage. The contribution is therefore a separation in representational power, rather than an empirical claim that every deep model will learn better than every shallow model.
summary.tldr: Some function families require substantially fewer hidden units in deep sum-product networks than in single-hidden-layer networks.

title: Shallow vs. Deep Sum-Product Networks

abstract: We address the problem of general supervised learning when data can only be accessed through an (indefinite) similarity function between data points. Existing work on learning with indefinite kernels has concentrated solely on binary/multiclass classification problems. We propose a model that is generic enough to handle any supervised learning task and also subsumes the model previously proposed for classification. We give a ''goodness'' criterion for similarity functions w.r.t. a given supervised learning task and then adapt a well-known landmarking technique to provide efficient algorithms for supervised learning using ''good'' similarity functions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our model on three important supervised learning problems: a) real-valued regression, b) ordinal regression and c) ranking where we show that our method guarantees bounded generalization error. Furthermore, for the case of real-valued regression, we give a natural goodness definition that, when used in conjunction with a recent result in sparse vector recovery, guarantees a sparse predictor with bounded generalization error. Finally, we report results of our learning algorithms on regression and ordinal regression tasks using non-PSD similarity functions and demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithms, especially that of the sparse landmark selection algorithm that achieves significantly higher accuracies than the baseline methods while offering reduced computational costs.

paragraphs: The paper considers supervised learning when data are accessible only through pairwise similarity scores, including similarities that are not positive semidefinite. Previous work had concentrated on classification. The authors propose a broader model intended to cover general supervised tasks while including the earlier classification framework.

They define what makes a similarity function good for a particular task and adapt a landmarking technique to obtain efficient algorithms from such functions. For real-valued regression, ordinal regression, and ranking, they establish bounded generalization error. In real-valued regression, an additional goodness definition combined with a sparse-recovery result yields a sparse predictor with a generalization bound.

Experiments examine regression and ordinal regression with non-positive-semidefinite similarities. The authors report particularly strong results for sparse landmark selection, which improves accuracy over their baselines while reducing computational cost. The contribution connects task-specific conditions on similarity quality to both learning guarantees and practical algorithms, extending the usefulness of similarity-based access beyond classification.
summary.tldr: Task-specific similarity conditions and landmarking support efficient regression and ranking with generalization guarantees, including sparse predictors.

title: Supervised Learning with Similarity Functions

abstract: This paper is concerned with finding a solution x to a quadratic system of equations y i = |< a i, x >|^2, i = 1, 2, ..., m. We prove that it is possible to solve unstructured quadratic systems in n variables exactly from O(n) equations in linear time, that is, in time proportional to reading and evaluating the data. This is accomplished by a novel procedure, which starting from an initial guess given by a spectral initialization procedure, attempts to minimize a non-convex objective. The proposed algorithm distinguishes from prior approaches by regularizing the initialization and descent procedures in an adaptive fashion, which discard terms bearing too much influence on the initial estimate or search directions. These careful selection rules---which effectively serve as a variance reduction scheme---provide a tighter initial guess, more robust descent directions, and thus enhanced practical performance. Further, this procedure also achieves a near-optimal statistical accuracy in the presence of noise. Finally, we demonstrate empirically that the computational cost of our algorithm is about four times that of solving a least-squares problem of the same size.

paragraphs: The paper studies recovering an unknown vector from measurements that square the magnitude of its inner products with known vectors. These quadratic measurements lead to a nonconvex recovery problem. For the random, unstructured systems studied, the authors prove exact recovery from a number of equations proportional to the number of variables, with time proportional to reading and evaluating the data.

The algorithm begins with a spectral estimate and then minimizes a nonconvex objective. Its distinguishing feature is adaptive filtering during both initialization and descent. Terms with excessive influence are discarded, preventing them from dominating the initial guess or subsequent search directions. The authors interpret these selection rules as variance reduction, producing tighter initialization and more robust updates.

The method also achieves near-optimal statistical accuracy when measurements contain noise. Empirically, its computational cost is reported as about four times that of a same-sized least-squares problem. That comparison supports the title’s practical message for the studied systems, while the exact-recovery and noisy-data claims describe different measurement settings.
summary.tldr: Adaptive filtering enables efficient recovery in the studied random quadratic systems, with exact noiseless recovery and near-optimal accuracy under noise.

title: Solving Random Quadratic Systems of Equations Is Nearly as Easy as Solving Linear Systems

abstract: Compact explicit feature maps provide a practical framework to scale kernel methods to large-scale learning, but deriving such maps for many types of kernels remains a challenging open problem. Among the commonly used kernels for nonlinear classification are polynomial kernels, for which low approximation error has thus far necessitated explicit feature maps of large dimensionality, especially for higher-order polynomials. Meanwhile, because polynomial kernels are unbounded, they are frequently applied to data that has been normalized to unit l2 norm. The question we address in this work is: if we know a priori that data is so normalized, can we devise a more compact map? We show that a putative affirmative answer to this question based on Random Fourier Features is impossible in this setting, and introduce a new approximation paradigm, Spherical Random Fourier (SRF) features, which circumvents these issues and delivers a compact approximation to polynomial kernels for data on the unit sphere. Compared to prior work, SRF features are less rank-deficient, more compact, and achieve better kernel approximation, especially for higher-order polynomials. The resulting predictions have lower variance and typically yield better classification accuracy.

paragraphs: Explicit feature maps can make kernel methods easier to scale, but accurately approximating polynomial kernels has required many features, especially for higher-degree polynomials. This paper asks whether a common preprocessing choice can help: when every input has unit Euclidean norm, all the data lies on the unit sphere.

The authors show that a proposed affirmative route using Random Fourier Features is impossible in this setting. They then introduce Spherical Random Fourier features, an alternative approximation approach designed for data on the sphere. The construction uses the normalization assumption to obtain compact approximations to polynomial kernels.

Compared with prior work, the resulting features are reported to be more compact, less rank deficient, and more accurate at approximating the kernel, with particularly strong benefits for higher-order polynomials. Predictions also have lower variance and typically better classification accuracy. The contribution shows how a known property of the input domain can shape a more effective approximation, while keeping the classification improvement appropriately qualified as typical.
summary.tldr: Spherical random features exploit unit-normalized inputs to approximate polynomial kernels more compactly and accurately, typically improving classification.

title: Spherical Random Features for Polynomial Kernels

abstract: Feature construction is of vital importance in reinforcement learning, as the quality of a value function or policy is largely determined by the corresponding features. The recent successes of deep reinforcement learning (RL) only increase the importance of understanding feature construction. Typical deep RL approaches use a linear output layer, which means that deep RL can be interpreted as a feature construction/encoding network followed by linear value function approximation. This paper develops and evaluates a theory of linear feature encoding. We extend theoretical results on feature quality for linear value function approximation from the uncontrolled case to the controlled case. We then develop a supervised linear feature encoding method that is motivated by insights from linear value function approximation theory, as well as empirical successes from deep RL. The resulting encoder is a surprisingly effective method for linear value function approximation using raw images as inputs.

paragraphs: In reinforcement learning, the features used to represent observations strongly influence the quality of a value function or policy. This paper studies feature construction through the lens of linear value approximation. Its motivation comes partly from deep reinforcement learning systems whose final output layer is linear, allowing the preceding network to be viewed as a feature encoder.

The authors extend theoretical results about feature quality from the uncontrolled setting to the controlled setting. This brings the analysis into a setting where actions are part of the learning problem. They then use insights from that theory, together with empirical lessons from deep reinforcement learning, to develop a supervised method for linear feature encoding.

The resulting encoder is evaluated with raw images as inputs and is reported to be surprisingly effective for linear value-function approximation. The significance is a connection between representation theory and a practical encoding method: understanding which features help a linear value predictor can guide how those features are constructed, even when observations begin as images.
summary.tldr: The paper extends feature-quality theory to controlled reinforcement learning and develops an effective supervised linear encoder for raw images.

title: Linear Feature Encoding for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The inverse covariance matrix provides considerable insight for understanding statistical models in the multivariate setting. In particular, when the distribution over variables is assumed to be multivariate normal, the sparsity pattern in the inverse covariance matrix, commonly referred to as the precision matrix, corresponds to the adjacency matrix representation of the Gauss-Markov graph, which encodes conditional independence statements between variables. Minimax results under the spectral norm have previously been established for covariance matrices, both sparse and banded, and for sparse precision matrices. We establish minimax estimation bounds for estimating banded precision matrices under the spectral norm. Our results greatly improve upon the existing bounds; in particular, we find that the minimax rate for estimating banded precision matrices matches that of estimating banded covariance matrices. The key insight in our analysis is that we are able to obtain barely-noisy estimates of $k \times k$ subblocks of the precision matrix by inverting slightly wider blocks of the empirical covariance matrix along the diagonal. Our theoretical results are complemented by experiments demonstrating the sharpness of our bounds.

paragraphs: A precision matrix is the inverse of a covariance matrix. Under a multivariate normal assumption, its pattern of zero and nonzero entries describes conditional independence relationships among variables. Estimating this matrix accurately is therefore useful for understanding multivariate structure. This paper establishes minimax estimation bounds for banded precision matrices under spectral-norm error.

The key construction estimates small blocks of the precision matrix by inverting slightly wider blocks of the empirical covariance matrix along its diagonal. The authors show that this produces estimates with very little noise. This local block strategy supplies the central insight needed to sharpen the theoretical bounds.

The resulting minimax rate matches the rate for estimating banded covariance matrices and substantially improves the existing precision-matrix bounds. Minimax analysis concerns the best achievable worst-case error over the matrix class under study, so the result characterizes the statistical difficulty of the estimation problem. Experiments complement the theory by demonstrating the sharpness of the bounds, supporting their relevance to observed estimation behavior.
summary.tldr: A local block-inversion analysis yields sharper minimax bounds for banded precision matrices, matching the rate for banded covariance estimation.

title: Minimax Estimation of Bandable Precision Matrices

abstract: In this paper, we propose ELF, an Extensive, Lightweight and Flexible platform for fundamental reinforcement learning research. Using ELF, we implement a highly customizable real-time strategy (RTS) engine with three game environments (Mini-RTS, Capture the Flag and Tower Defense). Mini-RTS, as a miniature version of StarCraft, captures key game dynamics and runs at 165K frame-per-second (FPS) on a laptop. When coupled with modern reinforcement learning methods, the system can train a full-game bot against built-in AIs end-to-end in one day with 6 CPUs and 1 GPU. In addition, our platform is flexible in terms of environment-agent communication topologies, choices of RL methods, changes in game parameters, and can host existing C/C++-based game environments like ALE. Using ELF, we thoroughly explore training parameters and show that a network with Leaky ReLU and Batch Normalization coupled with long-horizon training and progressive curriculum beats the rule-based built-in AI more than 70% of the time in the full game of Mini-RTS. Strong performance is also achieved on the other two games. In game replays, we show our agents learn interesting strategies. ELF, along with its RL platform, is open-sourced at https://github.com/facebookresearch/ELF.

paragraphs: ELF is a platform for reinforcement learning research built around fast, configurable game environments. The authors implement a real-time strategy engine with Mini-RTS, Capture the Flag, and Tower Defense. Mini-RTS preserves key dynamics of a larger strategy game while running at 165,000 frames per second on a laptop, enabling substantial simulated experience.

The platform supports different arrangements for communication between environments and agents, different learning methods, and changes to game parameters. It can also host existing C/C++ game environments. With six CPUs and one GPU, the reported system trains a bot end to end against built-in opponents in one day.

The authors investigate training choices and report that Leaky ReLU, Batch Normalization, long-horizon training, and a progressive curriculum together produce a Mini-RTS agent that beats the rule-based opponent more than 70% of the time. They also report strong performance in the other games and interesting strategies in replays. These findings demonstrate the platform's usefulness for testing how training choices affect complete game behavior.
summary.tldr: ELF provides fast, configurable strategy games that support end-to-end reinforcement learning and systematic experiments with training choices.

title: ELF: An Extensive, Lightweight and Flexible Research Platform for Real-time Strategy Games

abstract: Regression with group-sparsity penalty plays a central role in high-dimensional prediction problems. Most of existing methods require the group structure to be known a priori. In practice, this may be a too strong assumption, potentially hampering the effectiveness of the regularization method. To circumvent this issue, we present a method to estimate the group structure by means of a continuous bilevel optimization problem where the data is split into training and validation sets. Our approach relies on an approximation scheme where the lower level problem is replaced by a smooth dual forward-backward algorithm with Bregman distances. We provide guarantees regarding the convergence of the approximate procedure to the exact problem and demonstrate the well behaviour of the proposed method on synthetic experiments. Finally, a preliminary application to genes expression data is tackled with the purpose of unveiling functional groups.

paragraphs: Group-sparse regression encourages predictors to be selected or suppressed in groups. Its usefulness therefore depends on how those groups are defined. Most methods assume the grouping is supplied in advance, but that information may be unavailable or unsuitable. This paper treats the group structure as something to estimate from data.

The authors formulate this estimation as a continuous bilevel optimization problem using separate training and validation data. The two levels connect fitting the regression model with learning its grouping structure. To make the nested optimization tractable, they replace the lower-level problem with an approximation based on a smooth dual forward-backward algorithm using Bregman distances.

The paper provides guarantees that relate the approximate procedure to the exact problem as the approximation converges. Synthetic experiments demonstrate favorable behavior, and a preliminary application to gene expression data explores the discovery of functional groups. The contribution is a way to learn the structure controlling regularization, supported by convergence analysis and initial empirical evidence.
summary.tldr: A bilevel optimization method learns the grouping structure used by group-sparse regression instead of requiring it in advance.

title: Bilevel learning of the Group Lasso structure

abstract: We algorithmically construct multi-output Gaussian process priors which satisfy linear differential equations. Our approach attempts to parametrize all solutions of the equations using Gröbner bases. If successful, a push forward Gaussian process along the paramerization is the desired prior. We consider several examples from physics, geomathmatics and control, among them the full inhomogeneous system of Maxwell's equations. By bringing together stochastic learning and computeralgebra in a novel way, we combine noisy observations with precise algebraic computations.

paragraphs: This paper constructs Gaussian process priors for several related outputs whose behavior must satisfy linear differential equations. The goal is to combine uncertain, noisy measurements with mathematical relationships that are specified precisely. Instead of treating those equations as information separate from the probabilistic model, the construction incorporates them into the prior itself.

The method uses Gröbner bases, an algebraic computational tool, to attempt to describe all solutions through a parameterization. If that attempt succeeds, a Gaussian process is passed through the parameterization to obtain the desired constrained prior. The conditional nature of this step matters: the abstract does not claim that the required parameterization can always be found.

The authors consider examples from physics, geomathematics, and control, including the full inhomogeneous Maxwell equations. These examples illustrate the intended connection between symbolic computation and statistical learning. The contribution is an algorithmic route from equations to probabilistic models, allowing exact algebraic structure and noisy observations to participate in the same modeling framework.
summary.tldr: An algebraic construction produces Gaussian process priors satisfying linear differential equations when a suitable solution parameterization can be found.

title: Algorithmic Linearly Constrained Gaussian Processes

abstract: We present foundations for using Model Predictive Control (MPC) as a differentiable policy class for reinforcement learning. This provides one way of leveraging and combining the advantages of model-free and model-based approaches. Specifically, we differentiate through MPC by using the KKT conditions of the convex approximation at a fixed point of the controller. Using this strategy, we are able to learn the cost and dynamics of a controller via end-to-end learning. Our experiments focus on imitation learning in the pendulum and cartpole domains, where we learn the cost and dynamics terms of an MPC policy class. We show that our MPC policies are significantly more data-efficient than a generic neural network and that our method is superior to traditional system identification in a setting where the expert is unrealizable.

Using this strategy, we are able to learn the cost and dynamics of a controller via end-to-end learning. paragraphs: The paper makes Model Predictive Control usable as a differentiable policy class. This allows a structured controller to participate in end-to-end learning, offering a way to combine advantages of model-based and model-free approaches. The quantities learned include both the controller's cost terms and its model of dynamics.

The technical step is to differentiate through the controller using the optimality conditions of a convex approximation at a fixed point. These conditions, known as KKT conditions, provide the connection between controller parameters and the learning objective. Consequently, learning can adjust the components that determine the controller's behavior through the control computation itself.

Experiments focus on imitation learning for pendulum and cartpole tasks. The resulting MPC policies are reported to be significantly more data-efficient than a generic neural network. The method also outperforms traditional system identification in a setting where the expert is unrealizable. These findings support learning controller components directly for the imitation objective in the evaluated domains.
summary.tldr: Differentiating through MPC enables end-to-end learning of controller costs and dynamics, with strong data efficiency in imitation experiments.

title: Differentiable MPC for End-to-end Planning and Control

abstract: In real-world applications of education, an effective teacher adaptively chooses the next example to teach based on the learner’s current state. However, most existing work in algorithmic machine teaching focuses on the batch setting, where adaptivity plays no role. In this paper, we study the case of teaching consistent, version space learners in an interactive setting. At any time step, the teacher provides an example, the learner performs an update, and the teacher observes the learner’s new state. We highlight that adaptivity does not speed up the teaching process when considering existing models of version space learners, such as the “worst-case” model (the learner picks the next hypothesis randomly from the version space) and the “preference-based” model (the learner picks hypothesis according to some global preference). Inspired by human teaching, we propose a new model where the learner picks hypotheses according to some local preference defined by the current hypothesis. We show that our model exhibits several desirable properties, e.g., adaptivity plays a key role, and the learner’s transitions over hypotheses are smooth/interpretable. We develop adaptive teaching algorithms, and demonstrate our results via simulation and user studies.

We highlight that adaptivity does not speed up the teaching process when considering existing models of version space learners, such as the “worst-case” model (the learner picks the next hypothesis randomly from the version space) and the “preference-based” model (the learner picks hypothesis according to some global preference). We develop adaptive teaching algorithms, and demonstrate our results via simulation and user studies.

paragraphs: The paper asks when a teacher benefits from choosing each example after observing a learner's current state. It studies consistent version-space learners, which maintain hypotheses compatible with the examples received. In the interactive setup, teaching proceeds through an example, a learner update, and an observation of the resulting state.

The authors show that adaptivity does not accelerate teaching under the existing learner models they consider. These include a model that chooses randomly from the version space and one governed by a global preference over hypotheses. Thus, allowing a teacher to react to the learner is not sufficient by itself to make teaching faster.

Inspired by human teaching, the authors introduce preferences that depend locally on the learner's current hypothesis. In this model, adaptivity plays a key role and hypothesis transitions are smooth and interpretable. They develop adaptive teaching algorithms and demonstrate their findings through simulations and user studies. The contribution ties the value of interaction to how a learner moves between possible explanations.
summary.tldr: Adaptivity becomes valuable in machine teaching when learners' hypothesis preferences depend on their current state.

title: Understanding the Role of Adaptivity in Machine Teaching: The Case of Version Space Learners

abstract: We address the problem of regret minimization in logistic contextual bandits, where a learner decides among sequential actions or arms given their respective contexts to maximize binary rewards. Using a fast inference procedure with Polya-Gamma distributed augmentation variables, we propose an improved version of Thompson Sampling, a Bayesian formulation of contextual bandits with near-optimal performance. Our approach, Polya-Gamma augmented Thompson Sampling (PG-TS), achieves state-of-the-art performance on simulated and real data. PG-TS explores the action space efficiently and exploits high-reward arms, quickly converging to solutions of low regret. Its explicit estimation of the posterior distribution of the context feature covariance leads to substantial empirical gains over approximate approaches. PG-TS is the first approach to demonstrate the benefits of Polya-Gamma augmentation in bandits and to propose an efficient Gibbs sampler for approximating the analytically unsolvable integral of logistic contextual bandits.

Our approach, Polya-Gamma augmented Thompson Sampling (PG-TS), achieves state-of-the-art performance on simulated and real data. PG-TS explores the action space efficiently and exploits high-reward arms, quickly converging to solutions of low regret. Its explicit estimation of the posterior distribution of the context feature covariance leads to substantial empirical gains over approximate approaches. paragraphs: This paper studies sequential decisions with binary rewards, where each available action has contextual features. The learner must discover which actions work well while also choosing actions likely to pay off. The objective is low regret: limiting the reward lost through imperfect choices while learning from experience.

The proposed method, PG-TS, improves Thompson sampling through fast Bayesian inference using Polya-Gamma augmentation variables. An efficient Gibbs sampler approximates an integral in logistic contextual bandits that cannot be solved analytically. The approach explicitly estimates the posterior distribution of the context-feature covariance, making that uncertainty structure part of the decision process.

On simulated and real data, the authors report state-of-the-art performance, efficient exploration, and rapid convergence toward low-regret solutions. They attribute substantial empirical gains over approximate approaches to explicit covariance-posterior estimation. The contribution is both an inference procedure and evidence that Polya-Gamma augmentation is useful for bandit decisions. Its reported advantage comes from the evaluated settings, where improved uncertainty estimation supports the balance between exploration and reward-seeking.
summary.tldr: PG-TS uses Polya-Gamma Bayesian inference to improve exploration and reduce regret in logistic contextual bandit experiments.

title: PG-TS: Improved Thompson Sampling for Logistic Contextual Bandits

abstract: This paper proposes to learn reliable dense correspondence from videos in a self-supervised manner. Our learning process integrates two highly related tasks: tracking large image regions and establishing fine-grained pixel-level associations between consecutive video frames. We exploit the synergy between both tasks through a shared inter-frame affinity matrix, which simultaneously models transitions between video frames at both the region- and pixel-levels. While region-level localization helps reduce ambiguities in fine-grained matching by narrowing down search regions; fine-grained matching provides bottom-up features to facilitate region-level localization. Our method outperforms the state-of-the-art self-supervised methods on a variety of visual correspondence tasks, including video-object and part-segmentation propagation, keypoint tracking, and object tracking. Our self-supervised method even surpasses the fully-supervised affinity feature representation obtained from a ResNet-18 pre-trained on the ImageNet.

This paper learns these two kinds of correspondence together through self-supervision. Each task therefore supplies information that supports the other.

The broader contribution is evidence that coordinating coarse and fine temporal matching can produce strong correspondence features from self-supervised learning.
summary.tldr: Jointly learning region tracking and pixel matching improves self-supervised video correspondence through a shared cross-frame affinity representation.

title: Joint-task Self-supervised Learning for Temporal Correspondence

abstract: Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods generate samples that are asymptotically distributed from a target distribution of interest as the number of iterations goes to infinity. Various theoretical results provide upper bounds on the distance between the target and marginal distribution after a fixed number of iterations. These upper bounds are on a case by case basis and typically involve intractable quantities, which limits their use for practitioners. We introduce L-lag couplings to generate computable, non-asymptotic upper bound estimates for the total variation or the Wasserstein distance of general Markov chains. We apply L-lag couplings to the tasks of (i) determining MCMC burn-in, (ii) comparing different MCMC algorithms with the same target, and (iii) comparing exact and approximate MCMC. Lastly, we (iv) assess the bias of sequential Monte Carlo and self-normalized importance samplers.

paragraphs: Markov chain Monte Carlo produces samples whose distribution approaches a target as the number of iterations grows. In practice, the relevant question is how far the chain remains from that target after a finite run. Existing theoretical bounds often depend on quantities that are difficult to calculate and require separate analysis for each case.

The paper introduces L-lag couplings to obtain computable estimates of non-asymptotic upper bounds on distributional distance. The approach addresses both total variation and Wasserstein distance, giving ways to quantify discrepancy at a specified stage of a Markov chain. The distinction between an estimated upper bound and an exactly known distance is central to what the method provides.

The authors apply these estimates to choosing burn-in, comparing MCMC algorithms that share a target, and comparing exact with approximate MCMC. They also assess bias in sequential Monte Carlo and self-normalized importance sampling. These applications connect finite-run convergence assessment to concrete choices about sampling methods and the reliability of their output.
summary.tldr: L-lag couplings provide computable estimates of finite-run convergence bounds for assessing and comparing Monte Carlo methods.

title: Estimating Convergence of Markov chains with L-Lag Couplings

abstract: We revisit two algorithms, matrix stochastic gradient (MSG) and $\ell_2$-regularized MSG (RMSG), that are instances of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on a convex relaxation to principal component analysis (PCA). These algorithms have been shown to outperform Oja’s algorithm, empirically, in terms of the iteration complexity, and to have runtime comparable with Oja’s. However, these findings are not supported by existing theoretical results. While the iteration complexity bound for $\ell_2$-RMSG was recently shown to match that of Oja’s algorithm, its theoretical efficiency was left as an open problem. In this work, we give improved bounds on per iteration cost of mini-batched variants of both MSG and $\ell_2$-RMSG and arrive at an algorithm with total computational complexity matching that of Oja's algorithm.

paragraphs: This paper revisits streaming principal component analysis through two methods: matrix stochastic gradient and its squared-norm-regularized variant. Both apply stochastic gradient descent to a convex relaxation of PCA. Earlier empirical work suggested that these methods could need fewer iterations than Oja's algorithm while having comparable runtime, but theory had not fully accounted for that efficiency.

The distinction between iteration count and total computation is central. An algorithm can make good progress per iteration yet remain expensive if each update costs too much. Although a previous iteration bound for the regularized method already matched Oja's, a corresponding theoretical account of computational efficiency was still missing.

The authors improve bounds on the cost of each iteration for mini-batched versions of both methods. Combining this analysis with iteration requirements yields an algorithm whose total computational complexity matches Oja's algorithm. The contribution closes an important theoretical gap around convex approaches to streaming PCA. It establishes comparable overall complexity, rather than proving that the earlier empirical advantage in iteration count must occur on every problem.
summary.tldr: Sharper per-iteration bounds give a convex-relaxation approach to streaming PCA total computational complexity matching Oja's algorithm.

title: Efficient Convex Relaxations for Streaming PCA

abstract: Learning from different data types is a long-standing goal in machine learning research, as multiple information sources co-occur when describing natural phenomena. However, existing generative models that approximate a multimodal ELBO rely on difficult or inefficient training schemes to learn a joint distribution and the dependencies between modalities. In this work, we propose a novel, efficient objective function that utilizes the Jensen-Shannon divergence for multiple distributions. It simultaneously approximates the unimodal and joint multimodal posteriors directly via a dynamic prior. In addition, we theoretically prove that the new multimodal JS-divergence (mmJSD) objective optimizes an ELBO. In extensive experiments, we demonstrate the advantage of the proposed mmJSD model compared to previous work in unsupervised, generative learning tasks.

This paper targets the difficulty and inefficiency of training existing models that use a multimodal evidence lower bound, or ELBO, as their learning objective.

The authors propose a new objective based on Jensen-Shannon divergence for multiple distributions. It uses a dynamic prior to approximate both unimodal posteriors, based on individual modalities, and a joint posterior, based on modalities together. Handling these approximations simultaneously gives the training objective a direct role in connecting separate information sources with their combined representation.

The paper proves that the resulting multimodal Jensen-Shannon divergence objective, called mmJSD, optimizes an ELBO. This supplies a theoretical foundation alongside the proposed efficiency benefit. Extensive experiments report advantages over previous work on unsupervised generative learning tasks. The findings support the objective as a useful way to train multimodal models while retaining an established lower-bound formulation.
summary.tldr: mmJSD uses a dynamic prior and multimodal Jensen-Shannon divergence to train generative models with a proven ELBO objective.

title: Multimodal Generative Learning Utilizing Jensen-Shannon-Divergence

abstract: We present a novel texture synthesis framework, enabling the generation of infinite, high-quality 3D textures given a 2D exemplar image. Inspired by recent advances in natural texture synthesis, we train deep neural models to generate textures by non-linearly combining learned noise frequencies. To achieve a highly realistic output conditioned on an exemplar patch, we propose a novel loss function that combines ideas from both style transfer and generative adversarial networks. In particular, we train the synthesis network to match the Gram matrices of deep features from a discriminator network. In addition, we propose two architectural concepts and an extrapolation strategy that significantly improve generalization performance. In particular, we inject both model input and condition into hidden network layers by learning to scale and bias hidden activations. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations on a diverse set of exemplars motivate our design decisions and show that our system performs superior to previous state of the art. Finally, we conduct a user study that confirms the benefits of our framework.

paragraphs: GramGAN generates three-dimensional textures from a two-dimensional example image. Its goal is to produce high-quality texture that can extend indefinitely while remaining conditioned on the example patch. The synthesis network builds texture by combining learned noise frequencies through nonlinear transformations, giving it a learned mechanism for producing spatial variation.

Its training objective combines ideas from style transfer and generative adversarial networks. The synthesis network matches Gram matrices computed from a discriminator's deep features. These matrices summarize relationships among features, so the objective gives the generator a statistical target for matching the exemplar's appearance through a learned feature representation.

The paper also introduces architectural changes and an extrapolation strategy to improve generalization. In particular, both input and conditioning information influence hidden layers through learned scaling and shifting of activations. Quantitative and visual evaluations across diverse exemplars support the design choices and report better results than previous leading methods. A user study also supports the framework's benefits, adding perceptual evidence to the reported evaluations.
summary.tldr: GramGAN learns indefinitely extendable 3D textures from 2D examples by matching discriminator feature statistics and conditioning hidden activations.

title: GramGAN: Deep 3D Texture Synthesis From 2D Exemplars

abstract: Solving optimization problem is the key to decision making in many real-life analytics applications. However, the coefficients of the optimization problems are often uncertain and dependent on external factors, such as future demand or energy- or stock prices. Machine learning (ML) models, especially neural networks, are increasingly being used to estimate these coefficients in a data-driven way. Hence, end-to-end predict-and-optimize approaches, which consider how effective the predicted values are to solve the optimization problem, have received increasing attention. In case of integer linear programming problems, a popular approach to overcome their non-differentiabilty is to add a quadratic penalty term to the continuous relaxation, such that results from differentiating over quadratic programs can be used. Instead we investigate the use of the more principled logarithmic barrier term, as widely used in interior point solvers for linear programming. Instead of differentiating the KKT conditions, we consider the homogeneous self-dual formulation of the LP and we show the relation between the interior point step direction and corresponding gradients needed for learning. Finally, our empirical experiments demonstrate our approach performs as good as if not better than the state-of-the-art QPTL (Quadratic Programming task loss) formulation of Wilder et al. and SPO approach of Elmachtoub and Grigas.

paragraphs: Many decision systems first predict uncertain quantities and then use them as coefficients in an optimization problem. End-to-end prediction and optimization trains those predictions according to the decisions they produce. This paper investigates how to obtain the learning gradients needed when the decision stage involves linear programming.

A popular treatment of integer linear programs adds a quadratic penalty to their continuous relaxation so that differentiation methods for quadratic programs apply. The authors instead investigate a logarithmic barrier, a component used in interior-point methods for linear programming. They work with the homogeneous self-dual formulation of the linear program and relate the solver's interior-point step direction to the gradients required for learning.

The approach makes the connection between optimization steps and predictive training explicit through this formulation. In empirical experiments, the authors report performance as good as, or better than, the QPTL and SPO approaches. The stated evidence supports an alternative route to training predictions for downstream optimization, with competitive results obtained from the machinery of interior-point solving.
summary.tldr: An interior-point formulation supplies gradients for training predictions through linear optimization and achieves competitive empirical decision performance.

title: Interior Point Solving for LP-based prediction+optimisation

abstract: One of the primary goals of systems neuroscience is to relate the structure of neural circuits to their function, yet patterns of connectivity are difficult to establish when recording from large populations in behaving organisms. Many previous approaches have attempted to estimate functional connectivity between neurons using statistical modeling of observational data, but these approaches rely heavily on parametric assumptions and are purely correlational. Recently, however, holographic photostimulation techniques have made it possible to precisely target selected ensembles of neurons, offering the possibility of establishing direct causal links. A naive method for inferring functional connections is to stimulate each individual neuron multiple times and observe the responses of cells in the local network, but this approach scales poorly with the number of neurons. Here, we propose a method based on noisy group testing that drastically increases the efficiency of this process in sparse networks. By stimulating small ensembles of neurons, we show that it is possible to recover binarized network connectivity with a number of tests that grows only logarithmically with population size under minimal statistical assumptions. Moreover, we prove that our approach, which reduces to an efficiently solvable convex optimization problem, can be related to Variational Bayesian inference on the binary connection weights, and we derive rigorous bounds on the posterior marginals. This allows us to extend our method to the streaming setting, where continuously updated posteriors allow for optional stopping, and we demonstrate the feasibility of inferring connectivity for networks of up to tens of thousands of neurons online.

This paper proposes stimulating small groups and interpreting their responses through noisy group testing.

summary.tldr: Noisy group testing uses small-group stimulation to efficiently infer sparse binary neural connectivity and update connection probabilities online.

title: Online Neural Connectivity Estimation with Noisy Group Testing

abstract: The challenge of generalizing causal knowledge across different environments is pervasive in scientific explorations, including in AI, ML, and Data Science. Experiments are usually performed in one environment (e.g., in a lab, on Earth) with the intent, almost invariably, of being used elsewhere (e.g., outside the lab, on Mars), where the conditions are likely to be different. In the causal inference literature, this generalization task has been formalized under the rubric of transportability (Pearl and Bareinboim, 2011), where a number of criteria and algorithms have been developed for various settings. Despite the generality of such results, transportability theory has been confined to atomic, do()-interventions. In practice, many real-world applications require more complex, stochastic interventions; for instance, in reinforcement learning, agents need to continuously adapt to the changing conditions of an uncertain and unknown environment. In this paper, we extend transportability theory to encompass these more complex types of interventions, which are known as "soft," both relative to the input as well as the target distribution of the analysis. Specifically, we develop a graphical condition that is both necessary and sufficient for deciding soft-transportability. Second, we develop an algorithm to determine whether a non-atomic intervention is computable from a combination of the distributions available across domains. As a corollary, we show that the $\sigma$-calculus is complete for the task of soft-transportability.

paragraphs: Causal experiments are often conducted in one environment with the aim of informing decisions elsewhere. Transportability asks when knowledge can be transferred despite differences between environments. This paper extends that question beyond atomic interventions to more complex, potentially stochastic interventions, referred to as soft interventions.

The extension applies both to the interventions represented in the available information and to the target distribution being analyzed. The contribution provides a formal basis for combining causal information across environments when interventions are more flexible than setting a variable to a fixed value.
summary.tldr: The paper gives a necessary-and-sufficient graphical criterion and a complete algorithmic framework for transporting soft-intervention effects across environments.

title: General Transportability of Soft Interventions: Completeness Results

abstract: We consider the problem of wisely using a limited budget to label a small subset of a large unlabeled dataset. For example, consider the NLP problem of word sense disambiguation. For any word, we have a set of candidate labels from a knowledge base, but the label set is not necessarily representative of what occurs in the data: there may exist labels in the knowledge base that very rarely occur in the corpus because the sense is rare in modern English; and conversely there may exist true labels that do not exist in our knowledge base. Our aim is to obtain a classifier that performs as well as possible on examples of each “common class” that occurs with frequency above a given threshold in the unlabeled set while annotating as few examples as possible from “rare classes” whose labels occur with less than this frequency. The challenge is that we are not informed which labels are common and which are rare, and the true label distribution may exhibit extreme skew. We describe an active learning approach that (1) explicitly searches for rare classes by leveraging the contextual embedding spaces provided by modern language models, and (2) incorporates a stopping rule that ignores classes once we prove that they occur below our target threshold with high probability. We prove that our algorithm only costs logarithmically more than a hypothetical approach that knows all true label frequencies and show experimentally that incorporating automated search can significantly reduce the number of samples needed to reach target accuracy levels.
