paragraphs: With a limited labeling budget, a learner needs to discover which classes deserve attention. A knowledge base may list classes that barely occur in the data and omit classes that actually appear. The paper targets accurate classification of classes above a chosen frequency threshold while spending few annotations on classes below it.

The difficulty is that those frequencies are initially unknown and may be extremely uneven. The proposed active learning method uses contextual representations from language models to search explicitly for rare classes. It pairs that search with a statistical stopping rule: once a class is shown with high probability to fall below the target frequency, the algorithm stops devoting attention to it.

Searching for rare classes therefore helps determine when further annotation is unnecessary. The authors prove that their algorithm's cost is only a logarithmic factor above a hypothetical method given the true label frequencies. Experiments also show that automated search can substantially reduce the samples needed to reach target accuracy, supporting the value of combining targeted discovery with principled stopping.
summary.tldr: Targeted class search and a statistical stopping rule help spend labeling budgets on sufficiently common classes.

title: Exemplar Guided Active Learning

abstract: While semi-supervised learning (SSL) has proven to be a promising way for leveraging unlabeled data when labeled data is scarce, the existing SSL algorithms typically assume that training class distributions are balanced. However, these SSL algorithms trained under imbalanced class distributions can severely suffer when generalizing to a balanced testing criterion, since they utilize biased pseudo-labels of unlabeled data toward majority classes. To alleviate this issue, we formulate a convex optimization problem to softly refine the pseudo-labels generated from the biased model, and develop a simple algorithm, named Distribution Aligning Refinery of Pseudo-label (DARP) that solves it provably and efficiently. Under various class imbalanced semi-supervised scenarios, we demonstrate the effectiveness of DARP and its compatibility with state-of-the-art SSL schemes.

However, these SSL algorithms trained under imbalanced class distributions can severely suffer when generalizing to a balanced testing criterion, since they utilize biased pseudo-labels of unlabeled data toward majority classes. To alleviate this issue, we formulate a convex optimization problem to softly refine the pseudo-labels generated from the biased model, and develop a simple algorithm, named Distribution Aligning Refinery of Pseudo-label (DARP) that solves it provably and efficiently. Under various class imbalanced semi-supervised scenarios, we demonstrate the effectiveness of DARP and its compatibility with state-of-the-art SSL schemes.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning uses unlabeled examples to supplement a limited labeled dataset. A common mechanism assigns model-generated labels, or pseudo-labels, to unlabeled data. When training classes are imbalanced, these predictions can favor majority classes, creating problems when evaluation gives balanced importance to the classes rather than following the training imbalance.

DARP addresses this problem by refining the pseudo-labels produced by the biased model. The authors express the refinement as a convex optimization problem and develop an algorithm that solves it provably and efficiently. The adjustment is soft, allowing the label information to be refined rather than treating every original prediction as an unquestionable class assignment.

Experiments across several imbalanced semi-supervised scenarios demonstrate the method's effectiveness and compatibility with leading semi-supervised learning schemes. The contribution targets a specific source of error: the class bias carried into training through pseudo-labels. Its compatibility matters because pseudo-label refinement can improve how existing schemes use unlabeled data without requiring a wholly separate approach to semi-supervised learning.
summary.tldr: DARP efficiently refines biased pseudo-labels to improve semi-supervised learning with imbalanced classes.

title: Distribution Aligning Refinery of Pseudo-label for Imbalanced Semi-supervised Learning

abstract: A key tool for building differentially private systems is adding Gaussian noise to the output of a function evaluated on a sensitive dataset. Unfortunately, using a continuous distribution presents several practical challenges. First and foremost, finite computers cannot exactly represent samples from continuous distributions, and previous work has demonstrated that seemingly innocuous numerical errors can entirely destroy privacy. Moreover, when the underlying data is itself discrete (e.g., population counts), adding continuous noise makes the result less interpretable. With these shortcomings in mind, we introduce and analyze the discrete Gaussian in the context of differential privacy. Specifically, we theoretically and experimentally show that adding discrete Gaussian noise provides essentially the same privacy and accuracy guarantees as the addition of continuous Gaussian noise. We also present an simple and efficient algorithm for exact sampling from this distribution. This demonstrates its applicability for privately answering counting queries, or more generally, low-sensitivity integer-valued queries.

paragraphs: Adding Gaussian noise is a common way to protect sensitive data through differential privacy. Continuous noise creates an implementation challenge because finite computers cannot represent continuous samples exactly. The abstract notes that numerical errors can destroy privacy guarantees. Continuous outputs can also be awkward to interpret when the original query produces an integer count.

The authors show theoretically and experimentally that it provides essentially the same privacy and accuracy guarantees as continuous Gaussian noise. This preserves the main benefits of the Gaussian mechanism while working with a distribution suited to discrete outputs.

The results establish applicability to private counting queries and, more generally, integer-valued queries with low sensitivity, connecting mathematical privacy analysis to a concrete mechanism that finite computers can implement.
summary.tldr: Discrete Gaussian noise offers essentially continuous-Gaussian privacy and accuracy guarantees with efficient exact sampling for integer-valued queries.

title: The Discrete Gaussian for Differential Privacy

abstract: A recent Graph Neural Network (GNN) approach for learning to branch has been shown to successfully reduce the running time of branch-and-bound algorithms for Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP). While the GNN relies on a GPU for inference, MILP solvers are purely CPU-based. This severely limits its application as many practitioners may not have access to high-end GPUs. In this work, we ask two key questions. First, in a more realistic setting where only a CPU is available, is the GNN model still competitive? Second, can we devise an alternate computationally inexpensive model that retains the predictive power of the GNN architecture? We answer the first question in the negative, and address the second question by proposing a new hybrid architecture for efficient branching on CPU machines. The proposed architecture combines the expressive power of GNNs with computationally inexpensive multi-layer perceptrons (MLP) for branching. We evaluate our methods on four classes of MILP problems, and show that they lead to up to 26% reduction in solver running time compared to state-of-the-art methods without a GPU, while extrapolating to harder problems than it was trained on. The code for this project is publicly available at https://github.com/pg2455/Hybrid-learn2branch.

paragraphs: Branch-and-bound solvers for mixed integer linear programming must repeatedly choose how to branch during search. A graph neural network approach had reduced solver running time, but relied on GPU inference even though the solvers themselves run on CPUs. This paper asks whether that approach remains competitive when practitioners have only a CPU available.

The authors find that the existing GNN approach is not competitive in the CPU-only setting they examine. They propose a hybrid architecture that combines the expressive capabilities of a GNN with computationally inexpensive multilayer perceptrons for branching. The aim is to retain useful predictive power while making the cost of choosing branches suitable for CPU-based solving.

Evaluation covers four classes of mixed integer linear programming problems. The hybrid methods reduce solver running time by up to 26% compared with state-of-the-art methods without a GPU and extrapolate to harder problems than those used for training. The result illustrates why the computational cost of a learned decision rule matters alongside its predictions when it operates inside an optimization solver.
summary.tldr: A hybrid GNN–MLP branching model cuts CPU-only solver time by up to 26% in the reported evaluations and generalizes to harder problems.

title: Hybrid Models for Learning to Branch

abstract: Various Neural Networks employ time-consuming matrix operations like matrix inversion. Many such matrix operations are faster to compute given the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD). Techniques from (Zhang et al., 2018; Mhammedi et al., 2017) allow using the SVD in Neural Networks without computing it. In theory, the techniques can speed up matrix operations, however, in practice, they are not fast enough. We present an algorithm that is fast enough to speed up several matrix operations. The algorithm increases the degree of parallelism of an underlying matrix multiplication H*X where H is an orthogonal matrix represented by a product of Householder matrices.

paragraphs: Some neural networks require expensive matrix operations, including matrix inversion. Having a matrix’s singular value decomposition can make several such operations faster. Earlier techniques allowed neural networks to use an SVD without computing the decomposition directly, but their practical execution was too slow to deliver the anticipated speed benefits.

This paper targets the computation underlying those techniques. The relevant operation multiplies an input matrix X by an orthogonal matrix H represented as a product of Householder matrices. The authors introduce an algorithm that increases the parallelism of this multiplication, addressing the execution bottleneck in the representation.

The reported result is an algorithm fast enough to accelerate several matrix operations in practice. Its significance lies in making an existing theoretical opportunity computationally useful: avoiding explicit SVD computation helps only if the associated operations can also run efficiently. The contribution concerns the speed of those matrix computations, with increased parallelism providing the route from an appealing representation to practical acceleration.
summary.tldr: More parallel multiplication of Householder-represented orthogonal matrices makes SVD-based acceleration practical for several neural-network matrix operations.

title: What if Neural Networks had SVDs?

abstract: We improve the effectiveness of propagation- and linear-optimization-based neural network verification algorithms with a new tightened convex relaxation for ReLU neurons. Unlike previous single-neuron relaxations which focus only on the univariate input space of the ReLU, our method considers the multivariate input space of the affine pre-activation function preceding the ReLU. Using results from submodularity and convex geometry, we derive an explicit description of the tightest possible convex relaxation when this multivariate input is over a box domain. We show that our convex relaxation is significantly stronger than the commonly used univariate-input relaxation which has been proposed as a natural convex relaxation barrier for verification. While our description of the relaxation may require an exponential number of inequalities, we show that they can be separated in linear time and hence can be efficiently incorporated into optimization algorithms on an as-needed basis. Based on this novel relaxation, we design two polynomial-time algorithms for neural network verification: a linear-programming-based algorithm that leverages the full power of our relaxation, and a fast propagation algorithm that generalizes existing approaches. In both cases, we show that for a modest increase in computational effort, our strengthened relaxation enables us to verify a significantly larger number of instances compared to similar algorithms.

paragraphs: Neural-network verification often replaces difficult neuron behavior with convex approximations that are easier to analyze. This paper strengthens those approximations for ReLU neurons. Its key move is to retain the multiple inputs to the affine computation preceding a ReLU, rather than considering only the resulting single scalar input.

Using submodularity and convex geometry, the authors characterize the tightest convex relaxation when those multivariate inputs lie in a box domain. This relaxation is substantially stronger than the usual scalar-input version. Although its description can contain exponentially many inequalities, a linear-time separation procedure identifies needed constraints, allowing optimization algorithms to incorporate them as required.

The paper builds two polynomial-time verification algorithms from this result. One uses linear programming to exploit the complete relaxation; the other provides a fast propagation approach that generalizes existing methods. Both verify substantially more instances than comparable algorithms for a modest increase in computational effort. The findings show that a purported barrier for single-neuron relaxations can be improved by retaining richer information about each neuron’s inputs.
summary.tldr: Stronger multivariate ReLU relaxations let verification algorithms certify more instances with only a modest increase in computation.

title: The Convex Relaxation Barrier, Revisited: Tightened Single-Neuron Relaxations for Neural Network Verification

abstract: In this work, we propose a unified framework, called Visual Reasoning with Differ-entiable Physics (VRDP), that can jointly learn visual concepts and infer physics models of objects and their interactions from videos and language. This is achieved by seamlessly integrating three components: a visual perception module, a concept learner, and a differentiable physics engine. The visual perception module parses each video frame into object-centric trajectories and represents them as latent scene representations. The concept learner grounds visual concepts (e.g., color, shape, and material) from these object-centric representations based on the language, thus providing prior knowledge for the physics engine. The differentiable physics model, implemented as an impulse-based differentiable rigid-body simulator, performs differentiable physical simulation based on the grounded concepts to infer physical properties, such as mass, restitution, and velocity, by fitting the simulated trajectories into the video observations. Consequently, these learned concepts and physical models can explain what we have seen and imagine what is about to happen in future and counterfactual scenarios. Integrating differentiable physics into the dynamic reasoning framework offers several appealing benefits. More accurate dynamics prediction in learned physics models enables state-of-the-art performance on both synthetic and real-world benchmarks while still maintaining high transparency and interpretability; most notably, VRDP improves the accuracy of predictive and counterfactual questions by 4.5% and 11.5% compared to its best counterpart. VRDP is also highly data-efficient: physical parameters can be optimized from very few videos, and even a single video can be sufficient. Finally, with all physical parameters inferred, VRDP can quickly learn new concepts from a few examples.

paragraphs: Understanding a moving scene involves recognizing objects and reasoning about how their interactions unfold. VRDP combines visual perception, language-grounded concept learning, and differentiable physics to learn both kinds of information. Its perception component extracts object trajectories from video, while its concept learner associates object representations with concepts such as color, shape, and material.

An impulse-based rigid-body simulator then fits simulated motion to the observed trajectories. Because the simulator is differentiable, the system can optimize physical properties such as mass, restitution, and velocity using that fit. The learned concepts provide prior information for this process. Together, the concepts and physical model support explanations of observed events, predictions, and counterfactual reasoning.

They also find that physical parameters can be learned from very few videos, with one video sometimes sufficient. Once those parameters are inferred, the system can acquire new concepts from a few examples.
summary.tldr: VRDP combines language-grounded visual concepts with differentiable physics to improve predictions and counterfactual reasoning about moving objects.

title: Dynamic Visual Reasoning by Learning Differentiable Physics Models from Video and Language

abstract: This paper underlines an elegant property of batch-normalization (BN): Successive batch normalizations with random linear updates make samples increasingly orthogonal. We establish a non-asymptotic characterization of the interplay between depth, width, and the orthogonality of deep representations. More precisely, we prove, under a mild assumption, the deviation of the representations from orthogonality rapidly decays with depth up to a term inversely proportional to the network width. This result has two main theoretical and practical implications: 1) Theoretically, as the depth grows, the distribution of the outputs contracts to a Wasserstein-2 ball around an isotropic normal distribution. Furthermore, the radius of this Wasserstein ball shrinks with the width of the network. 2) Practically, the orthogonality of the representations directly influences the performance of stochastic gradient descent (SGD). When representations are initially aligned, we observe SGD wastes many iterations to disentangle representations before the classification. Nevertheless, we experimentally show that starting optimization from orthogonal representations is sufficient to accelerate SGD, with no need for BN.

paragraphs: This paper studies how batch normalization changes the geometry of representations in deep random networks. Its central observation is that repeatedly combining random linear transformations with batch normalization makes the representations of different samples increasingly orthogonal. In geometric terms, the samples become less aligned with one another as they pass through successive layers.

Under a mild assumption, the authors prove that deviation from orthogonality decreases rapidly with depth, down to a remaining term inversely proportional to network width. They also connect this behavior to the distribution of network outputs: increasing depth brings that distribution into a Wasserstein-2 neighborhood of an isotropic normal distribution, and increasing width shrinks the neighborhood.

The experiments connect this geometry to optimization. When representations initially align, stochastic gradient descent spends many iterations separating them before classification. Starting with orthogonal representations is experimentally sufficient to accelerate training even without batch normalization. This identifies one useful effect of normalization while keeping the theoretical claim tied to the random-network setting.
summary.tldr: In deep random networks, batch normalization progressively orthogonalizes sample representations, a geometry that experiments link to faster training.

title: Batch Normalization Orthogonalizes Representations in Deep Random Networks

abstract: Visual search is a ubiquitous and often challenging daily task, exemplified by looking for the car keys at home or a friend in a crowd. An intriguing property of some classical search tasks is an asymmetry such that finding a target A among distractors B can be easier than finding B among A. To elucidate the mechanisms responsible for asymmetry in visual search, we propose a computational model that takes a target and a search image as inputs and produces a sequence of eye movements until the target is found. The model integrates eccentricity-dependent visual recognition with target-dependent top-down cues. We compared the model against human behavior in six paradigmatic search tasks that show asymmetry in humans. Without prior exposure to the stimuli or task-specific training, the model provides a plausible mechanism for search asymmetry. We hypothesized that the polarity of search asymmetry arises from experience with the natural environment. We tested this hypothesis by training the model on augmented versions of ImageNet where the biases of natural images were either removed or reversed. The polarity of search asymmetry disappeared or was altered depending on the training protocol. This study highlights how classical perceptual properties can emerge in neural network models, without the need for task-specific training, but rather as a consequence of the statistical properties of the developmental diet fed to the model. All source code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/kreimanlab/VisualSearchAsymmetry.

paragraphs: Finding one kind of target among distractors can be easier than reversing their roles. This paper investigates that visual-search asymmetry with a model that receives a target and a search image, then generates eye movements until it finds the target. The model combines recognition that varies with viewing eccentricity and target-dependent guidance.

Across six classical search tasks showing human asymmetry, the model offers a plausible mechanism without prior exposure to the task stimuli or task-specific training. The authors then test whether the direction of asymmetry could arise from experience with natural images. They train the model on modified ImageNet data whose natural-image biases are removed or reversed.

Depending on the training protocol, the direction of search asymmetry disappears or changes. This supports the hypothesis that visual experience can shape the asymmetries exhibited by the model. The result shows how a classical perceptual property can emerge from the statistics of training data without dedicated search-task training. It provides a computational explanation consistent with human behavior, rather than establishing that humans necessarily acquire the bias through exactly the same mechanism.
summary.tldr: A visual-search model exhibits human-like asymmetries whose direction changes when biases in its visual training experience are removed or reversed.

title: Visual Search Asymmetry: Deep Nets and Humans Share Similar Inherent Biases

abstract: Agents trained by reinforcement learning (RL) often fail to generalize beyond the environment they were trained in, even when presented with new scenarios that seem similar to the training environment. We study the query complexity required to train RL agents that generalize to multiple environments. Intuitively, tractable generalization is only possible when the environments are similar or close in some sense. To capture this, we introduce Weak Proximity, a natural structural condition that requires the environments to have highly similar transition and reward functions and share a policy providing optimal value. Despite such shared structure, we prove that tractable generalization is impossible in the worst case. This holds even when each individual environment can be efficiently solved to obtain an optimal linear policy, and when the agent possesses a generative model. Our lower bound applies to the more complex task of representation learning for efficient generalization to multiple environments. On the positive side, we introduce Strong Proximity, a strengthened condition which we prove is sufficient for efficient generalization.
originalAbstract: Agents trained by reinforcement learning (RL) often fail to generalize beyond the environment they were trained in, even when presented with new scenarios that seem similar to the training environment. We study the query complexity required to train RL agents that generalize to multiple environments. Intuitively, tractable generalization is only possible when the environments are similar or close in some sense. To capture this, we introduce Weak Proximity, a natural structural condition that requires the environments to have highly similar transition and reward functions and share a policy providing optimal value. Despite such shared structure, we prove that tractable generalization is impossible in the worst case. This holds even when each individual environment can be efficiently solved to obtain an optimal linear policy, and when the agent possesses a generative model. Our lower bound applies to the more complex task of representation learning for efficient generalization to multiple environments. On the positive side, we introduce Strong Proximity, a strengthened condition which we prove is sufficient for efficient generalization.

paragraphs: A reinforcement-learning agent may solve its training environment yet fail in other environments that appear similar. This paper studies how many queries are required to learn agents that generalize across environments. It asks whether shared structure is enough to make that learning problem computationally manageable in terms of query complexity.

The authors define Weak Proximity: environments have highly similar transition and reward functions and share a policy attaining optimal value. They prove that even this structure does not ensure efficient generalization in the worst case. The difficulty remains when each environment individually admits efficient recovery of an optimal linear policy and the learner has access to a generative model.

The lower bound also applies to learning representations for efficient generalization across environments. On the positive side, the paper introduces Strong Proximity and proves that it is sufficient for efficient generalization. The contrast identifies a gap between intuitive similarity and a stronger condition that supports a tractability guarantee. Strong Proximity is established as sufficient, without the abstract claiming that it is necessary.
summary.tldr: Similar environments sharing an optimal policy can still make generalization intractable, while a stronger proximity condition suffices for efficiency.

title: When Is Generalizable Reinforcement Learning Tractable?

abstract: We consider the problem of generating rankings that are fair towards both users and item producers in recommender systems. We address both usual recommendation (e.g., of music or movies) and reciprocal recommendation (e.g., dating). Following concepts of distributive justice in welfare economics, our notion of fairness aims at increasing the utility of the worse-off individuals, which we formalize using the criterion of Lorenz efficiency. It guarantees that rankings are Pareto efficient, and that they maximally redistribute utility from better-off to worse-off, at a given level of overall utility. We propose to generate rankings by maximizing concave welfare functions, and develop an efficient inference procedure based on the Frank-Wolfe algorithm. We prove that unlike existing approaches based on fairness constraints, our approach always produces fair rankings. Our experiments also show that it increases the utility of the worse-off at lower costs in terms of overall utility.

paragraphs: Recommendation rankings affect both the people receiving recommendations and the people producing or being represented by the recommended items. This paper studies fairness across both sides, including ordinary recommendations such as music and reciprocal recommendations such as dating. Its objective emphasizes improving utility for individuals who are worse off.

The authors formalize fairness through Lorenz efficiency, drawing on distributive justice in welfare economics. Their criterion combines Pareto efficiency with maximal redistribution toward worse-off individuals at a given total utility. They generate rankings by maximizing concave welfare functions and develop an efficient inference procedure using the Frank–Wolfe algorithm.

The paper proves that the approach always produces fair rankings under its specified fairness notion, unlike the fairness-constraint approaches considered. Experiments also show improvements for worse-off individuals at a lower cost to overall utility. The result connects a formal distributional criterion to a computational ranking procedure, making the balance between aggregate benefit and the distribution of benefit explicit.
summary.tldr: Concave welfare optimization produces Lorenz-efficient rankings that address fairness for both users and producers while improving outcomes for worse-off individuals.

title: Two-sided fairness in rankings via Lorenz dominance

abstract: Compressive phase retrieval is a popular variant of the standard compressive sensing problem in which the measurements only contain magnitude information. In this paper, motivated by recent advances in deep generative models, we provide recovery guarantees with near-optimal sample complexity for phase retrieval with generative priors. We first show that when using i.i.d. Gaussian measurements and an $L$-Lipschitz continuous generative model with bounded $k$-dimensional inputs, roughly $O(k \log L)$ samples suffice to guarantee that any signal minimizing an amplitude-based empirical loss function is close to the true signal. Attaining this sample complexity with a practical algorithm remains a difficult challenge, and finding a good initialization for gradient-based methods has been observed to pose a major bottleneck. To partially address this, we further show that roughly $O(k \log L)$ samples ensure sufficient closeness between the underlying signal and any {\em globally optimal} solution to an optimization problem designed for spectral initialization (though finding such a solution may still be challenging). We also adapt this result to sparse phase retrieval, and show that $O(s \log n)$ samples are sufficient for a similar guarantee when the underlying signal is $s$-sparse and $n$-dimensional, matching an information-theoretic lower bound. While these guarantees do not directly correspond to a practical algorithm, we propose a practical spectral initialization method motivated by our findings, and experimentally observe performance gains over various existing spectral initialization methods for sparse phase retrieval.

paragraphs: Phase retrieval reconstructs a signal from measurements containing magnitude information alone. This paper studies how structural knowledge about the signal can reduce the required measurements. With independent Gaussian measurements and an L-Lipschitz generative model having bounded k-dimensional inputs, it shows that roughly O(k log L) samples suffice for an amplitude-loss minimizer to be close to the true signal.

Turning this sample guarantee into a practical method is difficult, particularly because gradient-based methods need a good initialization. The authors establish a related guarantee for globally optimal solutions of an optimization problem designed for spectral initialization. These results do not directly provide a practical algorithm with those guarantees. The authors nevertheless derive a practical spectral initializer inspired by the theory and observe gains over existing sparse phase-retrieval initialization methods.
summary.tldr: Near-optimal measurement guarantees for phase retrieval motivate a practical initializer, while computing the globally optimal solutions covered by the theory remains challenging.

title: Towards Sample-Optimal Compressive Phase Retrieval with Sparse and Generative Priors

abstract: As machine learning models are increasingly deployed in high-stakes domains such as legal and financial decision-making, there has been growing interest in post-hoc methods for generating counterfactual explanations. Such explanations provide individuals adversely impacted by predicted outcomes (e.g., an applicant denied a loan) with recourse---i.e., a description of how they can change their features to obtain a positive outcome. We propose a novel algorithm that leverages adversarial training and PAC confidence sets to learn models that theoretically guarantee recourse to affected individuals with high probability without sacrificing accuracy. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach via extensive experiments on real data.

Such explanations provide individuals adversely impacted by predicted outcomes (e.g., an applicant denied a loan) with recourse---i.e., a description of how they can change their features to obtain a positive outcome. We propose a novel algorithm that leverages adversarial training and PAC confidence sets to learn models that theoretically guarantee recourse to affected individuals with high probability without sacrificing accuracy. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach via extensive experiments on real data.

paragraphs: When a model gives someone an unfavorable decision, an explanation may describe changes to their features that would produce a favorable outcome. This is actionable recourse. The paper considers this need in high-stakes settings such as financial and legal decision-making, using a denied loan application as an example of the problem.

The authors address recourse during model learning. Their algorithm combines adversarial training with PAC confidence sets to learn models with a theoretical, high-probability recourse guarantee for affected individuals. This places the availability of a route to a positive prediction within the training objective, extending the usual focus on predictive accuracy.

The abstract states that the guarantee is achieved without sacrificing accuracy and reports extensive experiments on real data demonstrating the approach's efficacy. The probability qualification matters: the claim is a high-probability guarantee rather than an unconditional promise for every decision. The resulting contribution connects model construction with the ability to provide people a description of changes that would alter an unfavorable prediction.
summary.tldr: The paper trains models with high-probability recourse guarantees using adversarial training and PAC confidence sets, without sacrificing accuracy.

title: Learning Models for Actionable Recourse

abstract: When engineers train deep learning models, they are very much "flying blind". Commonly used methods for real-time training diagnostics, such as monitoring the train/test loss, are limited. Assessing a network's training process solely through these performance indicators is akin to debugging software without access to internal states through a debugger. To address this, we present Cockpit, a collection of instruments that enable a closer look into the inner workings of a learning machine, and a more informative and meaningful status report for practitioners. It facilitates the identification of learning phases and failure modes, like ill-chosen hyperparameters. These instruments leverage novel higher-order information about the gradient distribution and curvature, which has only recently become efficiently accessible. We believe that such a debugging tool, which we open-source for PyTorch, is a valuable help in troubleshooting the training process. By revealing new insights, it also more generally contributes to explainability and interpretability of deep nets.

paragraphs: Training and test losses summarize how a neural network is performing, but they reveal only part of what is happening during optimization. A disappointing curve may signal trouble without making its cause clear. Cockpit addresses this visibility problem by providing instruments for inspecting the internal training process, much as a software debugger exposes internal program states.

Its instruments use higher-order information about gradient distributions and curvature that has become efficiently accessible. Gradients describe how the model is being pushed to change, while curvature concerns the shape of the optimization landscape. Inspecting these quantities provides a richer status report than observing performance indicators alone.

The tool is designed to help practitioners distinguish learning phases and recognize failure modes, including poorly chosen hyperparameters. The authors release Cockpit for PyTorch and argue that it can support troubleshooting while offering additional insight into neural-network behavior. Its contribution is a practical way to observe training more closely: the abstract presents diagnostic instruments and their intended value, rather than a claim that the tool automatically repairs training problems.
summary.tldr: Cockpit exposes gradient and curvature information during neural-network training to help practitioners understand learning phases and diagnose failures.

title: Cockpit: A Practical Debugging Tool for the Training of Deep Neural Networks

abstract: Encoder-decoder networks with attention have proven to be a powerful way to solve many sequence-to-sequence tasks. In these networks, attention aligns encoder and decoder states and is often used for visualizing network behavior. However, the mechanisms used by networks to generate appropriate attention matrices are still mysterious. Moreover, how these mechanisms vary depending on the particular architecture used for the encoder and decoder (recurrent, feed-forward, etc.) are also not well understood. In this work, we investigate how encoder-decoder networks solve different sequence-to-sequence tasks. We introduce a way of decomposing hidden states over a sequence into temporal (independent of input) and input-driven (independent of sequence position) components. This reveals how attention matrices are formed: depending on the task requirements, networks rely more heavily on either the temporal or input-driven components. These findings hold across both recurrent and feed-forward architectures despite their differences in forming the temporal components. Overall, our results provide new insight into the inner workings of attention-based encoder-decoder networks.

paragraphs: Attention in encoder-decoder networks aligns representations of an input sequence with states used to generate an output sequence. Attention matrices are often visualized to inspect model behavior, but the mechanisms that produce those alignments are less clear. This paper investigates how those mechanisms depend on both the task and the network architecture.

The authors introduce a decomposition of hidden states into temporal and input-driven components. The temporal component is independent of the input, while the input-driven component is independent of sequence position. Separating these contributions makes it possible to examine whether attention is primarily organized by position-related structure or by information from the input.

The analysis finds that networks rely more strongly on one component or the other depending on task requirements. This pattern appears in both recurrent and feed-forward architectures, despite differences in how they create temporal components. The findings offer a shared way to understand attention across these architectures. They move beyond inspecting an alignment matrix by examining the distinct contributions within hidden states that help generate it.
summary.tldr: Decomposing hidden states reveals how temporal and input-driven information contribute to attention across recurrent and feed-forward encoder-decoder networks.

title: Understanding How Encoder-Decoder Architectures Attend

abstract: Unsupervised domain adaptation, as a prevalent transfer learning setting, spans many real-world applications. With the increasing representational power and applicability of neural networks, state-of-the-art domain adaptation methods make use of deep architectures to map the input features $X$ to a latent representation $Z$ that has the same marginal distribution across domains. This has been shown to be insufficient for generating optimal representation for classification, and to find conditionally invariant representations, usually strong assumptions are needed. We provide reasoning why when the supports of the source and target data from overlap, any map of $X$ that is fixed across domains may not be suitable for domain adaptation via invariant features. Furthermore, we develop an efficient technique in which the optimal map from $X$ to $Z$ also takes domain-specific information as input, in addition to the features $X$. By using the property of minimal changes of causal mechanisms across domains, our model also takes into account the domain-specific information to ensure that the latent representation $Z$ does not discard valuable information about $Y$. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method via synthetic and real-world data experiments. The code is available at: \texttt{https://github.com/DMIRLAB-Group/DSAN}.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation often learns a representation whose overall distribution looks the same in source and target domains. However, making these distributions match does not by itself produce the best representation for classification. This paper examines the transformation used to create that representation and asks whether the same transformation should be applied in every domain.

The authors argue that when source and target data supports overlap, a domain-independent map may be unsuitable for adaptation through invariant features. Their proposed technique gives the transformation both the input features and information about the domain. This allows the mapping into the latent representation to depend on the context in which an input occurs.

The model also uses the property that causal mechanisms change minimally across domains to preserve information relevant to the prediction target. The aim is to achieve useful invariance without discarding valuable classification information. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate the method's effectiveness, supporting the value of domain-aware transformations in the settings studied.
summary.tldr: Domain-aware representation mappings can preserve predictive information while addressing shortcomings of fixed invariant-feature transformations.

title: Domain Adaptation with Invariant Representation Learning: What Transformations to Learn?

abstract: In federated learning (FL), a number of distributed clients targeting the same task collaborate to train a single global model without sharing their data. The learning process typically starts from a randomly initialized or some pretrained model. In this paper, we aim at designing an initial model based on which an arbitrary group of clients can obtain a global model for its own purpose, within only a few rounds of FL. The key challenge here is that the downstream tasks for which the pretrained model will be used are generally unknown when the initial model is prepared. Our idea is to take a meta-learning approach to construct the initial model so that any group with a possibly unseen task can obtain a high-accuracy global model within only R rounds of FL. Our meta-learning itself could be done via federated learning among willing participants and is based on an episodic arrangement to mimic the R rounds of FL followed by inference in each episode. Extensive experimental results show that our method generalizes well for arbitrary groups of clients and provides large performance improvements given the same overall communication/computation resources, compared to other baselines relying on known pretraining methods.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets clients train a shared model without sharing their underlying data. This paper asks how to prepare an initial model that a later group of clients can adapt within only a few communication rounds. The difficulty is that the group's eventual task may be unknown when that starting model is constructed.

The authors use meta-learning to train the initialization for the adaptation process itself. Training episodes imitate a prescribed number, R, of federated learning rounds followed by inference. This arrangement makes the short federated training process part of what the initialization is optimized to support. The meta-learning stage can itself be carried out through federated learning among willing participants.

Experiments report good generalization across client groups and large performance improvements over baselines using other pretraining methods at the same overall communication and computation resources. The intended benefit is rapid adaptation, including to possibly unseen tasks. The evidence supports preparing an initialization around the downstream collaboration procedure rather than judging its usefulness only before that procedure begins.
summary.tldr: The method meta-learns an initialization designed to help new client groups train effective federated models in only a few rounds.

title: Few-Round Learning for Federated Learning

abstract: There has been rapidly growing interest in meta-learning as a method for increasing the flexibility and sample efficiency of reinforcement learning. One problem in this area of research, however, has been a scarcity of adequate benchmark tasks. In general, the structure underlying past benchmarks has either been too simple to be inherently interesting, or too ill-defined to support principled analysis. In the present work, we introduce a new benchmark for meta-RL research, emphasizing transparency and potential for in-depth analysis as well as structural richness. Alchemy is a 3D video game, implemented in Unity, which involves a latent causal structure that is resampled procedurally from episode to episode, affording structure learning, online inference, hypothesis testing and action sequencing based on abstract domain knowledge. We evaluate a pair of powerful RL agents on Alchemy and present an in-depth analysis of one of these agents. Results clearly indicate a frank and specific failure of meta-learning, providing validation for Alchemy as a challenging benchmark for meta-RL. Concurrent with this report, we are releasing Alchemy as public resource, together with a suite of analysis tools and sample agent trajectories.

paragraphs: Alchemy tests whether reinforcement learning agents can learn how to adapt when the hidden rules of an environment change. The authors argue that previous benchmarks often offered either overly simple structure or structure too poorly defined for careful analysis. Their goal is a task that combines a rich learning problem with enough transparency to explain an agent’s behavior.

The benchmark is a three-dimensional game built in Unity. Its hidden causal structure is generated anew between episodes, giving agents opportunities to discover relationships, update their understanding during play, test hypotheses, and choose sequences of actions using abstract knowledge. This makes adaptation to the current episode’s rules a central part of the challenge.

The authors evaluate two strong reinforcement learning agents and examine one in depth. Their results identify a specific failure of meta-learning in the tested agents, supporting Alchemy’s usefulness as a demanding benchmark. The public release includes analysis tools and example agent trajectories, so researchers can investigate how agents behave as well as compare their performance.
summary.tldr: Alchemy provides a game with changing hidden causal rules and analysis tools that expose specific adaptation failures in tested reinforcement learning agents.

title: Alchemy: A benchmark and analysis toolkit for meta-reinforcement learning agents

abstract: Room impulse response (RIR) functions capture how the surrounding physical environment transforms the sounds heard by a listener, with implications for various applications in AR, VR, and robotics. Whereas traditional methods to estimate RIRs assume dense geometry and/or sound measurements throughout the environment, we explore how to infer RIRs based on a sparse set of images and echoes observed in the space. Towards that goal, we introduce a transformer-based method that uses self-attention to build a rich acoustic context, then predicts RIRs of arbitrary query source-receiver locations through cross-attention. Additionally, we design a novel training objective that improves the match in the acoustic signature between the RIR predictions and the targets. In experiments using a state-of-the-art audio-visual simulator for 3D environments, we demonstrate that our method successfully generates arbitrary RIRs, outperforming state-of-the-art methods and---in a major departure from traditional methods---generalizing to novel environments in a few-shot manner. Project: http://vision.cs.utexas.edu/projects/fs_rir

paragraphs: A room impulse response describes how an environment transforms sound traveling from a source to a listener. Estimating it can support augmented reality, virtual reality, and robotics. This paper asks whether a few images and observed echoes can provide enough information to predict these responses, reducing reliance on dense geometry or sound measurements.

The proposed transformer first uses self-attention to combine the sparse observations into an acoustic context. It then uses cross-attention to predict a response for a queried source and receiver location. This separates gathering evidence about the environment from answering a particular acoustic query. A new training objective also encourages predictions to match the acoustic signature of the target responses.

Experiments in an audio-visual simulator for three-dimensional environments show successful predictions at arbitrary query locations and improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The model also transfers to new environments from a small set of observations. These findings support learning a reusable relationship between visual evidence, echoes, and environment acoustics, with the reported evaluation conducted in simulation.
summary.tldr: A transformer predicts environment acoustics from sparse images and echoes, showing few-shot transfer to new simulated environments.

title: Few-Shot Audio-Visual Learning of Environment Acoustics

abstract: Bilevel optimization has arisen as a powerful tool in modern machine learning. However, due to the nested structure of bilevel optimization, even gradient-based methods require second-order derivative approximations via Jacobian- or/and Hessian-vector computations, which can be costly and unscalable in practice. Recently, Hessian-free bilevel schemes have been proposed to resolve this issue, where the general idea is to use zeroth- or first-order methods to approximate the full hypergradient of the bilevel problem. However, we empirically observe that such approximation can lead to large variance and unstable training, but estimating only the response Jacobian matrix as a partial component of the hypergradient turns out to be extremely effective. To this end, we propose a new Hessian-free method, which adopts the zeroth-order-like method to approximate the response Jacobian matrix via taking difference between two optimization paths. Theoretically, we provide the convergence rate analysis for the proposed algorithms, where our key challenge is to characterize the approximation and smoothness properties of the trajectory-dependent estimator, which can be of independent interest. This is the first known convergence rate result for this type of Hessian-free bilevel algorithms. Experimentally, we demonstrate that the proposed algorithms outperform baseline bilevel optimizers on various bilevel problems. Particularly, in our experiment on few-shot meta-learning with ResNet-12 network over the miniImageNet dataset, we show that our algorithm outperforms baseline meta-learning algorithms, while other baseline bilevel optimizers do not solve such meta-learning problems within a comparable time frame.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization nests one optimization problem inside another, making even gradient-based learning potentially expensive. Computing the outer problem's hypergradient can involve costly second-order derivative operations. This paper investigates Hessian-free alternatives and reports that approximating the entire hypergradient can introduce substantial variance and unstable training.

The proposed method approximates only the response Jacobian, the component describing how the inner solution responds to changes in the outer variables. It estimates that response by taking the difference between two optimization trajectories. The authors analyze the estimator's approximation quality and smoothness despite its dependence on those trajectories, obtaining the first known convergence-rate result for this type of Hessian-free bilevel algorithm.

Experiments report improvements over baseline bilevel optimizers across several problems. In few-shot meta-learning with ResNet-12 on miniImageNet, the method outperforms baseline meta-learning algorithms, while other tested bilevel optimizers do not solve the problem within comparable time. The findings favor a more targeted approximation strategy and connect its empirical effectiveness to a convergence analysis.
summary.tldr: A Hessian-free bilevel method estimates only the response Jacobian through two optimization paths, with convergence guarantees and favorable empirical results.

title: On the Convergence Theory for Hessian-Free Bilevel Algorithms

abstract: Treatment effect estimation is a fundamental problem in causal inference. We focus on designing efficient randomized controlled trials, to accurately estimate the effect of some treatment on a population of $n$ individuals. In particular, we study \textit{sample-constrained treatment effect estimation}, where we must select a subset of $s \ll n$ individuals from the population to experiment on. This subset must be further partitioned into treatment and control groups. Algorithms for partitioning the entire population into treatment and control groups, or for choosing a single representative subset, have been well-studied. The key challenge in our setting is jointly choosing a representative subset and a partition for that set. We focus on both individual and average treatment effect estimation, under a linear effects model. We give provably efficient experimental designs and corresponding estimators, by identifying connections to discrepancy minimization and leverage-score-based sampling used in randomized numerical linear algebra. Our theoretical results obtain a smooth transition to known guarantees when $s$ equals the population size. We also empirically demonstrate the performance of our algorithms.

paragraphs: A randomized controlled trial may have resources to experiment on only a small fraction of a population. That creates two linked decisions: which individuals to include and how to divide them between treatment and control. This paper studies those choices jointly, aiming to estimate treatment effects accurately despite a restricted sample.

Under a linear effects model, the authors consider both individual treatment effects and the population's average effect. They develop efficient experimental designs together with corresponding estimators. Their approach draws connections to discrepancy minimization and leverage-score sampling, tools that help address balance and informative selection in mathematical computations.

The theoretical guarantees connect smoothly to established results when the experimental sample expands to include the whole population. This makes the constrained setting part of a broader design problem with a familiar full-population endpoint. The authors also demonstrate their algorithms empirically. The main contribution is treating representative selection and treatment-control assignment as a coordinated task under the stated linear modeling assumption.
summary.tldr: Under a linear effects model, the paper jointly designs participant selection and treatment-control assignment for trials with severely limited sample sizes.

title: Sample Constrained Treatment Effect Estimation

abstract: Meaningful uncertainty quantification in computer vision requires reasoning about semantic information---say, the hair color of the person in a photo or the location of a car on the street. To this end, recent breakthroughs in generative modeling allow us to represent semantic information in disentangled latent spaces, but providing uncertainties on the semantic latent variables has remained challenging. In this work, we provide principled uncertainty intervals that are guaranteed to contain the true semantic factors for any underlying generative model. The method does the following: (1) it uses quantile regression to output a heuristic uncertainty interval for each element in the latent space (2) calibrates these uncertainties such that they contain the true value of the latent for a new, unseen input. The endpoints of these calibrated intervals can then be propagated through the generator to produce interpretable uncertainty visualizations for each semantic factor. This technique reliably communicates semantically meaningful, principled, and instance-adaptive uncertainty in inverse problems like image super-resolution and image completion. Project page: https://swamiviv.github.io/semantic_uncertainty_intervals/

paragraphs: An uncertainty estimate for an image is easier to interpret when it concerns a meaningful attribute, such as hair color or an object's location. Generative models can represent such factors in disentangled latent spaces, where separate latent variables encode semantic information. This paper develops uncertainty intervals for those variables, connecting statistical uncertainty to interpretable image characteristics.

The method first uses quantile regression to propose an interval for each latent coordinate. These initial intervals are heuristic, so a calibration step adjusts them to provide coverage of the true latent value for a new input. The paper presents coverage guarantees that apply regardless of the underlying generative model.

The interval endpoints are then passed through the generator to visualize the uncertainty associated with each semantic factor. This lets the output communicate possible variation in meaningful image content, rather than presenting an unexplained numerical score. The authors demonstrate the approach for inverse problems including super-resolution and image completion, reporting principled uncertainty that adapts to the individual input and remains semantically interpretable.
summary.tldr: Calibrated intervals in disentangled latent spaces turn uncertainty about semantic image factors into interpretable visualizations with coverage guarantees.

title: Semantic uncertainty intervals for disentangled latent spaces

abstract: A longstanding challenge in neuroscience is to understand neural mechanisms underlying the brain’s remarkable ability to learn and detect transformations of objects due to motion. Translations and rotations of images can be viewed as orthogonal transformations in the space of pixel intensity vectors. Every orthogonal transformation can be decomposed into rotations within irreducible two-dimensional subspaces (or representations). For sets of commuting transformations, known as toroidal groups, Cohen and Welling proposed a mathematical framework for learning the irreducible representations. We explore the possibility that the brain also learns irreducible representations using a biologically plausible learning mechanism. The first is based on SVD of the anti-symmetrized outer product of the vectors representing consecutive images and is implemented by a single-layer neural network. The second is based on PCA of the difference between consecutive frames and is implemented in a two-layer network but with greater biological plausibility. Both networks learn image rotations (replicating Cohen and Welling’s results) as well as translations. It would be interesting to search for the proposed networks in nascent connectomics and physiology datasets.

paragraphs: The paper asks how neural circuits might learn the transformations that occur when objects move. It represents images as vectors of pixel intensities and considers translations and rotations through orthogonal transformations. The mathematical framework breaks transformations into smaller rotational components, focusing on commuting transformations, whose order of application does not matter.

The authors propose two learning mechanisms for these irreducible representations. The first uses a singular value decomposition of an anti-symmetrized outer product formed from consecutive images and has a single-layer neural implementation. The second applies principal component analysis to differences between successive frames. It requires two layers but is described as more biologically plausible.

Both networks learn image rotations and translations, with the rotation results reproducing earlier work. The contribution connects a mathematical account of visual transformations to candidate neural learning mechanisms. Its biological claim remains a possibility: the paper proposes looking for these networks in connectivity and physiology data, rather than reporting that the brain has already been shown to implement them.
summary.tldr: Two biologically motivated neural mechanisms learn component representations of commuting image transformations.

title: Biological Learning of Irreducible Representations of Commuting Transformations

abstract: We study the problem of meta-learning with task-level differential privacy. Meta-learning has received increasing attention recently because of its ability to enable fast generalization to new task with small number of data points. However, the training process of meta learning likely involves exchange of task specific information, which may pose privacy risk especially in some privacy-sensitive applications. Therefore, it is important to provide strong privacy guarantees such that the learning process will not reveal any task sensitive information. To this end, existing works have proposed meta learning algorithms with record-level differential privacy, which is not sufficient in many scenarios since it does not protect the aggregated statistics based on the task dataset as a whole. Moreover, the utility guarantees in the prior work are based on assuming that the loss function satisfies both smoothness and quadratic growth conditions, which do not necessarily hold in practice. To address these issues, we propose meta learning algorithms with task-level differential privacy; that is, our algorithms protect the privacy of the entire dataset for each task. In the case when a single meta model is trained, we give both privacy and utility guarantees assuming only that the loss is convex and Lipschitz. Moreover, we propose a new private clustering-based meta-learning algorithm that enables private meta learning of multiple meta models. This can provide significant accuracy gains over the single meta model paradigm, especially when the tasks distribution cannot be well represented by a single meta model. Finally, we conduct several experiments demonstrating the effectiveness of our proposed algorithms.

paragraphs: Meta-learning uses experience across tasks to support adaptation to new tasks with little data. Sharing information during training can expose sensitive properties of an entire task dataset. This paper targets task-level differential privacy, extending protection beyond individual records to the dataset associated with each task.

For learning a single meta model, the authors provide privacy and utility guarantees assuming convex, Lipschitz losses. These assumptions avoid the smoothness and quadratic-growth requirements used in earlier utility guarantees. summary.tldr: Task-level private meta-learning protects whole task datasets and supports either one shared model or multiple privately clustered models.

title: Task-level Differentially Private Meta Learning

abstract: Despite recent success in using the invariance principle for out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization on Euclidean data (e.g., images), studies on graph data are still limited. Different from images, the complex nature of graphs poses unique challenges to adopting the invariance principle. In particular, distribution shifts on graphs can appear in a variety of forms such as attributes and structures, making it difficult to identify the invariance. Moreover, domain or environment partitions, which are often required by OOD methods on Euclidean data, could be highly expensive to obtain for graphs. To bridge this gap, we propose a new framework, called Causality Inspired Invariant Graph LeArning (CIGA), to capture the invariance of graphs for guaranteed OOD generalization under various distribution shifts. Specifically, we characterize potential distribution shifts on graphs with causal models, concluding that OOD generalization on graphs is achievable when models focus only on subgraphs containing the most information about the causes of labels. Accordingly, we propose an information-theoretic objective to extract the desired subgraphs that maximally preserve the invariant intra-class information. Learning with these subgraphs is immune to distribution shifts. Extensive experiments on 16 synthetic or real-world datasets, including a challenging setting -- DrugOOD, from AI-aided drug discovery, validate the superior OOD performance of CIGA.

abstract: We explore the minimax optimal error associated with a demographic parity-constrained regression problem within the context of a linear model. Our proposed model encompasses a broader range of discriminatory bias sources compared to the model presented by Chzhen and Schreuder. Our analysis reveals that the minimax optimal error for the demographic parity-constrained regression problem under our model is characterized by $\Theta(\frac{dM}{n})$, where $n$ denotes the sample size, $d$ represents the dimensionality, and $M$ signifies the number of demographic groups arising from sensitive attributes. Moreover, we demonstrate that the minimax error increases in conjunction with a larger bias present in the model.

paragraphs: This paper studies the fundamental prediction error achievable when regression must satisfy demographic parity under a linear model. Its focus is minimax error: the best worst-case performance available within the specified problem setting. That perspective asks how difficult the constrained learning problem is, rather than assessing only the behavior of one particular fitted predictor.

The proposed model includes a broader range of discriminatory bias sources than the earlier model identified in the abstract. Within this expanded setting, the authors establish that the minimax error scales as dM/n, up to constant factors. Here n is the number of samples, d is the feature dimension, and M is the number of demographic groups defined by sensitive attributes.

The rate describes how sample availability, dimensionality, and group count enter the problem’s statistical difficulty together. The analysis also shows that greater bias in the model increases minimax error. These conclusions concern demographic-parity-constrained regression under the studied linear model; they characterize its attainable error rather than asserting a universal relationship for every fairness criterion or model family.
summary.tldr: Under the studied linear model, demographic-parity-constrained regression has minimax error scaling as dM/n, with greater model bias increasing that error.

title: Demographic Parity Constrained Minimax Optimal Regression under Linear Model

abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel and powerful method to harness Bayesian optimization for variational quantum eigensolvers (VQEs) - a hybrid quantum-classical protocol used to approximate the ground state of a quantum Hamiltonian. Specifically, we derive a *VQE-kernel* which incorporates important prior information about quantum circuits: the kernel feature map of the VQE-kernel exactly matches the known functional form of the VQE's objective function and thereby significantly reduces the posterior uncertainty.Moreover, we propose a novel acquisition function for Bayesian optimization called \emph{Expected Maximum Improvement over Confident Regions} (EMICoRe) which can actively exploit the inductive bias of the VQE-kernel by treating regions with low predictive uncertainty as indirectly "observed". As a result, observations at as few as three points in the search domain are sufficient to determine the complete objective function along an entire one-dimensional subspace of the optimization landscape. Our numerical experiments demonstrate that our approach improves over state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: Variational quantum eigensolvers combine quantum and classical computation to approximate a quantum Hamiltonian's ground state. Their optimization objective has a known mathematical form arising from the quantum circuit. This paper uses that structure to guide Bayesian optimization, so each observation can provide more information about the objective being searched.

The proposed VQE-kernel has a feature map that exactly matches the objective's known functional form. Incorporating this information substantially reduces posterior uncertainty. The authors pair the kernel with EMICoRe, an acquisition function that treats confidently predicted regions as indirectly observed, allowing the search to use information beyond the points that were directly evaluated.

With this structure, observations at as few as three points can be sufficient to determine the objective along an entire one-dimensional subspace. That statement concerns a one-dimensional slice of the optimization landscape. Numerical experiments report improvements over state-of-the-art baselines, supporting the benefit of combining a physics-informed model with an acquisition rule designed to exploit its confidence.
summary.tldr: A quantum-circuit-informed kernel and confidence-aware acquisition rule make Bayesian optimization more effective for variational quantum eigensolvers.

title: Physics-Informed Bayesian Optimization of Variational Quantum Circuits

abstract: In this work, we study how the performance of a given direction changes with its sampling ratio in Multilingual Neural Machine Translation (MNMT). By training over 200 multilingual models with various model sizes, data sizes, and language directions, we find it interesting that the performance of certain translation direction does not always improve with the increase of its weight in the multi-task optimization objective. Accordingly, scalarization method leads to a multitask trade-off front that deviates from the traditional Pareto front when there exists data imbalance in the training corpus, which poses a great challenge to improve the overall performance of all directions. Based on our observations, we propose the Double Power Law to predict the unique performance trade-off front in MNMT, which is robust across various languages, data adequacy, and the number of tasks. Finally, we formulate the sample ratio selection problem in MNMT as an optimization problem based on the Double Power Law. Extensive experiments show that it achieves better performance than temperature searching and gradient manipulation methods with only 1/5 to 1/2 of the total training budget. We release the code at https://github.com/pkunlp-icler/ParetoMNMT for reproduction.

paragraphs: Multilingual translation training must decide how frequently to sample each translation direction. Increasing one direction's share might seem like a straightforward way to improve it. After training more than 200 models across model sizes, data sizes, and language directions, the authors find that giving a direction more weight does not always improve its performance.

With imbalanced training data, the tradeoff curve produced by weighting tasks can depart from the traditional Pareto front. This complicates efforts to improve all directions together. The authors propose a Double Power Law to predict the observed performance tradeoffs, reporting robustness across different languages, levels of data adequacy, and numbers of tasks.

They then use that predictive relationship to formulate sampling-ratio selection as an optimization problem. Experiments show better performance than temperature searching and gradient manipulation methods while using one fifth to one half of the total training budget. The practical contribution is a model of how sampling affects multilingual performance that can guide allocation more efficiently than the compared selection methods.
summary.tldr: A Double Power Law models multilingual translation tradeoffs and guides sampling ratios more efficiently than the compared selection methods.

title: On the Pareto Front of Multilingual Neural Machine Translation

abstract: The recent emergence of Large Language Models based on the Transformer architecture has enabled dramatic advancements in the field of Natural Language Processing. However, these models have long inference latency, which limits their deployment and makes them prohibitively expensive for various real-time applications. The inference latency is further exacerbated by autoregressive generative tasks, as models need to run iteratively to generate tokens sequentially without leveraging token-level parallelization. To address this, we propose Big Little Decoder (BiLD), a framework that can improve inference efficiency and latency for a wide range of text generation applications. The BiLD framework contains two models with different sizes that collaboratively generate text. The small model runs autoregressively to generate text with a low inference cost, and the large model is only invoked occasionally to refine the small model’s inaccurate predictions in a non-autoregressive manner. To coordinate the small and large models, BiLD introduces two simple yet effective policies: (1) the fallback policy that determines when to hand control over to the large model; and (2) the rollback policy that determines when the large model needs to correct the small model's inaccurate predictions. To evaluate our framework across different tasks and models, we apply BiLD to various text generation scenarios encompassing machine translation on IWSLT 2017 De-En and WMT 2014 De-En, and summarization on XSUM and CNN/DailyMail. On an NVIDIA T4 GPU, our framework achieves a speedup of up to 2.12x speedup with minimal generation quality degradation. Furthermore, our framework is fully plug-and-play and can be applied without any modifications in the training process or model architecture. Our code is open-sourced.

summary.tldr: BiLD coordinates small-model generation with occasional large-model corrections, achieving up to 2.12-fold speedups with minimal quality degradation.

title: Speculative Decoding with Big Little Decoder

abstract: In this paper, we introduce a novel MCMC sampler, PARNI-DAG, for a fully-Bayesian approach to the problem of structure learning under observational data. Under the assumption of causal sufficiency, the algorithm allows for approximate sampling directly from the posterior distribution on Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs). PARNI-DAG performs efficient sampling of DAGs via locally informed, adaptive random neighborhood proposal that results in better mixing properties. In addition, to ensure better scalability with the number of nodes, we couple PARNI-DAG with a pre-tuning procedure of the sampler's parameters that exploits a skeleton graph derived through some constraint-based or scoring-based algorithms. Thanks to these novel features, PARNI-DAG quickly converges to high-probability regions and is less likely to get stuck in local modes in the presence of high correlation between nodes in high-dimensional settings. After introducing the technical novelties in PARNI-DAG, we empirically demonstrate its mixing efficiency and accuracy in learning DAG structures on a variety of experiments.

paragraphs: Learning a directed acyclic graph from observational data involves uncertainty about which relationships between variables are supported. PARNI-DAG takes a fully Bayesian approach by approximately sampling graphs from their posterior distribution. Its stated setup assumes causal sufficiency, so the treatment of graph structure rests on the assumption that relevant shared causes are accounted for.

The sampler uses proposals built from adaptive random neighborhoods and local information. These proposals aim to improve mixing, meaning the sampler's ability to move through plausible graph structures. To scale with the number of variables, a preliminary tuning procedure uses a skeleton graph obtained from an existing constraint-based or score-based algorithm.

Together, these mechanisms help the sampler reach high-probability regions quickly and reduce its tendency to become trapped in local modes, including high-dimensional settings with strongly correlated variables. Experiments demonstrate mixing efficiency and accuracy in learning graph structures. The contribution is an improved procedure for exploring posterior uncertainty over graphs, with approximate sampling and causal sufficiency remaining explicit parts of its scope.
summary.tldr: PARNI-DAG improves Bayesian graph-structure sampling through adaptive local proposals and skeleton-based tuning under causal sufficiency.

title: Structure Learning with Adaptive Random Neighborhood Informed MCMC

abstract: One of the grand enduring goals of AI is to create generalist agents that can learn multiple different tasks from diverse data via multitask learning (MTL). However, in practice, applying gradient descent (GD) on the average loss across all tasks may yield poor multitask performance due to severe under-optimization of certain tasks. Previous approaches that manipulate task gradients for a more balanced loss decrease require storing and computing all task gradients ($\mathcal{O}(k)$ space and time where $k$ is the number of tasks), limiting their use in large-scale scenarios. In this work, we introduce Fast Adaptive Multitask Optimization (FAMO), a dynamic weighting method that decreases task losses in a balanced way using $\mathcal{O}(1)$ space and time. We conduct an extensive set of experiments covering multi-task supervised and reinforcement learning problems. Our results indicate that FAMO achieves comparable or superior performance to state-of-the-art gradient manipulation techniques while offering significant improvements in space and computational efficiency. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/Cranial-XIX/FAMO}.
