paragraphs: Training several tasks together by minimizing their average loss can leave some tasks poorly optimized. Methods that directly manipulate task gradients seek a more balanced decrease in losses, but computing and storing every task's gradient costs time and memory proportional to the number of tasks. That overhead makes scaling more difficult.

Fast Adaptive Multitask Optimization, or FAMO, addresses this problem through dynamic task weighting. It adjusts how tasks contribute to optimization so that their losses decrease in a balanced way. The paper describes the method as using O(1) space and time, compared with the O(k) requirements of the gradient manipulation approaches under discussion, where k counts tasks.

Experiments cover both supervised multitask learning and reinforcement learning. The reported results match or exceed state-of-the-art gradient manipulation methods while substantially improving computational and memory efficiency. The significance is that balancing progress across tasks need not carry the same task-gradient handling costs as earlier methods, making this approach useful for pursuing more scalable multitask training.
summary.tldr: FAMO dynamically balances task losses while reducing the time and memory costs associated with manipulating every task's gradient.

title: FAMO: Fast Adaptive Multitask Optimization

abstract: In this work, we consider the problem of matrix sensing over graphs (MSoG). As a general case of matrix completion and matrix sensing problems, the MSoG problem has not been analyzed in the literature and the existing results cannot be directly applied to the MSoG problem. This work provides the first theoretical results on the optimization landscape of the MSoG problem. More specifically, we propose a new condition, named the $\Omega$-RIP condition, to characterize the optimization complexity of the problem. In addition, with an improved regularizer of the incoherence, we prove that the strict saddle property holds for the MSoG problem with high probability under the incoherence condition and the $\Omega$-RIP condition, which guarantees the polynomial-time global convergence of saddle-avoiding methods. Compared with state-of-the-art results, the bounds in this work are tight up to a constant. Besides the theoretical guarantees, we numerically illustrate the close relation between the $\Omega$-RIP condition and the optimization complexity.

paragraphs: Matrix sensing over graphs generalizes matrix completion and matrix sensing, but the existing analyses do not directly cover this broader problem. This paper studies its optimization landscape: the structure that determines whether an optimization method can reach a globally correct solution or encounter troublesome stationary points.

The authors introduce a condition called Ω-RIP to characterize optimization complexity. They combine it with an improved regularizer for incoherence, a property imposed in their analysis. Under both the incoherence and Ω-RIP conditions, they prove that the problem has the strict saddle property with high probability. This structure supports methods designed to avoid saddles, giving those methods polynomial-time global convergence guarantees.

The conditions are central to the result: the guarantee applies to the analyzed setting when those requirements hold. The authors report bounds that are tight up to a constant compared with state-of-the-art results. Numerical illustrations also show a close relationship between Ω-RIP and optimization complexity, connecting the new theoretical condition to observed optimization behavior.
summary.tldr: A new Ω-RIP condition supports conditional guarantees that saddle-avoiding methods solve matrix sensing over graphs in polynomial time.

title: Geometric Analysis of Matrix Sensing over Graphs

abstract: In this work, we propose a new class of learnable optimizers, called Mnemosyne. It is based on the novel spatio-temporal low-rank implicit attention Transformers that can learn to train entire neural network architectures, including other Transformers, without any task-specific optimizer tuning. We show that Mnemosyne: (a) outperforms popular LSTM optimizers (also with new feature engineering to mitigate catastrophic forgetting of LSTMs), (b) can successfully train Transformers while using simple meta-training strategies that require minimal computational resources, (c) matches accuracy-wise SOTA hand-designed optimizers with carefully tuned hyper-parameters (often producing top performing models). Furthermore, Mnemosyne provides space complexity comparable to that of its hand-designed first-order counterparts, which allows it to scale to training larger sets of parameters. We conduct an extensive empirical evaluation of Mnemosyne on: (a) fine-tuning a wide range of Vision Transformers (ViTs) from medium-size architectures to massive ViT-Hs (36 layers, 16 heads), (b) pre-training BERT models and (c) soft prompt-tuning large 11B+ T5XXL models. We complement our results with a comprehensive theoretical analysis of the compact associative memory used by Mnemosyne which we believe was never done before.

paragraphs: Mnemosyne is a learned optimizer: a model trained to update another neural network's parameters. The paper uses Transformers with a low-rank implicit attention mechanism operating across parameters and training time. The aim is to train entire networks, including other Transformers, without tuning the optimizer separately for each task.

The authors report that Mnemosyne outperforms LSTM-based learned optimizers, including versions with additional features intended to reduce forgetting. It also matches the accuracy achieved by leading hand-designed optimizers with carefully tuned hyperparameters, often producing the best-performing models. Mnemosyne's memory complexity is comparable to hand-designed first-order optimizers, which supports scaling to larger parameter sets. The paper also analyzes its compact associative memory theoretically. Together, these contributions address both the effectiveness of learned update rules and the memory requirements that determine where such optimizers can be used.
summary.tldr: Mnemosyne uses Transformers as learned optimizers, matching carefully tuned conventional optimizers in reported accuracy while retaining comparable memory complexity.

title: Mnemosyne: Learning to Train Transformers with Transformers

abstract: The alignment of large language models (LLMs) is critical for developing effective and safe language models. Traditional approaches focus on aligning models during the instruction tuning or reinforcement learning stages, referred to in this paper as `\textit{post alignment}'. We argue that alignment during the pre-training phase, which we term 'native alignment', warrants investigation. Native alignment aims to prevent unaligned content from the beginning, rather than relying on post-hoc processing. This approach leverages extensively aligned pre-training data to enhance the effectiveness and usability of pre-trained models. Our study specifically explores the application of native alignment in the context of Arabic LLMs. We conduct comprehensive experiments and ablation studies to evaluate the impact of native alignment on model performance and alignment stability. Additionally, we release open-source Arabic LLMs that demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on various benchmarks, providing significant benefits to the Arabic LLM community.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether language-model alignment should begin during pre-training. The authors call this approach native alignment, distinguishing it from alignment performed later through instruction tuning or reinforcement learning. Their focus is Arabic language models, where they examine how changing the model's initial learning material affects both its capabilities and alignment.

The proposed approach uses extensively aligned pre-training data. Its aim is to prevent unaligned content from being learned from the beginning and to make the resulting pre-trained models more useful. This makes the choice of pre-training material part of the alignment strategy, extending the question beyond how a completed base model should subsequently be adapted.

The study includes experiments and ablations examining model performance and alignment stability. The authors also release open-source Arabic models that achieve reported state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks. These findings support investigating alignment at the pre-training stage; the stated aim of preventing unaligned content should be understood as a design objective, rather than a guarantee established by benchmark performance.
summary.tldr: The paper studies alignment through Arabic pre-training data and releases models with reported state-of-the-art benchmark performance.

title: Alignment at Pre-training! Towards Native Alignment for Arabic LLMs

abstract: We propose a novel stochastic bandit algorithm that employs reward estimates using a tree ensemble model. Specifically, our focus is on a soft tree model, a variant of the conventional decision tree that has undergone both practical and theoretical scrutiny in recent years. By deriving several non-trivial properties of soft trees, we extend the existing analytical techniques used for neural bandit algorithms to our soft tree-based algorithm. We demonstrate that our algorithm achieves a smaller cumulative regret compared to the existing ReLU-based neural bandit algorithms. We also show that this advantage comes with a trade-off: the hypothesis space of the soft tree ensemble model is more constrained than that of a ReLU-based neural network.

paragraphs: A stochastic bandit algorithm must choose actions while learning their uncertain rewards. The model used to estimate rewards affects how effectively it can make those choices. This paper proposes a bandit algorithm based on an ensemble of soft trees, a variant of conventional decision trees that has received both practical and theoretical study.

The authors derive several properties of soft trees and use them to extend analytical techniques previously developed for neural bandit algorithms. This makes it possible to analyze the tree-based method within a related theoretical framework. They show smaller cumulative regret than existing bandit algorithms based on ReLU neural networks, meaning a smaller accumulated shortfall in reward under the analyzed comparison.

The advantage comes with an explicit trade-off: the soft-tree ensemble can represent a more restricted set of functions than a ReLU-based neural network. The result therefore links improved regret behavior to reduced representational flexibility. The paper's contribution is both an alternative reward model for bandit exploration and an analysis clarifying the cost associated with its theoretical advantage.
summary.tldr: Soft-tree bandits achieve smaller analyzed cumulative regret than existing ReLU neural bandits, with a more restricted hypothesis space.

title: No-Regret Bandit Exploration based on Soft Tree Ensemble Model

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are trained on vast amounts of data, most of which is automatically scraped from the internet. This data includes encyclopedic documents that harbor a vast amount of general knowledge (*e.g.*, Wikipedia) but also potentially overlap with benchmark datasets used for evaluating LLMs. Consequently, evaluating models on test splits that might have leaked into the training set is prone to misleading conclusions. To foster sound evaluation of language models, we introduce a new test dataset named RepLiQA, suited for question-answering and topic retrieval tasks. RepLiQA is a collection of five splits of test sets, four of which have not been released to the internet or exposed to LLM APIs prior to this publication. Each sample in RepLiQA comprises (1) a reference document crafted by a human annotator and depicting an imaginary scenario (*e.g.*, a news article) absent from the internet; (2) a question about the document’s topic; (3) a ground-truth answer derived directly from the information in the document; and (4) the paragraph extracted from the reference document containing the answer. As such, accurate answers can only be generated if a model can find relevant content within the provided document. We run a large-scale benchmark comprising several state-of-the-art LLMs to uncover differences in performance across models of various types and sizes in a context-conditional language modeling setting. Released splits of RepLiQA can be found here: https://huggingface.co/datasets/ServiceNow/repliqa.

summary.tldr: RepLiQA tests language models on human-written imaginary documents to assess their use of unfamiliar reference content.

title: RepLiQA: A Question-Answering Dataset for Benchmarking LLMs on Unseen Reference Content

abstract: With the surging growth of model parameters, foundation models pose unprecedented challenges to traditional computational infrastructures. These large models inherently require substantial accelerator memory to accommodate massive tensors during pre-training, fine-tuning, and even inference stages, making it even more challenging to deploy a model with restricted computational resources. Given this challenge, distribution and offloading the model states are two major solutions. Partitioning the required states to participating workers, and storing them in lower speed media, such as host DRAM and block devices, largely alleviate the accelerator memory pressure. However, the prohibitive costs of tensor communication render it a theoretically plausible yet practically inefficient solution. Previous efforts to improve efficiency include maximizing rematerialization and employing chunk-based tensor management to reduce host-device communication. Despite these efforts, the reported training throughput only achieves 36.54% of model FLOPs utilization (MFUs), still not comparable to full on-device training. In this work, we redesign the data flow of heterogeneous hardware and sharded model training to minimize the excessive communication overhead. Our proposed scheme significantly enhances training and inference throughput of large language models under restrictive computational resources. We confirmed a large leap in effective compute time by looking into the kernel-level runtime behavior of our trials, where the MFUs can achieve up to 51%. Compared to the state-of-the-art approach, our framework robustly achieves remarkable speedups from 3x to 30x in multiple distributed heterogeneous training setups and inference speedups of 1.5x to 2.35x without compromising arithmetic precision.

summary.tldr: SpeedLoader reduces tensor communication overhead, delivering substantial training and inference speedups in evaluated memory-constrained distributed systems.

title: SpeedLoader: An I/O efficient scheme for heterogeneous and distributed LLM operation

abstract: Many zeroth-order (ZO) optimization algorithms have been developed to solve nonconvex minimax problems in machine learning and computer vision areas. However, existing ZO minimax algorithms have high complexity and rely on some strict restrictive conditions for ZO estimations. To address these issues, we design a new unified ZO gradient descent extragradient ascent (ZO-GDEGA) algorithm, which reduces the overall complexity to $\mathcal{O}(d\epsilon^{-6})$ to find an $\epsilon$-stationary point of the function $\psi$ for nonconvex-concave (NC-C) problems, where $d$ is the variable dimension. To the best of our knowledge, ZO-GDEGA is the first ZO algorithm with complexity guarantees to solve stochastic NC-C problems. Moreover, ZO-GDEGA requires weaker conditions on the ZO estimations and achieves more robust theoretical results. As a by-product, ZO-GDEGA has advantages on the condition number for the NC-strongly concave case. Experimentally, ZO-GDEGA can generate more effective poisoning attack data with an average accuracy reduction of 5\%. The improved AUC performance also verifies the robustness of gradient estimations.

paragraphs: Zeroth-order optimization works from function evaluations when gradients are unavailable. In minimax problems, one part of the problem is minimized while another is maximized, making efficient estimation especially important. This paper addresses the high complexity and restrictive estimation conditions of existing zeroth-order methods for nonconvex minimax optimization.

The proposed ZO-GDEGA algorithm combines gradient descent with extragradient ascent using zeroth-order estimates. For nonconvex-concave problems, it reaches an epsilon-stationary point of the studied function with complexity O(d epsilon^-6), where d is the variable dimension. The authors also give complexity guarantees for the stochastic setting and require weaker conditions on the estimates. For nonconvex-strongly-concave problems, the method additionally improves dependence on the condition number.

Experiments report more effective poisoning data, producing an average accuracy reduction of 5%, alongside improved AUC performance that supports the robustness of the gradient estimates. These findings accompany the theoretical contribution: a unified algorithm with better computational guarantees and less restrictive estimation requirements. Its stationarity guarantee concerns approximate optimization progress, rather than a claim of finding a global optimum.
summary.tldr: ZO-GDEGA improves zeroth-order minimax complexity guarantees while weakening estimation conditions and showing empirical robustness benefits.

title: Robust and Faster Zeroth-Order Minimax Optimization: Complexity and Applications

abstract: The generation of equilibrium samples of molecular systems has been a long-standing problem in statistical physics. Boltzmann Generators are a generative machine learning method that addresses this issue by learning a transformation via a normalizing flow from a simple prior distribution to the target Boltzmann distribution of interest. Recently, flow matching has been employed to train Boltzmann Generators for small molecular systems in Cartesian coordinates. We extend this work and propose a first framework for Boltzmann Generators that are transferable across chemical space, such that they predict zero-shot Boltzmann distributions for test molecules without being retraining for these systems. These transferable Boltzmann Generators allow approximate sampling from the target distribution of unseen systems, as well as efficient reweighting to the target Boltzmann distribution. The transferability of the proposed framework is evaluated on dipeptides, where we show that it generalizes efficiently to unseen systems.Furthermore, we demonstrate that our proposed architecture enhances the efficiency of Boltzmann Generators trained on single molecular systems.

paragraphs: Boltzmann Generators learn to produce equilibrium samples of molecular systems by transforming a simple probability distribution into a target Boltzmann distribution. This paper extends work that trains such generators using flow matching in Cartesian coordinates. Its goal is transfer across chemical space: a trained generator should make predictions for new molecules without being retrained separately for each molecular system.

The proposed framework provides approximate samples for unseen systems and supports efficient reweighting to the target Boltzmann distribution. That distinction matters because direct generated samples are described as approximate, while reweighting supplies a way to account for their relationship to the desired distribution. The intended benefit is reuse of a learned generator across molecular systems.

The authors evaluate transferability on dipeptides and report efficient generalization to unseen systems within that evaluation. They also show that the proposed architecture improves the efficiency of generators trained for individual molecular systems. The findings therefore support both a transferable sampling framework and an architectural improvement for the single-system setting, with the transfer evidence grounded in dipeptide experiments.
summary.tldr: Transferable Boltzmann Generators approximately sample unseen molecular systems without retraining and support efficient reweighting to their target distributions.

title: Transferable Boltzmann Generators

abstract: Recent methods are proposed to improve performance of domain adaptation by inferring domain index under an adversarial variational bayesian framework, where domain index is unavailable. However, existing methods typically assume that the global domain indices are sampled from a vanilla gaussian prior, overlooking the inherent structures among different domains.To address this challenge, we propose a Bayesian Domain Adaptation with Gaussian Mixture Domain-Indexing(GMDI) algorithm. GMDI employs a Gaussian Mixture Model for domain indices, with the number of component distributions in the "domain-themes'' space adaptively determined by a Chinese Restaurant Process. By dynamically adjusting the mixtures at the domain indices level, GMDI significantly improves domain adaptation performance. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that GMDI achieves a more stringent evidence lower bound, closer to the log-likelihood. For classification, GMDI outperforms all approaches, and surpasses the state-of-the-art method, VDI, by up to 3.4%, reaching 99.3%. For regression, GMDI reduces MSE by up to 21% (from 3.160 to 2.493), achieving the lowest errors among all methods.

GMDI employs a Gaussian Mixture Model for domain indices, with the number of component distributions in the "domain-themes'' space adaptively determined by a Chinese Restaurant Process. By dynamically adjusting the mixtures at the domain indices level, GMDI significantly improves domain adaptation performance. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that GMDI achieves a more stringent evidence lower bound, closer to the log-likelihood. For classification, GMDI outperforms all approaches, and surpasses the state-of-the-art method, VDI, by up to 3.4%, reaching 99.3%. paragraphs: Domain adaptation aims to maintain performance across different data domains. Some Bayesian approaches infer a hidden domain index when domain labels are unavailable, but assume those indices follow a single Gaussian distribution. This paper argues that such a prior overlooks structure among domains, treating their organization too simply.

GMDI replaces that single distribution with a Gaussian mixture over domain indices. A Chinese Restaurant Process adaptively determines how many mixture components are used in the domain-theme space. This lets the representation accommodate multiple groups of domains while adjusting the mixture structure during learning. The theoretical analysis shows a tighter evidence lower bound, meaning the variational bound lies closer to the log-likelihood.

The reported classification results outperform the compared approaches, exceeding VDI by up to 3.4% and reaching 99.3%. For regression, mean squared error falls by up to 21%, from 3.160 to 2.493. Together, these findings support modeling relationships among hidden domains more flexibly, with both a stronger variational bound and improved predictive results in the reported comparisons.
summary.tldr: GMDI adaptively models hidden domain indices with a Gaussian mixture, tightening the variational bound and improving reported adaptation results.

title: Bayesian Domain Adaptation with Gaussian Mixture Domain-Indexing

abstract: The Normalized cut (NCut) problem is a fundamental and yet notoriously difficult one in the unsupervised clustering field. Because the NCut problem is fractionally structured, the fractional programming (FP) based approach has worked its way into a new frontier. However, the conventional FP techniques are insufficient: the classic Dinkelbach's transform can only deal with a single ratio and hence is limited to the two-class clustering, while the state-of-the-art quadratic transform accounts for multiple ratios but fails to convert the NCut problem to a tractable form. This work advocates a novel extension of the quadratic transform to the multidimensional ratio case, thereby recasting the fractional 0-1 NCut problem into a bipartite matching problem---which can be readily solved in an iterative manner. Furthermore, we explore the connection between the proposed multidimensional FP method and the minorization-maximization theory to verify the convergence.

paragraphs: Normalized cut is a difficult clustering problem whose objective contains ratios. That structure makes fractional programming a natural candidate for solving it. However, existing transformations have important restrictions: Dinkelbach’s transform handles a single ratio and is limited here to two-class clustering, while the quadratic transform handles several ratios but does not make this problem tractable.

The paper extends the quadratic transform to a multidimensional ratio setting. This reformulates the fractional problem with binary decisions as a bipartite matching problem, which can be solved through an iterative procedure. The key contribution is therefore a transformation that connects the original clustering objective to a form that supports manageable computation.

The authors also investigate the relationship between their method and minorization-maximization theory to verify convergence. This supplies theoretical support for the iterative process alongside the new reformulation. The stated advance addresses both obstacles highlighted in the abstract: handling the richer ratio structure of normalized cuts and obtaining a tractable form for the resulting optimization.
summary.tldr: A multidimensional fractional-programming transformation turns normalized-cut clustering into an iterative bipartite matching problem with convergence support.

title: Multidimensional Fractional Programming for Normalized Cuts

abstract: We study private stochastic convex optimization (SCO) under user-level differential privacy (DP) constraints. In this setting, there are $n$ users (e.g., cell phones), each possessing $m$ data items (e.g., text messages), and we need to protect the privacy of each user's entire collection of data items. Existing algorithms for user-level DP SCO are impractical in many large-scale machine learning scenarios because: (i) they make restrictive assumptions on the smoothness parameter of the loss function and require the number of users to grow polynomially with the dimension of the parameter space; or (ii) they are prohibitively slow, requiring at least $(mn)^{3/2}$ gradient computations for smooth losses and $(mn)^3$ computations for non-smooth losses. To address these limitations, we provide novel user-level DP algorithms with state-of-the-art excess risk and runtime guarantees, without stringent assumptions. First, we develop a linear-time algorithm with state-of-the-art excess risk (for a non-trivial linear-time algorithm) under a mild smoothness assumption. Our second algorithm applies to arbitrary smooth losses and achieves optimal excess risk in $\approx (mn)^{9/8}$ gradient computations. Third, for non-smooth loss functions, we obtain optimal excess risk in $n^{11/8} m^{5/4}$ gradient computations. Moreover, our algorithms do not require the number of users to grow polynomially with the dimension.

paragraphs: This paper studies convex learning when privacy must cover each user's entire collection of data. With n users holding m items each, protecting a user means protecting all m items together. Existing algorithms can require restrictive smoothness assumptions, a number of users that grows polynomially with parameter dimension, or prohibitively many gradient computations.

The third handles nonsmooth losses with optimal excess risk using n^(11/8) m^(5/4) gradient computations.

These results improve the stated computational requirements while maintaining strong guarantees on excess risk, the gap from the best achievable objective value. None of the proposed algorithms requires the user count to grow polynomially with dimension. The distinctions among their assumptions matter: the linear-time result carries a mild smoothness condition, while the other algorithms address broader loss classes.
summary.tldr: New user-level private convex optimization algorithms reduce computation while retaining strong excess-risk guarantees under their respective smoothness conditions.

title: Faster Algorithms for User-Level Private Stochastic Convex Optimization

abstract: Diffusion-based video generation models have demonstrated remarkable success in obtaining high-fidelity videos through the iterative denoising process. However, these models require multiple denoising steps during sampling, resulting in high computational costs. In this work, we propose a novel approach to obtain single-step video generation models by leveraging adversarial training to fine-tune pre-trained video diffusion models. We show that, through the adversarial training, the multi-steps video diffusion model, i.e., Stable Video Diffusion (SVD), can be trained to perform single forward pass to synthesize high-quality videos, capturing both temporal and spatial dependencies in the video data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves competitive generation quality of synthesized videos with significantly reduced computational overhead for the denoising process (i.e., around $23\times$ speedup compared with SVD and $6\times$ speedup compared with existing works, with even better generation quality), paving the way for real-time video synthesis and editing.

We show that, through the adversarial training, the multi-steps video diffusion model, i.e., Stable Video Diffusion (SVD), can be trained to perform single forward pass to synthesize high-quality videos, capturing both temporal and spatial dependencies in the video data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves competitive generation quality of synthesized videos with significantly reduced computational overhead for the denoising process (i.e., around $23\times$ speedup compared with SVD and $6\times$ speedup compared with existing works, with even better generation quality), paving the way for real-time video synthesis and editing.

paragraphs: Video diffusion models generate detailed videos through repeated denoising steps, but those repeated passes make sampling computationally expensive. SF-V targets this bottleneck by adapting a pretrained video diffusion model to generate a video in a single forward pass. The goal is to preserve useful video quality while sharply reducing denoising work.

The approach uses adversarial training to fine-tune Stable Video Diffusion. The resulting model captures both spatial dependencies within frames and temporal dependencies across frames in its single-step output. This matters because shortening generation must still account for the structure of individual images and the relationships that make them form a coherent video.

Experiments report competitive generation quality with about a 23-fold denoising speedup over Stable Video Diffusion. Against existing works, the abstract reports approximately sixfold speedup with better generation quality. These findings establish a substantially faster generation approach in the evaluated settings and suggest a route toward real-time video synthesis and editing.
summary.tldr: SF-V uses adversarial fine-tuning for single-pass video generation, reporting roughly 23× faster denoising than Stable Video Diffusion.

title: SF-V: Single Forward Video Generation Model

abstract: A challenging problem in many modern machine learning tasks is to process weight-space features, i.e., to transform or extract information from the weights and gradients of a neural network. Recent works have developed promising weight-space models that are equivariant to the permutation symmetries of simple feedforward networks. However, they are not applicable to general architectures, since the permutation symmetries of a weight space can be complicated by recurrence or residual connections. This work proposes an algorithm that automatically constructs permutation equivariant models, which we refer to as universal neural functionals (UNFs), for any weight space. Among other applications, we demonstrate how UNFs can be substituted into existing learned optimizer designs, and find promising improvements over prior methods when optimizing small image classifiers and language models. Our results suggest that learned optimizers can benefit from considering the (symmetry) structure of the weight space they optimize.

However, they are not applicable to general architectures, since the permutation symmetries of a weight space can be complicated by recurrence or residual connections. This work proposes an algorithm that automatically constructs permutation equivariant models, which we refer to as universal neural functionals (UNFs), for any weight space. Among other applications, we demonstrate how UNFs can be substituted into existing learned optimizer designs, and find promising improvements over prior methods when optimizing small image classifiers and language models. paragraphs: Some machine learning systems operate on another network's weights or gradients, rather than directly on ordinary input data. These systems need to account for permutation symmetries in how network parameters are organized. Previous models handle the symmetries of simple feedforward networks, but recurrence and residual connections can make the structure more complicated.

Universal Neural Functionals provide an algorithm for automatically constructing permutation-equivariant models for any weight space. Equivariance means that a relevant reordering of the input parameters leads to the corresponding reordering of the output. The construction extends this structured treatment of weights beyond the simpler architectures addressed by earlier approaches.

The authors demonstrate applications including replacing components of existing learned optimizers with these functionals. They find promising improvements when optimizing small image classifiers and language models. These results suggest that learned optimizers can benefit from explicitly respecting the symmetry structure of the parameters they update. The broader contribution is an automatic way to build that architectural awareness into models that process other networks.
summary.tldr: Universal Neural Functionals automatically construct symmetry-respecting models for network weights and show promising gains in learned optimization.

title: Universal Neural Functionals

abstract: Linear temporal logic (LTL) and, more generally, $\omega$-regular objectives are alternatives to the traditional discount sum and average reward objectives in reinforcement learning (RL), offering the advantage of greater comprehensibility and hence explainability. In this work, we study the relationship between these objectives. Our main result is that each RL problem for $\omega$-regular objectives can be reduced to a limit-average reward problem in an optimality-preserving fashion, via (finite-memory) reward machines. Furthermore, we demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by showing that optimal policies for limit-average problems can be found asymptotically by solving a sequence of discount-sum problems approximately. Consequently, we resolve an open problem: optimal policies for LTL and $\omega$-regular objectives can be learned asymptotically.
originalAbstract: Linear temporal logic (LTL) and, more generally, $\omega$-regular objectives are alternatives to the traditional discount sum and average reward objectives in reinforcement learning (RL), offering the advantage of greater comprehensibility and hence explainability. In this work, we study the relationship between these objectives. Our main result is that each RL problem for $\omega$-regular objectives can be reduced to a limit-average reward problem in an optimality-preserving fashion, via (finite-memory) reward machines. Furthermore, we demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by showing that optimal policies for limit-average problems can be found asymptotically by solving a sequence of discount-sum problems approximately. Consequently, we resolve an open problem: optimal policies for LTL and $\omega$-regular objectives can be learned asymptotically.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning objectives need not be expressed only as accumulated numerical rewards. Linear temporal logic and the broader class of omega-regular objectives describe desired behavior over time, offering a more comprehensible way to specify goals. This paper studies how these objectives relate to familiar average-reward and discounted-reward formulations.

The main result translates every reinforcement learning problem with an omega-regular objective into a limit-average reward problem. The translation uses reward machines with finite memory and preserves optimality. That preservation is the essential connection: solving the translated reward problem optimally also provides an optimal solution for the original behavioral objective.

The authors then show that optimal policies for the limit-average formulation can be learned asymptotically by approximately solving a sequence of discounted-sum problems. Combining the two results establishes asymptotic learnability of optimal policies for temporal-logic and omega-regular objectives, resolving the stated open problem. The guarantee concerns convergence in the limit, so the contribution is a theoretical route to optimal learning rather than a finite-training-time claim.
summary.tldr: An optimality-preserving translation to average rewards establishes asymptotic learning of optimal policies for temporal-logic and omega-regular objectives.

title: Reinforcement Learning with LTL and $\omega$-Regular Objectives via Optimality-Preserving Translation to Average Rewards

abstract: We present a new angle on the expressive power of graph neural networks (GNNs) by studying how the predictions of real-valued GNN classifiers, such as those classifying graphs probabilistically, evolve as we apply them on larger graphs drawn from some random graph model. We show that the output converges to a constant function, which upper-bounds what these classifiers can uniformly express. This strong convergence phenomenon applies to a very wide class of GNNs, including state of the art models, with aggregates including mean and the attention-based mechanism of graph transformers. Our results apply to a broad class of random graph models, including sparse and dense variants of the Erdős-Rényi model, the stochastic block model, and the Barabási-Albert model. We empirically validate these findings, observing that the convergence phenomenon appears not only on random graphs but also on some real-world graphs.

We show that the output converges to a constant function, which upper-bounds what these classifiers can uniformly express. This strong convergence phenomenon applies to a very wide class of GNNs, including state of the art models, with aggregates including mean and the attention-based mechanism of graph transformers. paragraphs: Graph neural networks are often studied through the graph structures they can distinguish. This paper takes a different perspective: what happens to their real-valued classification outputs as the input graphs become larger? The setting considers graphs drawn from random graph models, allowing the authors to analyze prediction behavior as graph size grows.

For a broad class of networks, the authors prove that the output converges to a constant. The covered architectures include models using mean aggregation and the attention mechanism used by graph transformers. The results span several random graph families, including sparse and dense Erdős-Rényi variants, stochastic block models, and the Barabási-Albert model.

Convergence toward a constant restricts what these classifiers can express uniformly as graph size increases: their outputs eventually lose variation in the analyzed settings. Experiments support the theoretical findings and also observe this behavior on some real-world graphs. That empirical extension is narrower than a universal claim about real data; the paper identifies a broad asymptotic phenomenon, not failure of every graph classifier on every finite graph.
summary.tldr: The paper proves that broad classes of graph neural classifiers approach constant outputs on growing graphs from several random graph models.

title: Almost Surely Asymptotically Constant Graph Neural Networks

abstract: The superior generation capabilities of Denoised Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs) have been effectively showcased across a multitude of domains. Recently, the application of DDPMs has extended to time series generation tasks, where they have significantly outperformed other deep generative models, often by a substantial margin. However, we have discovered two main challenges with these methods: 1) the inference time is excessively long; 2) there is potential for improvement in the quality of the generated time series. In this paper, we propose a method based on discrete token modeling technique called Similarity-driven Discrete Transformer (SDformer). Specifically, SDformer utilizes a similarity-driven vector quantization method for learning high-quality discrete token representations of time series, followed by a discrete Transformer for data distribution modeling at the token level. Comprehensive experiments show that our method significantly outperforms competing approaches in terms of the generated time series quality while also ensuring a short inference time. Furthermore, without requiring retraining, SDformer can be directly applied to predictive tasks and still achieve commendable results.

paragraphs: Generating realistic time series requires modeling the patterns present in sequential data. Diffusion models have achieved strong results on this task, but the authors identify slow inference and room for better sample quality as remaining problems. SDformer explores discrete token modeling as an alternative generation approach.

The method first learns discrete representations using similarity-driven vector quantization. This maps time-series information into tokens whose representation learning is guided by similarity. A discrete Transformer then models the distribution of those tokens. The design therefore separates learning an effective token representation from learning how the represented data are distributed.

Comprehensive experiments report substantially better generated time-series quality than competing approaches while maintaining short inference time. The authors also apply the trained model directly to predictive tasks without retraining and report good results. Together, these findings suggest that the learned discrete representation and Transformer distribution model can support both generation and the demonstrated predictive uses, while addressing the inference-speed concern that motivated the work.
summary.tldr: SDformer models similarity-based discrete time-series tokens to improve generation quality and speed, with prediction possible without retraining.

title: SDformer: Similarity-driven Discrete Transformer For Time Series Generation

abstract: Research in auditory, visual, and audiovisual speech recognition (ASR, VSR, and AVSR, respectively) has traditionally been conducted independently. Even recent self-supervised studies addressing two or all three tasks simultaneously tend to yield separate models, leading to disjoint inference pipelines with increased memory requirements and redundancies. This paper proposes unified training strategies for these systems. We demonstrate that training a single model for all three tasks enhances VSR and AVSR performance, overcoming typical optimisation challenges when training from scratch. Moreover, we introduce a greedy pseudo-labelling approach to more effectively leverage unlabelled samples, addressing shortcomings in related self-supervised methods. Finally, we develop a self-supervised pre-training method within our framework, proving its effectiveness alongside our semi-supervised approach. Despite using a single model for all tasks, our unified approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on LRS3 for ASR, VSR, and AVSR compared to recent methods. Code will be made publicly available.

paragraphs: Speech recognition from audio, visual input, and their combination is often handled by separate models. Even joint research efforts can leave separate inference pipelines, with duplicated components and increased memory requirements. This paper develops training strategies that let a single model perform all three tasks, unifying the recognition system across the available input types.

The authors find that joint training improves visual and audiovisual recognition and overcomes typical optimization difficulties encountered when training from scratch. They also introduce greedy pseudo-labeling to make better use of unlabeled samples. A further self-supervised pretraining method operates within the same framework, and the paper demonstrates its effectiveness alongside the semi-supervised approach.

On LRS3, the unified model achieves state-of-the-art performance relative to recent methods for auditory, visual, and audiovisual recognition. The result shows that sharing one model across these tasks can coexist with strong task-specific performance. The contribution spans both model unification and ways of learning from unlabeled data, addressing the training process as well as the fragmented inference setup.
summary.tldr: Unified training, pseudo-labeling, and self-supervised pretraining enable one model to achieve state-of-the-art LRS3 results across three speech-recognition input modes.

title: Unified Speech Recognition: A Single Model for Auditory, Visual, and Audiovisual Inputs

abstract: Recent work has shown that the attention maps of the widely popular DINOv2 model exhibit artifacts, which hurt both model interpretability and performance on dense image tasks. These artifacts emerge due to the model repurposing patch tokens with redundant local information for the storage of global image information. To address this problem, additional register tokens have been incorporated in which the model can store such information instead. We carefully examine the influence of these register tokens on the relationship between global and local image features, showing that while register tokens yield cleaner attention maps, these maps do not accurately reflect the integration of local image information in large models. Instead, global information is dominated by information extracted from register tokens, leading to a disconnect between local and global features. Inspired by these findings, we show that the [CLS] token itself leads to a very similar phenomenon in models without explicit register tokens. Our work shows that care must be taken when interpreting attention maps of large ViTs. Further, by clearly attributing the faulty behavior to register and [CLS] tokens, we show a path towards more interpretable vision models.

paragraphs: Vision transformers can repurpose image-patch tokens to store information about the whole image. In DINOv2, this produces attention-map artifacts that harm interpretability and dense image tasks. Adding register tokens gives the model dedicated places to store global information, producing cleaner attention maps. This paper investigates what those cleaner maps actually reveal.

The authors find that, in large models, cleaned-up attention maps do not accurately reflect how local image information contributes to global features. Instead, global information is dominated by information extracted from register tokens, creating a disconnect between local and global representations. The visual appearance of an attention map therefore does not by itself establish that it faithfully explains local information integration.

The analysis also identifies a similar phenomenon caused by the classification, or [CLS], token in models without explicit registers. This broadens the finding beyond register-equipped architectures. By attributing the behavior to these specific tokens, the work identifies an architectural source of interpretability problems and suggests a direction for developing more interpretable vision models.
summary.tldr: Register and [CLS] tokens can disconnect local and global features in large vision transformers, making clean attention maps misleading as explanations.

title: Register and [CLS] tokens induce a decoupling of local and global features in large ViTs

abstract: Deep graph clustering (DGC) aims to partition graph nodes into distinct clusters in an unsupervised manner. Despite rapid advancements in this field, DGC remains inherently challenging due to the absence of ground-truth, which complicates the design of effective algorithms and impedes the establishment of standardized benchmarks. The lack of unified datasets, evaluation protocols, and metrics further exacerbates these challenges, making it difficult to systematically assess and compare DGC methods. To address these limitations, we introduce $\texttt{DGCBench}$, the first comprehensive and unified benchmark for DGC methods. It evaluates 12 state-of-the-art DGC methods across 12 datasets from diverse domains and scales, spanning 6 critical dimensions: $\textbf{discriminability}$, $\textbf{effectiveness}$, $\textbf{scalability}$, $\textbf{efficiency}$, $\textbf{stability}$, and $\textbf{robustness}$. Additionally, we develop $\texttt{PyDGC}$, an open-source Python library that standardizes the DGC training and evaluation paradigm. Through systematic experiments, we reveal persistent limitations in existing methods, specifically regarding the homophily bottleneck, training instability, vulnerability to perturbations, efficiency plateau, scalability challenges, and poor discriminability, thereby offering actionable insights for future research. We hope that $\texttt{DGCBench}$, $\texttt{PyDGC}$, and our analyses will collectively accelerate the progress in the DGC community. The code is available at https://github.com/Marigoldwu/PyDGC.

paragraphs: Deep graph clustering groups graph nodes without using ground-truth cluster assignments during learning. Comparing methods is difficult when studies use different datasets, evaluation procedures, and metrics. DGCBench addresses this fragmentation by establishing a common framework for assessing methods across several practical dimensions.

The benchmark evaluates 12 methods on 12 datasets covering different domains and scales. Its six evaluation dimensions are discriminability, effectiveness, scalability, efficiency, stability, and robustness. This broad view makes it possible to examine both the quality of the resulting groups and the behavior of the methods under different computational and data conditions. The accompanying Python library, PyDGC, standardizes training and evaluation.

The experiments identify recurring weaknesses involving dependence on homophily, training instability, sensitivity to perturbations, limited efficiency improvements, scaling difficulties, and poor discriminability. Homophily concerns the tendency of similar nodes to be connected, so dependence on it is a structural vulnerability. The contribution is a shared evaluation foundation and an analysis of persistent obstacles that future clustering methods need to address.
summary.tldr: DGCBench standardizes deep graph clustering evaluation and exposes recurring weaknesses in quality, stability, robustness, efficiency, and scalability.

title: DGCBench: A Deep Graph Clustering Benchmark

abstract: The quality of foundation models depends heavily on their training data. Consequently, great efforts have been put into dataset curation. Yet most approaches rely on manual tuning of coarse-grained mixtures of large buckets of data, or filtering by hand-crafted heuristics. An approach that is ultimately more scalable (let alone more satisfying) is to \emph{learn} which data is actually valuable for training. This type of meta-learning could allow more sophisticated, fine-grained, and effective curation. Our proposed \emph{DataRater} is an instance of this idea. It estimates the value of training on any particular data point. This is done by meta-learning using `meta-gradients', with the objective of improving training efficiency on held out data. In extensive experiments across a range of model scales and datasets, we find that using our DataRater to filter data is highly effective, resulting in significantly improved compute efficiency.

paragraphs: Foundation-model training depends heavily on which examples enter the dataset. Common curation approaches adjust broad mixtures of data or apply manually designed filtering rules. DataRater instead learns to estimate the training value of individual examples, making data selection a learned component of the training process rather than only a set of human choices.

The method uses meta-learning with meta-gradients. Its objective is to improve training efficiency on held-out data, so the signal for judging an example comes from the training outcome the system is trying to improve. This connects example selection to measured learning usefulness and supports finer-grained decisions than treating a large bucket of data as uniformly valuable.

Across experiments involving different model scales and datasets, filtering with DataRater significantly improves compute efficiency. The stated finding supports learned curation as a practical way to make training resources more productive in the evaluated settings. Its broader contribution is a framework for learning which data to retain, with held-out training efficiency providing the objective that guides those judgments.
summary.tldr: DataRater learns the training value of individual examples and improves compute efficiency by using those estimates to filter datasets.

title: DataRater: Meta-Learned Dataset Curation

abstract: Personalized alignment is essential for enabling large language models (LLMs) to engage effectively in user-centric dialogue. While recent prompt-based and offline optimization methods offer preliminary solutions, they fall short in cold-start scenarios and long-term personalization due to their inherently static and shallow designs. In this work, we introduce the Reinforcement Learning for Personalized Alignment (RLPA) framework, in which an LLM interacts with a simulated user model to iteratively infer and refine user profiles through dialogue. The training process is guided by a dual-level reward structure: the Profile Reward encourages accurate construction of user representations, while the Response Reward incentivizes generation of responses consistent with the inferred profile. We instantiate RLPA by fine-tuning Qwen-2.5-3B-Instruct, resulting in Qwen-RLPA, which achieves state-of-the-art performance in personalized dialogue. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that Qwen-RLPA consistently outperforms prompting and offline fine-tuning baselines, and even surpasses advanced commercial models such as Claude-3.5 and GPT-4o. Further analysis highlights Qwen-RLPA's robustness in reconciling conflicting user preferences, sustaining long-term personalization and delivering more efficient inference compared to recent reasoning-focused LLMs. These results emphasize the potential of dynamic profile inference as a more effective paradigm for building personalized dialogue systems.

title: Teaching Language Models to Evolve with Users: Dynamic Profile Modeling for Personalized Alignment

abstract: We study the problem of learning a neural sampler to generate samples from discrete state spaces where the target probability mass function $\pi\propto\mathrm{e}^{-U}$ is known up to a normalizing constant, which is an important task in fields such as statistical physics, machine learning, combinatorial optimization, etc. To better address this challenging task when the state space has a large cardinality and the distribution is multi-modal, we propose **M**asked **D**iffusion **N**eural **S**ampler (**MDNS**), a novel framework for training discrete neural samplers by aligning two path measures through a family of learning objectives, theoretically grounded in the stochastic optimal control of the continuous-time Markov chains. We validate the efficiency and scalability of MDNS through extensive experiments on various distributions with distinct statistical properties, where MDNS learns to accurately sample from the target distributions despite the extremely high problem dimensions and outperforms other learning-based baselines by a large margin. A comprehensive study of ablations and extensions is also provided to demonstrate the efficacy and potential of the proposed framework. Our code is available at https://github.com/yuchen-zhu-zyc/MDNS.

paragraphs: This paper studies sampling from discrete distributions whose probabilities are known only up to a normalizing constant. The target assigns relative probability through an energy function, but the overall normalization is unavailable. Such problems arise in statistical physics, machine learning, and combinatorial optimization, and become especially challenging when there are many possible states and several distinct regions of high probability.

Masked Diffusion Neural Sampler, or MDNS, learns a neural sampling process by aligning two path measures. Here, the comparison concerns distributions over sampling trajectories, rather than only their final states. A family of learning objectives carries out this alignment, with its theoretical foundation supplied by stochastic optimal control of continuous-time Markov chains.

Experiments cover distributions with different statistical properties and extremely high dimensions. The authors report accurate sampling, strong efficiency and scalability, and large improvements over other learning-based baselines. Ablations and extensions further examine the framework’s components and potential. These findings support trajectory-distribution alignment as a practical training principle for difficult discrete sampling problems.
summary.tldr: MDNS learns to sample difficult discrete distributions by aligning sampling-path distributions using objectives grounded in stochastic optimal control.

title: MDNS: Masked Diffusion Neural Sampler via Stochastic Optimal Control

abstract: Designing wise AI policy is a grand challenge for society. To design such policy, policymakers should place a premium on rigorous evidence and scientific consensus. While several mechanisms exist for evidence generation, and nascent mechanisms tackle evidence synthesis, we identify a complete void on consensus formation. In this position paper, we argue NeurIPS should actively catalyze scientific consensus on AI policy. Beyond identifying the current deficit in consensus formation mechanisms, we argue that NeurIPS is the best option due its strengths and the paucity of compelling alternatives. To make progress, we recommend initial pilots for NeurIPS by distilling lessons from the IPCC's leadership to build scientific consensus on climate policy. We dispel predictable counters that AI researchers disagree too much to achieve consensus and that policy engagement is not the business of NeurIPS. NeurIPS leads AI on many fronts, and it should champion scientific consensus to create policy that better realizes the benefits of AI.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that sound AI policy needs mechanisms for forming scientific consensus alongside rigorous evidence. The authors distinguish producing evidence, synthesizing existing evidence, and establishing a shared scientific position. They identify an absence of mechanisms for the third activity, even as structures for the first two already exist or are beginning to develop.

Their proposal is for NeurIPS to help fill this institutional gap. They argue that its strengths and the lack of compelling alternatives make it the best available choice. As a practical starting point, they recommend initial pilots informed by lessons from the IPCC’s role in building scientific consensus relevant to climate policy.

The paper also addresses anticipated objections: that disagreement among AI researchers makes consensus unattainable, and that policy engagement falls outside NeurIPS’s responsibilities. Its contribution is an institutional argument and a proposed direction for action, rather than an experimental demonstration. The intended outcome is a stronger shared scientific foundation for policies that better realize AI’s benefits.
summary.tldr: This position paper argues that NeurIPS should pilot mechanisms for scientific consensus on AI policy, drawing lessons from the IPCC.

title: NeurIPS should lead scientific consensus on AI policy

abstract: This work studies fast adversarial training against sparse adversarial perturbations bounded by $l_0$ norm. We first demonstrate the unique challenges of employing $1$-step attacks on $l_0$ bounded perturbations, especially catastrophic overfitting (CO) that cannnot be properly addressed by existing fast adversarial training method for other $l_p$ norms ($p \geq 1$). We highlight that CO in $l_0$ adversarial training arises from sub-optimal perturbation locations of $1$-step attack. Some strategies like multi-$\epsilon$ can mitigate this sub-optimality to some extent, they lead to unstable training in turn. Theoretical and numerical analyses also reveal that the loss landscape of $l_0$ adversarial training is more craggy than its $l_\infty$, $l_2$ and $l_1$ counterparts, which exaggerates CO. To address this issue, we adopt soft labels and the trade-off loss function to smooth the adversarial loss landscape. Extensive experiments demonstrate our method can overcome the challenge of CO, achieve state-of-the-art performance, and narrow the performance gap between $1$-step and multi-step adversarial training against sparse attacks.

paragraphs: This paper studies fast adversarial training against sparse attacks, where the l0 bound limits how many input elements are changed. Training with one-step attacks is challenging because it can suffer catastrophic overfitting. The authors find that existing fast-training remedies developed for other norm constraints do not adequately address this sparse setting.

Their analysis identifies poorly chosen perturbation locations as a source of the problem. Some strategies reduce that suboptimality but introduce unstable training. Theoretical and numerical results also show a more rugged loss landscape than in the compared l-infinity, l2, and l1 settings, worsening catastrophic overfitting. This connects attack construction and optimization geometry as parts of the same difficulty.

The proposed remedy uses soft labels and a trade-off loss to smooth the adversarial loss landscape. Experiments show that the method overcomes catastrophic overfitting in the evaluated settings, achieves state-of-the-art performance, and reduces the gap between one-step and multistep training. The findings support tailoring fast adversarial training to sparse perturbations rather than assuming techniques transfer directly across norm constraints.
summary.tldr: Smoothing the loss landscape improves one-step adversarial training against sparse attacks and reduces catastrophic overfitting in the reported experiments.

title: Understanding and Improving Fast Adversarial Training against $l_0$ Bounded Perturbations

abstract: Audio super-resolution (SR), i.e., upsampling the low-resolution (LR) waveform to the high-resolution (HR) version, has recently been explored with diffusion and bridge models, while previous methods often suffer from sub-optimal upsampling quality due to their uninformative generation prior. Towards high-quality audio super-resolution, we present a new system with latent bridge models (LBMs), where we compress the audio waveform into a continuous latent space and design an LBM to enable a latent-to-latent generation process that naturally matches the LR-to-HR upsampling process, thereby fully exploiting the instructive prior information contained in the LR waveform. To further enhance the training results despite the limited availability of HR samples, we introduce frequency-aware LBMs, where the prior and target frequency are taken as model input, enabling LBMs to explicitly learn an any-to-any upsampling process at the training stage. Furthermore, we design cascaded LBMs and present two prior augmentation strategies, where we make the first attempt to unlock the audio upsampling beyond 48 kHz and empower a seamless cascaded SR process, providing higher flexibility for audio post-production. Comprehensive experimental results evaluated on the VCTK, ESC-50, Song-Describer benchmark datasets and two internal testsets demonstrate that we achieve state-of-the-art objective and perceptual quality for any-to-48 kHz SR across speech, audio, and music signals, as well as setting the first record for any-to-192kHz audio SR. Demo at https://AudioLBM.github.io/.

Towards high-quality audio super-resolution, we present a new system with latent bridge models (LBMs), where we compress the audio waveform into a continuous latent space and design an LBM to enable a latent-to-latent generation process that naturally matches the LR-to-HR upsampling process, thereby fully exploiting the instructive prior information contained in the LR waveform. To further enhance the training results despite the limited availability of HR samples, we introduce frequency-aware LBMs, where the prior and target frequency are taken as model input, enabling LBMs to explicitly learn an any-to-any upsampling process at the training stage. Furthermore, we design cascaded LBMs and present two prior augmentation strategies, where we make the first attempt to unlock the audio upsampling beyond 48 kHz and empower a seamless cascaded SR process, providing higher flexibility for audio post-production. Comprehensive experimental results evaluated on the VCTK, ESC-50, Song-Describer benchmark datasets and two internal testsets demonstrate that we achieve state-of-the-art objective and perceptual quality for any-to-48 kHz SR across speech, audio, and music signals, as well as setting the first record for any-to-192kHz audio SR. Demo at https://AudioLBM.github.io/.

paragraphs: Audio super-resolution produces a higher-resolution waveform from a lower-resolution recording. This paper argues that earlier generative approaches do not make enough use of the information already present in the input. Its system compresses waveforms into a continuous latent space and learns a bridge from the low-resolution representation to the high-resolution representation.

This construction makes the generation process correspond directly to the desired audio transformation. To improve training when high-resolution examples are limited, the authors also provide the source and target frequencies as inputs. This frequency-aware version learns different upsampling relationships within training. Cascaded bridges and two prior augmentation strategies then support successive upsampling stages and greater flexibility in audio post-production.

Across speech, general audio, and music evaluations, the authors report state-of-the-art objective and perceptual quality for upsampling to 48 kHz. They also report the first results for their any-to-192 kHz audio super-resolution setting. The contribution therefore combines stronger use of the original recording with a framework for multiple target resolutions and cascaded processing.
summary.tldr: Latent bridge models use the input recording to guide audio super-resolution, supporting frequency-aware training and cascaded upsampling to 192 kHz.

title: Audio Super-Resolution with Latent Bridge Models

abstract: Learning from human involvement aims to incorporate the human subject to monitor and correct agent behavior errors. Although most interactive imitation learning methods focus on correcting the agent’s action at the current state, they do not adjust its actions in future states, which may be potentially more hazardous. To address this, we introduce Predictive Preference Learning from Human Interventions (PPL), which leverages the implicit preference signals contained in human interventions to inform predictions of future rollouts. The key idea of PPL is to bootstrap each human intervention into L future time steps, called the preference horizon, with the assumption that the agent follows the same action and the human makes the same intervention in the preference horizon. By applying preference optimization on these future states, expert corrections are propagated into the safety-critical regions where the agent is expected to explore, significantly improving learning efficiency and reducing human demonstrations needed. We evaluate our approach with experiments on both autonomous driving and robotic manipulation benchmarks and demonstrate its efficiency and generality. Our theoretical analysis further shows that selecting an appropriate preference horizon L balances coverage of risky states with label correctness, thereby bounding the algorithmic optimality gap. Demo and code are available at: https://metadriverse.github.io/ppl.

paragraphs: A human intervention tells an agent that its current behavior needs correction, but the information may also be useful for states it will encounter next. Predictive Preference Learning from Human Interventions uses that implicit preference to train on predicted future states. The aim is to extend the value of each correction into potentially hazardous regions ahead.

The method propagates an intervention over a preference horizon of L future steps. It assumes that the agent repeats the same action and the human supplies the same intervention throughout that horizon. Preference optimization then applies the resulting corrections to those future states. This assumption is central because it determines when the projected preference labels remain appropriate.

Experiments in autonomous driving and robotic manipulation demonstrate improved learning efficiency and reduced need for human demonstrations. The theoretical analysis explains the tradeoff in choosing L: a longer horizon covers more risky states, while label correctness must also be maintained. Selecting an appropriate horizon balances these effects and bounds the algorithmic optimality gap.
summary.tldr: PPL extends human corrections into predicted future states, balancing broader risk coverage against the reliability of projected preference labels.

title: Predictive Preference Learning from Human Interventions

abstract: Existing code generation benchmarks primarily evaluate functional correctness, with limited attention to code efficiency, and they are often restricted to a single language such as Python. To address this gap, we introduce EffiBench‑X, the first large‑scale multi‑language benchmark specifically designed for robust efficiency evaluation of LLM‑generated code. EffiBench‑X supports Python, C++, Java, JavaScript, Ruby, and Go, and comprises competitive programming tasks paired with human‑expert solutions as efficiency baselines. Evaluating state‑of‑the‑art LLMs on EffiBench‑X reveals that while models frequently generate functionally correct code, they consistently underperform human experts in efficiency. Even the most efficient LLM‑generated solutions (e.g., Qwen3‑32B) achieve only around 62% of human efficiency on average, with significant language‑specific variation: models tend to perform better in Python, Ruby, and JavaScript than in Java, C++, and Go (e.g., DeepSeek‑R1’s Python code is markedly more efficient than its Java code). These findings highlight the need for research into optimization‑oriented methods to improve the efficiency of LLM‑generated code across diverse languages. The dataset and evaluation infrastructure are publicly available at https://github.com/EffiBench/EffiBench-X.git and https://huggingface.co/datasets/EffiBench/effibench-x.

paragraphs: A generated program can return the right answer while still using resources inefficiently. Many code-generation benchmarks emphasize correctness and cover only one programming language, leaving this distinction underexamined. EffiBench-X introduces a large-scale benchmark specifically for evaluating the efficiency of language-model-generated code across multiple languages.

The benchmark includes competitive programming tasks in Python, C++, Java, JavaScript, Ruby, and Go. Human-expert solutions provide the efficiency reference for each task. This design makes it possible to examine both the gap between generated and expert code and how that gap changes with the programming language, instead of treating performance in one language as representative of all six.

The evaluated models frequently produce correct programs but consistently trail human experts in efficiency. Even the strongest reported results, including Qwen3-32B, reach only about 62% of human efficiency on average. Models tend to fare better in Python, Ruby, and JavaScript than in Java, C++, and Go. These findings motivate optimization-focused research alongside continued improvements in functional correctness.
summary.tldr: EffiBench-X finds that functionally correct model-generated code still falls short of expert efficiency across six programming languages.

title: EffiBench-X: A Multi-Language Benchmark for Measuring Efficiency of LLM-Generated Code

abstract: Generalizing to complex and temporally extended task objectives and safety constraints remains a critical challenge in reinforcement learning (RL). Linear temporal logic (LTL) offers a unified formalism to specify such requirements, yet existing methods are limited in their abilities to handle nested long-horizon tasks and safety constraints, and cannot identify situations when a subgoal is not satisfiable and an alternative should be sought. In this paper, we introduce GenZ-LTL, a method that enables zero-shot generalization to arbitrary LTL specifications. GenZ-LTL leverages the structure of Büchi automata to decompose an LTL task specification into sequences of reach-avoid subgoals. Contrary to the current state-of-the-art method that conditions on subgoal sequences, we show that it is more effective to achieve zero-shot generalization by solving these reach-avoid problems $\textit{one subgoal at a time}$ through proper safe RL formulations. In addition, we introduce a novel subgoal-induced observation reduction technique that can mitigate the exponential complexity of subgoal-state combinations under realistic assumptions. Empirical results show that GenZ-LTL substantially outperforms existing methods in zero-shot generalization to unseen LTL specifications.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning tasks can require sequences of achievements while imposing safety constraints throughout execution. Linear temporal logic provides a formal language for these requirements, but nested and long-horizon specifications are difficult to generalize to. GenZ-LTL addresses zero-shot execution of new specifications by breaking them into smaller decisions.

The method uses Büchi automata to turn a specification into sequences of reach-avoid subgoals. Each subgoal combines something to reach with something to avoid. The authors show that solving these problems individually through suitable safe reinforcement-learning formulations is more effective for zero-shot generalization than conditioning on an entire sequence of subgoals.

GenZ-LTL also reduces observations according to the current subgoal. Under realistic assumptions, this can mitigate the exponential growth in combinations of subgoals and states. Experiments report substantial improvements over existing methods on previously unseen temporal-logic specifications. The findings support a modular strategy: exploit the formal structure of a complex requirement, then focus the learned controller on one appropriately formulated subproblem at a time.
summary.tldr: GenZ-LTL improves zero-shot generalization to temporal-logic tasks by decomposing them into reach-avoid problems solved one subgoal at a time.

title: One Subgoal at a Time: Zero-Shot Generalization to Arbitrary Linear Temporal Logic Requirements in Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The convergence of graph learning and multi-view learning has propelled the emergence of multi-view graph neural networks (MGNNs), offering unprecedented capabilities to address complex real-world data characterized by heterogeneous yet interconnected information. While existing MGNNs exploit the potential of multi-view graphs, they often fail to harmonize the dual inductive biases critical to multi-view learning: consistency (inherent inter-view agreement) and complementarity (view-specific distinctiveness). To bridge this gap, we propose Multi-view Collaborative Graph Experts (MvCGE), a novel framework grounded in the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) paradigm. MvCGE establishes architectural consistency through shared parameters while preserving complementarity via layer-wise collaborative graph experts, which are dynamically activated by a graph-aware routing mechanism that adapts to the structural nuances of each view. This dual-level design is further reinforced by two novel components: a load equilibrium loss to prevent expert collapse and ensure balanced specialization, and a graph discrepancy loss based on distributional divergence to enhance inter-view complementarity. Extensive experiments on diverse datasets demonstrate MvCGE’s superiority.
