paragraphs: Multi-view graph learning combines interconnected information represented through different views. The paper focuses on balancing two useful properties: agreement between views and information that is distinctive to each view. It argues that existing multi-view graph neural networks often do not coordinate these properties effectively.

Multi-view Collaborative Graph Experts, or MvCGE, uses a mixture-of-experts architecture to address that balance. Shared parameters establish consistency across views, while collaborative experts at each layer preserve view-specific information. A graph-aware routing mechanism dynamically activates experts according to the structural characteristics of each view. This makes expert participation responsive to the graph being processed.

Two training objectives reinforce the architecture. A load equilibrium loss is designed to prevent expert collapse and promote balanced specialization, while a graph discrepancy loss based on distributional divergence encourages complementarity between views. Experiments on diverse datasets report superior performance. The findings support coordinating shared representations with structurally informed expert specialization so that the model can use both cross-view agreement and distinctive information.
summary.tldr: MvCGE combines shared parameters and dynamically routed graph experts to balance agreement and distinctive information across graph views.

title: Where Graph Meets Heterogeneity: Multi-View Collaborative Graph Experts

abstract: We propose an algorithm with improved query-complexity for the problem of hypothesis selection under local differential privacy constraints. Given a set of $k$ probability distributions $Q$, we describe an algorithm that satisfies local differential privacy, performs $\tilde{O}(k^{3/2})$ non-adaptive queries to individuals who each have samples from a probability distribution $p$, and outputs a probability distribution from the set $Q$ which is nearly the closest to $p$. Previous algorithms required either $\Omega(k^2)$ queries or many rounds of interactive queries. Technically, we introduce a new object we dub the Scheff\'e graph, which captures structure of the differences between distributions in $Q$, and may be of more broad interest for hypothesis selection tasks.

Given a set of $k$ probability distributions $Q$, we describe an algorithm that satisfies local differential privacy, performs $\tilde{O}(k^{3/2})$ non-adaptive queries to individuals who each have samples from a probability distribution $p$, and outputs a probability distribution from the set $Q$ which is nearly the closest to $p$. paragraphs: Hypothesis selection asks which candidate probability distribution best matches the distribution that produced observed samples. This paper studies the task under local differential privacy, where queries to individuals must satisfy privacy constraints. Given k candidates, the goal is to return one nearly as close to the underlying distribution as the best available candidate.

The proposed algorithm uses approximately k to the three-halves non-adaptive queries, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Non-adaptive queries can be specified without choosing later questions based on earlier answers. Previous approaches required either at least quadratic query counts or many rounds of interactive querying, creating a tradeoff between query volume and interaction.

The technical tool is the Scheffé graph, which records structure in the differences between candidate distributions. Using that structure enables the improved query bound while retaining local privacy and near-best hypothesis selection. The authors suggest that this graph may also prove useful for other hypothesis-selection tasks. That broader relevance remains a possibility, while the demonstrated contribution is the more query-efficient, non-adaptive private selection algorithm.
summary.tldr: The Scheffé graph enables locally private hypothesis selection with roughly k to the three-halves non-adaptive queries.

title: Query-Efficient Locally Private Hypothesis Selection via the Scheffe Graph

abstract: Spatial Planning is a crucial part in the field of spatial intelligence, which requires the understanding and planning about object arrangements in space perspective. AI agents with the spatial planning ability can better adapt to various real-world applications, including robotic manipulation, automatic assembly, urban planning etc. Recent works have attempted to construct benchmarks for evaluating the spatial intelligence of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Nevertheless, these benchmarks primarily focus on spatial reasoning based on typical Visual Question-Answering (VQA) forms, which suffers from the gap between abstract spatial understanding and concrete task execution. In this work, we take a step further to build a comprehensive benchmark called MineAnyBuild, aiming to evaluate the spatial planning ability of open-world AI agents in the Minecraft game. Specifically, MineAnyBuild requires an agent to generate executable architecture building plans based on the given multi-modal human instructions. It involves 4,000 curated spatial planning tasks and also provides a paradigm for infinitely expandable data collection by utilizing rich player-generated content. MineAnyBuild evaluates spatial planning through four core supporting dimensions: spatial understanding, spatial reasoning, creativity, and spatial commonsense. Based on MineAnyBuild, we perform a comprehensive evaluation for existing MLLM-based agents, revealing the severe limitations but enormous potential in their spatial planning abilities. We believe our MineAnyBuild will open new avenues for the evaluation of spatial intelligence and help promote further development for open-world AI agents capable of spatial planning.

paragraphs: Understanding where objects belong is only part of spatial intelligence; an agent also needs to turn that understanding into an executable plan. MineAnyBuild evaluates this step through architectural building tasks in Minecraft. It targets the gap between answering spatial questions and planning concrete actions from human instructions that can combine multiple modalities.

The benchmark contains 4,000 curated spatial planning tasks. Agents must generate building plans that can actually be executed, with evaluation covering spatial understanding, spatial reasoning, creativity, and spatial commonsense. The authors also propose a data collection approach based on player-generated content, providing a route to continually expanding the task collection.

An evaluation of existing multimodal language model agents reveals severe limitations in their spatial planning abilities, alongside substantial potential for improvement. The benchmark's contribution is to make executable planning central to spatial evaluation. It provides a setting where interpreting an instruction and arranging a structure must connect through a usable plan, allowing future work to assess progress beyond question-answering performance.
summary.tldr: MineAnyBuild tests whether multimodal agents can turn human instructions into executable Minecraft building plans across 4,000 spatial planning tasks.

title: MineAnyBuild: Benchmarking Spatial Planning for Open-world AI Agents

abstract: We present a theoretical framework showing that popular LLM alignment methods—including RLHF and its variants—can be understood as divergence estimators between aligned (safe or preferred) and unaligned (harmful or less-preferred) distributions. This perspective explains the emergence of separation in the latent space between safe and harmful prompts after alignment. As an application of our general divergence framework, we propose KLDO, a novel KL divergence-based alignment method, and empirically validate its effectiveness. We further show that using compliance–refusal datasets, rather than standard preference-based datasets, leads to stronger separation and improved safety alignment. Finally, to quantify the separation effect, we propose a distance-based metric in the prompt representation space, which also acts as a statistically significant indicator for model safety.

paragraphs: Safety alignment changes how a language model responds to preferred and harmful inputs, but different alignment methods can appear to have separate mathematical foundations. This paper offers a common framework: popular approaches, including reinforcement learning from human feedback and its variants, can be interpreted as estimating divergence between aligned and unaligned distributions.

Divergence measures how distributions differ. Through this perspective, the authors explain why representations of safe and harmful prompts become separated in a model’s latent space after alignment. They use the framework to develop KLDO, an alignment method based on KL divergence, and provide empirical evidence of its effectiveness. The theory therefore motivates a concrete training approach.

The paper also finds that compliance–refusal datasets produce stronger separation and better safety alignment than standard preference datasets. To measure this effect, it introduces a distance-based statistic in the space of prompt representations. That statistic is a statistically significant indicator of model safety. Together, these results connect alignment objectives, training-data choices, and internal representations within one theoretical account.
summary.tldr: A divergence-estimation view of alignment explains representation separation and motivates a new method, dataset choice, and safety indicator.

title: LLM Safety Alignment is Divergence Estimation in Disguise

abstract: Recent works have introduced new equivariant neural networks, motivated by their improved generalization compared to traditional deep neural networks. While experiments support this advantage, the theoretical understanding of their generalization properties remains limited. In this paper, we analyze the generalization capabilities of Group Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) with the ReLU activation function through the lens of Vapnik-Chervonenkis (VC) dimension theory. We investigate how architectural factors—such as the number of layers, weights, and input dimensions—affect the VC dimension. A key challenge in our analysis is proving a lower bound on the VC dimension, for which we introduce new techniques, establishing a novel connection between GCNNs and standard deep neural networks. Additionally, we compare our derived bounds to those known for fully connected neural networks. Our results extend previous findings on the VC dimension of continuous GCNNs with two layers, offering new insights into their generalization behavior, particularly their dependence on input resolution.

paragraphs: Equivariant neural networks have shown empirical generalization advantages, but explaining those advantages theoretically remains difficult. This paper studies group convolutional neural networks with ReLU activations through VC dimension, a measure of a model class's capacity to represent classification patterns. The goal is to connect architectural choices with theoretical understanding of generalization.

The analysis examines how depth, the number of weights, and input dimensionality affect VC dimension. Establishing a lower bound is a central technical challenge. To address it, the authors develop techniques that reveal a connection between group convolutional networks and standard deep neural networks. They also compare their resulting bounds with known bounds for fully connected architectures.

The results extend earlier work on continuous group convolutional networks restricted to two layers. A particular focus is how capacity depends on input resolution, making the analysis relevant to understanding what changes when a network receives more detailed inputs. The contribution supplies architectural capacity bounds and new proof techniques, rather than an experimental demonstration that every group convolutional network generalizes better.
summary.tldr: The paper derives VC-dimension bounds for deep ReLU group convolutional networks, examining dependence on architecture and input resolution.

title: On the VC dimension of deep group convolutional neural networks

abstract: Chemical reaction prediction remains a fundamental challenge in organic chemistry, where existing machine learning models face two critical limitations: sensitivity to input permutations (molecule/atom orderings) and inadequate modeling of substructural interactions governing reactivity. These shortcomings lead to inconsistent predictions and poor generalization to real-world scenarios. To address these challenges, we propose ReaDISH, a novel reaction prediction model that learns permutation-invariant representations while incorporating interaction-aware features. It introduces two innovations: (1) symmetric difference shingle encoding, which computes molecular shingle differences to capture reaction-specific structural changes while eliminating order sensitivity; and (2) geometry-structure interaction attention, a mechanism that models intra- and inter-molecular interactions at the shingle level. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ReaDISH improves reaction prediction performance across diverse benchmarks. It shows enhanced robustness with an average improvement of 8.76\% on R$^2$ under permutation perturbations.

paragraphs: Chemical reaction predictors should respond to molecular structure rather than arbitrary choices about how atoms or molecules are ordered in the input. Existing models can be sensitive to those orderings and can also inadequately represent interactions between molecular substructures. ReaDISH addresses both issues by combining order-independent representations with explicit interaction modeling.

Its symmetric difference shingle encoding compares sets of molecular substructural pieces to capture changes specific to a reaction. Because the representation is built to be permutation invariant, reordering the input does not change the encoded representation. A second mechanism, geometry-structure interaction attention, models relationships between shingles both within a molecule and across molecules.

These components serve complementary purposes: the encoding removes an irrelevant source of variation, while attention represents interactions relevant to reactivity. Experiments report improved reaction prediction across diverse benchmarks. Under permutation perturbations, the authors report an average 8.76% improvement in R², supporting enhanced robustness to reordered inputs. The findings connect representation design with more consistent predictions and improved benchmark performance, addressing the two weaknesses that motivate the method.
summary.tldr: ReaDISH combines order-invariant molecular encoding with interaction attention to improve reaction prediction and robustness to input reordering.

title: Reaction Prediction via Interaction Modeling of Symmetric Difference Shingle Sets

abstract: Institutions with limited data and computing resources often outsource model training to third-party providers in a semi-honest setting, assuming adherence to prescribed training protocols with pre-defined learning paradigm (e.g., supervised or semi-supervised learning). However, this practice can introduce severe security risks, as adversaries may poison the training data to embed backdoors into the resulting model. Existing detection approaches predominantly rely on statistical analyses, which often fail to maintain universally accurate detection accuracy across different learning paradigms. To address this challenge, we propose a unified backdoor detection framework in the semi-honest setting that exploits cross-examination of model inconsistencies between two independent service providers. Specifically, we integrate central kernel alignment to enable robust feature similarity measurements across different model architectures and learning paradigms, thereby facilitating precise recovery and identification of backdoor triggers. We further introduce backdoor fine-tuning sensitivity analysis to distinguish backdoor triggers from adversarial perturbations, substantially reducing false positives. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves superior detection performance, improving accuracy by 4.4%, 1.7%, and 10.6% over SoTA baselines across supervised, semi-supervised, and autoregressive learning tasks, respectively. Notably, it is the first to effectively detect backdoors in multimodal large language models, further highlighting its broad applicability and advancing secure deep learning.

paragraphs: Outsourcing model training can expose an institution to backdoors inserted through poisoned training data. This paper studies a semi-honest setting in which providers are assumed to follow prescribed training protocols. Its detection strategy cross-examines models from two independent service providers, looking for inconsistencies that can reveal hidden trigger-dependent behavior across different learning paradigms.

Those comparisons support the recovery and identification of candidate backdoor triggers. It then analyzes sensitivity to fine-tuning to distinguish backdoor triggers from adversarial perturbations, reducing false positives caused by confusing these two kinds of model vulnerability.

The authors report detection accuracy improvements of 4.4%, 1.7%, and 10.6% over state-of-the-art baselines in supervised, semi-supervised, and autoregressive tasks, respectively. They also report effective backdoor detection in multimodal large language models. The approach's broad applicability comes from combining cross-provider comparisons with a second test of trigger behavior, within the stated outsourced-training setting.
summary.tldr: Lie Detector compares independently trained models and tests fine-tuning sensitivity to identify backdoors across several learning paradigms.

title: Lie Detector: Unified Backdoor Detection via Cross-Examination Framework

abstract: Data arrives at our senses as a continuous stream, smoothly transforming from one instant to the next. These smooth transformations can be viewed as continuous symmetries of the environment that we inhabit, defining equivalence relations between stimuli over time. In machine learning, neural network architectures that respect symmetries of their data are called equivariant and have provable benefits in terms of generalization ability and sample efficiency. To date, however, equivariance has been considered only for static transformations and feed-forward networks, limiting its applicability to sequence models, such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs), and corresponding time-parameterized sequence transformations. In this work, we extend equivariant network theory to this regime of 'flows' -- one-parameter Lie subgroups capturing natural transformations over time, such as visual motion. We begin by showing that standard RNNs are generally not flow equivariant: their hidden states fail to transform in a geometrically structured manner for moving stimuli. We then show how flow equivariance can be introduced, and demonstrate that these models significantly outperform their non-equivariant counterparts in terms of training speed, length generalization, and velocity generalization, on both next step prediction and sequence classification. We present this work as a first step towards building sequence models that respect the time-parameterized symmetries which govern the world around us.

This paper extends that idea to transformations unfolding continuously over time, such as visual motion. These transformations are described as flows, mathematically represented by one-parameter Lie subgroups, and require attention to how a sequence evolves.

The authors first show that ordinary recurrent neural networks generally lack flow equivariance. When a stimulus moves, their hidden states need not change in a way that respects the geometry of that motion. They then show how to introduce flow equivariance into recurrent models, extending symmetry-aware network theory beyond static transformations and feed-forward architectures.

These findings support encoding time-dependent symmetry directly in a sequence model. The work is presented as an initial step toward models whose internal dynamics respect continuous transformations in their inputs, with benefits demonstrated on the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: Flow-equivariant recurrent networks respect continuous transformations over time and improve training speed and length and velocity generalization in the reported experiments.

title: Flow Equivariant Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: Recent advancements in omnimodal learning have significantly improved understanding and generation across images, text, and speech, yet these developments remain predominantly confined to proprietary models. The lack of high-quality omnimodal datasets and the challenges of real-time emotional speech synthesis have notably hindered progress in open-source research. To address these limitations, we introduce OpenOmni, a two-stage training framework that integrates omnimodal alignment and speech generation to develop a state-of-the-art omnimodal large language model. In the alignment phase, a pretrained speech model undergoes further training on image-text tasks, enabling (near) zero-shot generalization from vision to speech, outperforming models trained on tri-modal datasets. In the speech generation phase, a lightweight decoder is trained on speech tasks with direct preference optimization, which enables real-time emotional speech synthesis with high fidelity. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OpenOmni surpasses state-of-the-art models across omnimodal, vision-language, and speech-language benchmarks. It achieves a 4-point absolute improvement on OmniBench over the leading open-source model VITA, despite using 5$\times$ fewer training examples and a smaller model size (7B vs. 7$\times$8B). Besides, OpenOmni achieves real-time speech generation with less than 1 second latency at non-autoregressive mode, reducing inference time by 5$\times$ compared to autoregressive methods, and improves emotion classification accuracy by 7.7\%. The codebase is available at https://github.com/RainBowLuoCS/OpenOmni.

title: OpenOmni: Advancing Open-Source Omnimodal Large Language Models with Progressive Multimodal Alignment and Real-time Emotional Speech Synthesis

abstract: A fine-grained account of functional selectivity in the cortex is essential for understanding how visual information is processed and represented in the brain. Classical studies using designed experiments have identified multiple category-selective regions; however, these approaches rely on preconceived hypotheses about categories. Subsequent data-driven discovery methods have sought to address this limitation but are often limited by simple, typically linear encoding models. We propose an in silico approach for data-driven discovery of novel category-selectivity hypotheses based on an encoder–decoder transformer model. The architecture incorporates a brain-region to image-feature cross-attention mechanism, enabling nonlinear mappings between high-dimensional deep network features and semantic patterns encoded in the brain activity. We further introduce a method to characterize the selectivity of individual parcels by leveraging diffusion-based image generative models and large-scale datasets to synthesize and select images that maximally activate each parcel. Our approach reveals regions with complex, compositional selectivity involving diverse semantic concepts, which we validate in silico both within and across subjects. Using a brain encoder as a “digital twin” offers a powerful, data-driven framework for generating and testing hypotheses about visual selectivity in the human brain—hypotheses that can guide future fMRI experiments. Our code is available at: https://kriegeskorte-lab.github.io/in-silico-mapping-web/.

paragraphs: Discovering what visual content different brain regions respond to can be constrained by the categories researchers choose to test. This paper develops a computational approach for generating new hypotheses about visual selectivity from data. It also addresses the limited expressiveness of earlier discovery methods that rely on simple, often linear models of brain responses.

An encoder–decoder transformer uses cross-attention between brain regions and image features to learn nonlinear relationships between visual representations and brain activity. The authors then combine diffusion-based image generation with large image datasets to synthesize and select images predicted to activate individual brain parcels most strongly. These images help characterize the semantic content associated with each parcel.

The approach identifies regions with selectivity for complex combinations of semantic concepts, and the authors validate those patterns computationally within and across subjects. The brain encoder functions as a digital model for exploring hypotheses about responses. The stated findings are in silico results intended to guide future fMRI experiments, providing a way to propose and computationally test richer categories before experimental investigation.
summary.tldr: A transformer brain model and generated images reveal computational hypotheses about complex visual selectivity that could guide future fMRI experiments.

title: In Silico Mapping of Visual Categorical Selectivity Across the Whole Brain

abstract: We introduce FlexOLMo, a new class of language models (LMs) that supports (1) distributed training without data sharing, where different model parameters are independently trained on private datasets, and (2) data-flexible inference, where these parameters along with their associated data can be easily included or excluded from model inferences with no further training. FlexOLMo employs a mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture where each expert is trained independently on private datasets and later integrated through a new nonparametric routing without any joint training across datasets. FlexOLMo is trained on FLEXMIX, a corpus we curate comprising seven restricted sets, either real or realistic approximations, alongside publicly available datasets. We evaluate models with up to 37 billion parameters (20 billion active) on 31 diverse downstream tasks. We show that a general expert trained on public data can be effectively combined with independently trained experts from other data owners significantly benefiting from these restricted sets (an average 41% relative improvement) while allowing flexible opt-out at inference time (e.g., for users without appropriate licenses or permissions). Our approach also outperforms prior model merging methods by 10.1% on average and surpasses the standard MoE trained without data restrictions using the same training FLOPs. Altogether, FlexOLMo enables training on restricted data while keeping data local and supports fine-grained control of data access at inference.

paragraphs: FlexOLMo addresses a practical problem: organizations may want language models to benefit from restricted datasets while retaining control over their use. It supports independent training on private data and lets the resulting model components be included or excluded during inference without further training. This connects data access decisions to which experts participate in a response.

The architecture is a mixture of experts. Each expert learns separately from its owner's dataset, and a nonparametric routing method combines the experts without joint training across datasets. A general expert trained on public data provides a component that can be combined with these independently trained specialists.

The authors evaluate models with up to 37 billion parameters, including 20 billion active parameters, across 31 tasks. They report an average 41% relative improvement from incorporating restricted-data experts and a 10.1% average advantage over earlier model-merging methods. FlexOLMo also exceeds a standard mixture of experts at the same training compute. These findings support modular data use alongside inference-time opt-outs for access or licensing needs.
summary.tldr: FlexOLMo combines independently trained experts while allowing their associated data contributions to be included or excluded at inference time.

title: FlexOLMo: Open Language Models for Flexible Data Use

abstract: Estimators in statistics and machine learning must typically trade off between efficiency, having low variance for a fixed target, and distributional robustness, such as \textit{multiaccuracy}, or having low bias over a range of possible targets. In this paper, we consider a simple estimator, \emph{ridge boosting}: starting with any initial predictor, perform a single boosting step with (kernel) ridge regression. Surprisingly, we show that ridge boosting simultaneously achieves both efficiency and distributional robustness: for target distribution shifts that lie within an RKHS unit ball, this estimator maintains low bias across all such shifts and has variance at the semiparametric efficiency bound for each target. In addition to bridging otherwise distinct research areas, this result has immediate practical value. Since ridge boosting uses only data from the source distribution, researchers can train a single model to obtain both robust and efficient estimates for multiple target estimands at the same time, eliminating the need to fit separate semiparametric efficient estimators for each target. We assess this approach through simulations and an application estimating the age profile of retirement income.

paragraphs: Statistical estimators often face a trade-off between low variance for a particular target and low bias across several possible targets. This paper studies a simple procedure called ridge boosting: begin with any predictor and apply one boosting step using ridge regression, potentially with a kernel. The surprising result is that this procedure can achieve both objectives within a specified family of distribution shifts.

The guarantee applies to target shifts lying in the unit ball of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. Across these shifts, ridge boosting maintains low bias and achieves variance at the semiparametric efficiency bound for each target. The restriction on the shift family is central to the stated robustness result.

Because the procedure uses only source-distribution data, a single fitted model can support robust and efficient estimation of multiple target quantities. This avoids fitting a separate efficient estimator for each target within the covered setting. The authors assess the method through simulations and an application estimating how retirement income varies with age, connecting the theoretical result to a practical estimation problem.
summary.tldr: One ridge-regression boosting step achieves low bias and efficient variance across target shifts within an RKHS unit ball.

title: Ridge Boosting is Both Robust and Efficient

abstract: Online social media provide a platform for people to discuss current events and exchange opinions with their peers. While interactions are predominantly positive, in recent years, there has been a lot of research to understand the conflicts in social networks and how they are based on different views and opinions. In this paper, we ask whether the conflicts in a network reveal a small and interpretable set of prevalent opinion ranges that explain the users' interactions. More precisely, we consider signed graphs, where the edge signs indicate positive and negative interactions of node pairs, and our goal is to infer opinion intervals that are consistent with the edge signs. We introduce an optimization problem that models this question, and we give strong hardness results and a polynomial-time approximation scheme by utilizing connections to interval graphs and the Correlation Clustering problem. We further provide scalable heuristics and show that in experiments they yield more expressive solutions than Correlation Clustering baselines. We also present a case study on a novel real-world dataset from the German parliament, showing that our algorithms can recover the political leaning of German parties based on co-voting behavior.

paragraphs: Positive and negative interactions in a network may reveal underlying differences in opinion. This paper asks whether those interactions can be explained by a small, interpretable collection of opinion ranges. Its input is a signed graph: nodes represent participants, and edge signs record positive or negative relationships between pairs.

The authors formulate an optimization problem that seeks opinion intervals consistent with those signs. This supports the idea that signed relationships can reveal interpretable opinion structure. The interval formulation provides a way to describe ranges of opinion while grounding the explanation in the observed pattern of agreement and conflict.
summary.tldr: The paper infers interpretable opinion intervals from positive and negative network interactions using approximation algorithms and scalable heuristics.

title: Discovering Opinion Intervals from Conflicts in Signed Graphs

abstract: Leveraging the coherent exploration of Hamiltonian flow, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo produces computationally efficient Monte Carlo estimators, even with respect to complex and high-dimensional target distributions. When confronted with data-intensive applications, however, the algorithm may be too expensive to implement, leaving us to consider the utility of approximations such as data subsampling. In this paper I demonstrate how data subsampling fundamentally compromises the scalability of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo.
originalAbstract: Leveraging the coherent exploration of Hamiltonian flow, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo produces computationally efficient Monte Carlo estimators, even with respect to complex and high-dimensional target distributions. When confronted with data-intensive applications, however, the algorithm may be too expensive to implement, leaving us to consider the utility of approximations such as data subsampling. In this paper I demonstrate how data subsampling fundamentally compromises the scalability of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo.

paragraphs: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo uses coherent Hamiltonian motion to explore a target distribution and construct Monte Carlo estimates. The abstract emphasizes that this can remain computationally efficient even for complicated, high-dimensional targets. Its usefulness therefore depends on how effectively the exploration produces estimates, alongside the computational cost of running it.

Large datasets can make the method too expensive, motivating approximations that use only subsets of the data. The paper examines this proposed shortcut and argues that naive data subsampling fundamentally compromises Hamiltonian Monte Carlo’s scalability. The issue is whether a cheaper approximation preserves the exploration behavior responsible for the original method’s efficiency.

The stated finding changes how the computational trade-off should be understood: reducing the data used by an approximation cannot by itself establish that the resulting sampler scales well. The paper’s contribution is an incompatibility argument concerning Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and naive subsampling. It directs attention to the relationship between approximation and coherent exploration when assessing whether a sampling method remains efficient for data-intensive problems.
summary.tldr: The paper argues that naive data subsampling undermines the coherent exploration underlying Hamiltonian Monte Carlo’s scalability.

title: The Fundamental Incompatibility of Scalable Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and Naive Data Subsampling

abstract: We study parameter estimation for sparse nonlinear regression. More specifically, we assume the data are given by y = f( \bf x^T \bf β^* ) + ε, where f is nonlinear. To recover \bf βs, we propose an \ell_1-regularized least-squares estimator. Unlike classical linear regression, the corresponding optimization problem is nonconvex because of the nonlinearity of f. In spite of the nonconvexity, we prove that under mild conditions, every stationary point of the objective enjoys an optimal statistical rate of convergence. Detailed numerical results are provided to back up our theory.

To recover \bf βs, we propose an \ell_1-regularized least-squares estimator. Unlike classical linear regression, the corresponding optimization problem is nonconvex because of the nonlinearity of f. In spite of the nonconvexity, we prove that under mild conditions, every stationary point of the objective enjoys an optimal statistical rate of convergence. Detailed numerical results are provided to back up our theory.

paragraphs: The paper studies regression in which an observation is a nonlinear function of a weighted combination of input features, plus noise. The unknown parameter vector is sparse, meaning only a limited set of its entries is nonzero. The goal is to recover that vector despite the nonlinear relationship between inputs and observations.

The authors propose least squares with an l1 penalty to encourage sparsity. Because the prediction passes through a nonlinear function, the resulting optimization problem is nonconvex. This creates a distinction between finding a globally optimal objective value and obtaining a statistically accurate estimate of the underlying parameters.

The main theorem shows that, under mild conditions, every stationary point of the objective achieves an optimal statistical convergence rate. The guarantee concerns estimation accuracy under those conditions; it does not assert that the objective becomes convex. Numerical results support the theoretical analysis. The contribution explains how nonconvex optimization can still yield statistically strong parameter estimates in this sparse nonlinear regression setting.
summary.tldr: Under mild conditions, every stationary point of an l1-regularized sparse nonlinear regression objective attains an optimal statistical convergence rate.

title: Sparse Nonlinear Regression: Parameter Estimation under Nonconvexity

abstract: We approach structured output prediction by optimizing a deep value network (DVN) to precisely estimate the task loss on different output configurations for a given input. Once the model is trained, we perform inference by gradient descent on the continuous relaxations of the output variables to find outputs with promising scores from the value network. When applied to image segmentation, the value network takes an image and a segmentation mask as inputs and predicts a scalar estimating the intersection over union between the input and ground truth masks. For multi-label classification, the DVN’s objective is to correctly predict the F1 score for any potential label configuration. The DVN framework achieves the state-of-the-art results on multi-label prediction and image segmentation benchmarks.

Once the model is trained, we perform inference by gradient descent on the continuous relaxations of the output variables to find outputs with promising scores from the value network. When applied to image segmentation, the value network takes an image and a segmentation mask as inputs and predicts a scalar estimating the intersection over union between the input and ground truth masks. For multi-label classification, the DVN’s objective is to correctly predict the F1 score for any potential label configuration. The DVN framework achieves the state-of-the-art results on multi-label prediction and image segmentation benchmarks.

paragraphs: The paper approaches structured prediction by teaching a neural network to evaluate candidate answers. A deep value network receives an input together with a proposed output configuration and estimates its task-specific quality. This makes evaluating whole output configurations the central learned operation, allowing the model to judge how well their parts work together.

After training, the method searches for promising outputs through gradient descent on continuous relaxations of the output variables. The relaxation supplies a representation that gradient-based optimization can adjust. The trained value network then guides iterative changes to the candidate output using its predicted score.

For image segmentation, the network examines an image and proposed mask and estimates the mask’s intersection-over-union score against the ground truth. For multi-label classification, it learns to estimate the F1 score of candidate label configurations. The framework achieves state-of-the-art results on the reported benchmarks for both tasks, supporting learned evaluation as a useful guide for structured-output refinement.
summary.tldr: Deep value networks learn to score candidate structured outputs and guide their iterative refinement through gradient-based inference.

title: Deep Value Networks Learn to Evaluate and Iteratively Refine Structured Outputs

abstract: The design of neural architectures for structured objects is typically guided by experimental insights rather than a formal process. In this work, we appeal to kernels over combinatorial structures, such as sequences and graphs, to derive appropriate neural operations. We introduce a class of deep recurrent neural operations and formally characterize their associated kernel spaces. Our recurrent modules compare the input to virtual reference objects (cf. filters in CNN) via the kernels. Similar to traditional neural operations, these reference objects are parameterized and directly optimized in end-to-end training. We empirically evaluate the proposed class of neural architectures on standard applications such as language modeling and molecular graph regression, achieving state-of-the-art results across these applications.

In this work, we appeal to kernels over combinatorial structures, such as sequences and graphs, to derive appropriate neural operations. We introduce a class of deep recurrent neural operations and formally characterize their associated kernel spaces. Our recurrent modules compare the input to virtual reference objects (cf. filters in CNN) via the kernels. Similar to traditional neural operations, these reference objects are parameterized and directly optimized in end-to-end training. We empirically evaluate the proposed class of neural architectures on standard applications such as language modeling and molecular graph regression, achieving state-of-the-art results across these applications.

paragraphs: Sequences and graphs have structure that a neural architecture needs to handle. Architecture design often relies on experimental intuition about suitable operations. This paper develops a more formal route: start from kernels over structured objects and use them to derive neural operations appropriate for those objects.

The authors introduce deep recurrent operations and characterize their associated kernel spaces mathematically. Each recurrent module compares an input with virtual reference objects through a kernel. These reference objects play a role analogous to filters in convolutional networks: they are parameterized and learned directly through end-to-end training. The architecture therefore combines a kernel-based interpretation with adaptable neural components.

The proposed architectures are evaluated on language modeling and molecular graph regression, with results reported as state of the art across these applications. Those findings show that the formal construction can also produce competitive predictive models. The broader contribution is a connection between structured similarity functions and trainable recurrent operations, giving architecture design an explicit mathematical starting point.
summary.tldr: The paper derives trainable recurrent neural operations from sequence and graph kernels and reports strong results on both types of data.

title: Deriving Neural Architectures from Sequence and Graph Kernels

abstract: We propose a novel, efficient approach for distributed sparse learning with observations randomly partitioned across machines. In each round of the proposed method, worker machines compute the gradient of the loss on local data and the master machine solves a shifted $\ell_1$ regularized loss minimization problem. After a number of communication rounds that scales only logarithmically with the number of machines, and independent of other parameters of the problem, the proposed approach provably matches the estimation error bound of centralized methods.
originalAbstract: We propose a novel, efficient approach for distributed sparse learning with observations randomly partitioned across machines. In each round of the proposed method, worker machines compute the gradient of the loss on local data and the master machine solves a shifted $\ell_1$ regularized loss minimization problem. After a number of communication rounds that scales only logarithmically with the number of machines, and independent of other parameters of the problem, the proposed approach provably matches the estimation error bound of centralized methods.

paragraphs: Distributed sparse learning fits a model using observations held across multiple machines, while favoring solutions with relatively few active coefficients. The central question here is whether those machines can reach the statistical accuracy of a centralized method without requiring many rounds of communication. The paper studies observations randomly partitioned across machines.

Each round divides the work between workers and a master. Workers compute loss gradients using their local observations. The master then solves a shifted loss minimization problem with an ℓ1 penalty, which promotes sparsity. This arrangement combines information from local datasets through gradient computations and an updated optimization problem at the master.

The authors prove that the method matches the estimation error bound of centralized approaches after a number of communication rounds growing only logarithmically with the number of machines. That round count is independent of the other problem parameters in the stated result. The finding connects distributed computation with centralized statistical accuracy under the random-partition setting considered.
summary.tldr: With randomly partitioned observations, a distributed sparse-learning method matches centralized error bounds after logarithmically many communication rounds.

title: Efficient Distributed Learning with Sparsity

abstract: We focus on predicting sleep stages from radio measurements without any attached sensors on subjects. We introduce a new predictive model that combines convolutional and recurrent neural networks to extract sleep-specific subject-invariant features from RF signals and capture the temporal progression of sleep. A key innovation underlying our approach is a modified adversarial training regime that discards extraneous information specific to individuals or measurement conditions, while retaining all information relevant to the predictive task. We analyze our game theoretic setup and empirically demonstrate that our model achieves significant improvements over state-of-the-art solutions.
originalAbstract: We focus on predicting sleep stages from radio measurements without any attached sensors on subjects. We introduce a new predictive model that combines convolutional and recurrent neural networks to extract sleep-specific subject-invariant features from RF signals and capture the temporal progression of sleep. A key innovation underlying our approach is a modified adversarial training regime that discards extraneous information specific to individuals or measurement conditions, while retaining all information relevant to the predictive task. We analyze our game theoretic setup and empirically demonstrate that our model achieves significant improvements over state-of-the-art solutions.

paragraphs: The paper aims to predict sleep stages from radio measurements without attaching sensors to the person being monitored. Its modeling challenge includes extracting information about sleep while handling differences between individuals and measurement conditions. The proposed predictor combines convolutional and recurrent neural networks to address these aspects together.

The architecture extracts sleep-related features from radio signals and models how sleep progresses over time. Its key innovation is a modified adversarial training regime designed to discard information specific to a person or recording condition while retaining information relevant to sleep-stage prediction. This makes the desired representation both task-focused and invariant to the subject.

The authors analyze the adversarial interaction through a game-theoretic setup and report significant empirical improvements over state-of-the-art solutions. The findings support combining temporal modeling with a training objective that separates predictive information from extraneous variation. The contribution is a method for learning which aspects of radio measurements matter for sleep staging while reducing dependence on who was measured or under what conditions.
summary.tldr: A convolutional-recurrent model uses adversarial training to predict sleep stages from radio signals while removing subject- and condition-specific information.

title: Learning Sleep Stages from Radio Signals: A Conditional Adversarial Architecture

abstract: Many graph analytics problems can be solved via iterative algorithms where the solutions are often characterized by a set of steady-state conditions. Different algorithms respect to different set of fixed point constraints, so instead of using these traditional algorithms, can we learn an algorithm which can obtain the same steady-state solutions automatically from examples, in an effective and scalable way? How to represent the meta learner for such algorithm and how to carry out the learning? In this paper, we propose an embedding representation for iterative algorithms over graphs, and design a learning method which alternates between updating the embeddings and projecting them onto the steady-state constraints. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework using a few commonly used graph algorithms, and show that in some cases, the learned algorithm can handle graphs with more than 100,000,000 nodes in a single machine.

paragraphs: Many graph algorithms repeatedly update quantities until they reach a steady state. The desired solution can often be described by fixed-point conditions: relationships that hold once further updates no longer change the result. This paper investigates learning an algorithm from examples while retaining those conditions as a guide to the intended solution.

The authors propose an embedding representation for iterative graph algorithms. Their learning procedure alternates between updating the embeddings and projecting them onto steady-state constraints. This couples learning from examples with the mathematical relationships that characterize the output of the underlying graph computation.

The framework is evaluated using several commonly used graph algorithms. The authors demonstrate effectiveness and report that, in some cases, a learned algorithm can handle graphs exceeding 100 million nodes on one machine. That scale result is explicitly case-dependent. The broader contribution is a way to combine learned representations with fixed-point structure, connecting data-driven algorithm learning to the steady-state solutions that graph analytics seeks.
summary.tldr: A learned embedding framework uses steady-state constraints to solve graph problems, reaching graphs above 100 million nodes in some evaluated cases.

title: Learning Steady-States of Iterative Algorithms over Graphs

abstract: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) with attention mechanisms have obtained state-of-the-art results for many sequence processing tasks. Most of these models use a simple form of encoder with attention that looks over the entire sequence and assigns a weight to each token independently. We present a mechanism for focusing RNN encoders for sequence modelling tasks which allows them to attend to key parts of the input as needed. We formulate this using a multi-layer conditional hierarchical sequence encoder that reads in one token at a time and makes a discrete decision on whether the token is relevant to the context or question being asked. The discrete gating mechanism takes in the context embedding and the current hidden state as inputs and controls information flow into the layer above. We train it using policy gradient methods. We evaluate this method on several types of tasks with different attributes. First, we evaluate the method on synthetic tasks which allow us to evaluate the model for its generalization ability and probe the behavior of the gates in more controlled settings. We then evaluate this approach on large scale Question Answering tasks including the challenging MS MARCO and SearchQA tasks. Our models shows consistent improvements for both tasks over prior work and our baselines. It has also shown to generalize significantly better on synthetic tasks as compared to the baselines.

paragraphs: A sequence-processing model often needs different parts of an input depending on the question or context. This paper builds that dependency into a recurrent encoder. It starts from the observation that many attention-based systems examine the whole sequence and assign token weights independently, and proposes a mechanism that focuses information flow during encoding.

The encoder has multiple hierarchical layers and reads tokens one at a time. A discrete gate uses the context embedding and current hidden state to decide whether information is relevant enough to pass to the next layer. Policy-gradient methods train these gating decisions, making the selection process part of the learned model.

The authors use synthetic tasks to inspect gate behavior and test generalization under controlled conditions. They also evaluate large-scale question answering on MS MARCO and SearchQA, reporting consistent improvements over prior work and their baselines on both. The synthetic experiments show substantially better generalization than the baselines, supporting the usefulness of context-dependent selection in the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: Context-dependent discrete gates focus hierarchical RNN encoders and improve the reported question-answering and synthetic-task results.

title: Focused Hierarchical RNNs for Conditional Sequence Processing

abstract: How does missing data affect our ability to learn signal structures? It has been shown that learning signal structure in terms of principal components is dependent on the ratio of sample size and dimensionality and that a critical number of observations is needed before learning starts (Biehl and Mietzner, 1993). Here we generalize this analysis to include missing data. Probabilistic principal component analysis is regularly used for estimating signal structures in datasets with missing data. Our analytic result suggest that the effect of missing data is to effectively reduce signal-to-noise ratio rather than - as generally believed - to reduce sample size. The theory predicts a phase transition in the learning curves and this is indeed found both in simulation data and in real datasets.

paragraphs: Principal component analysis aims to recover signal structure from data, but successful recovery depends on how many observations are available relative to dimensionality. Prior analysis established a critical observation threshold before learning begins. This paper extends that analysis to missing data, focusing on probabilistic PCA as a method for estimating signal structure in incomplete datasets.

The analytic result suggests that missing entries act by lowering the effective signal-to-noise ratio. This differs from interpreting missingness simply as having fewer samples. The distinction changes how the loss of information is understood: the proposed account emphasizes weaker recoverable signal relative to noise within the analyzed learning problem.

The theory predicts a phase transition in learning curves, meaning a threshold separates different regimes of signal recovery. The authors observe this behavior in both simulations and real datasets. These findings support the analysis and its interpretation of missing data, while retaining the qualified claim that reduced signal-to-noise ratio explains the effect studied.
summary.tldr: The analysis suggests missing data weakens PCA’s effective signal-to-noise ratio and predicts a recovery threshold observed in experiments.

title: Phase transition in PCA with missing data: Reduced signal-to-noise ratio, not sample size!

abstract: Stochastic multi-armed bandits form a class of online learning problems that have important applications in online recommendation systems, adaptive medical treatment, and many others. Even though potential attacks against these learning algorithms may hijack their behavior, causing catastrophic loss in real-world applications, little is known about adversarial attacks on bandit algorithms. In this paper, we propose a framework of offline attacks on bandit algorithms and study convex optimization based attacks on several popular bandit algorithms. We show that the attacker can force the bandit algorithm to pull a target arm with high probability by a slight manipulation of the rewards in the data. Then we study a form of online attacks on bandit algorithms and propose an adaptive attack strategy against any bandit algorithm without the knowledge of the bandit algorithm. Our adaptive attack strategy can hijack the behavior of the bandit algorithm to suffer a linear regret with only a logarithmic cost to the attacker. Our results demonstrate a significant security threat to stochastic bandits.

paragraphs: Stochastic bandit algorithms learn which actions to choose from the rewards they observe. This makes reward data a potential route for manipulating future decisions. The paper studies that vulnerability through both offline poisoning of recorded rewards and online attacks that adapt as the learning process unfolds.

For the offline setting, the authors introduce an attack framework and study attacks formulated through convex optimization against several popular bandit algorithms. They show that small changes to rewards in the data can make an algorithm choose an attacker-selected arm with high probability. The result connects corruption of learning evidence to control over the learner’s behavior.

For the online setting, the authors propose an adaptive strategy that does not require knowledge of the bandit algorithm. In their attack framework, it can induce regret that grows linearly while the attacker’s cost grows only logarithmically. This mismatch means sustained damage to learning can require comparatively slow growth in attack expenditure, demonstrating a significant security concern for systems that trust observed rewards.
summary.tldr: Reward poisoning can steer stochastic bandits toward attacker-chosen actions and induce linear regret at logarithmic attack cost.

title: Data Poisoning Attacks on Stochastic Bandits

abstract: In federated learning problems, data is scattered across different servers and exchanging or pooling it is often impractical or prohibited. We develop a Bayesian nonparametric framework for federated learning with neural networks. Each data server is assumed to provide local neural network weights, which are modeled through our framework. We then develop an inference approach that allows us to synthesize a more expressive global network without additional supervision, data pooling and with as few as a single communication round. We then demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on federated learning problems simulated from two popular image classification datasets.

paragraphs: Federated learning addresses situations where data lives on separate servers and cannot easily be collected in one place. This paper asks how to build a global neural network from knowledge already represented in local networks. Its starting assumption is that each server supplies its neural network weights, giving the central learning procedure model information without pooling the underlying data.

The authors develop a Bayesian nonparametric framework for modeling those local weights and an inference procedure for synthesizing a more expressive global network. The synthesis requires no additional supervision and can operate with as few as one communication round. This makes communication requirements part of the contribution alongside the statistical approach to combining local models.

The paper demonstrates the approach on federated learning settings simulated from two image classification datasets. These experiments support the usefulness of constructing a shared model from local weights. The stated result is a way to combine distributed neural networks while avoiding data pooling, with the possibility of very limited communication.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian framework combines local neural network weights into a more expressive global network without pooling data, potentially using one communication round.

title: Bayesian Nonparametric Federated Learning of Neural Networks

abstract: Linear quadratic regulator (LQR) is one of the most popular frameworks to tackle continuous Markov decision process tasks. With its fundamental theory and tractable optimal policy, LQR has been revisited and analyzed in recent years, in terms of reinforcement learning scenarios such as the model-free or model-based setting. In this paper, we introduce the Structured Policy Iteration (S-PI) for LQR, a method capable of deriving a structured linear policy. Such a structured policy with (block) sparsity or low-rank can have significant advantages over the standard LQR policy: more interpretable, memory-efficient, and well-suited for the distributed setting. In order to derive such a policy, we first cast a regularized LQR problem when the model is known. Then, our Structured Policy Iteration (S-PI) algorithm, which takes a policy evaluation step and a policy improvement step in an iterative manner, can solve this regularized LQR efficiently. We further extend the S-PI algorithm to the model-free setting where a smoothing procedure is adopted to estimate the gradient. In both the known-model and model-free setting, we prove convergence analysis under the proper choice of parameters. Finally, the experiments demonstrate the advantages of S-PI in terms of balancing the LQR performance and level of structure by varying the weight parameter.

paragraphs: Linear quadratic regulation offers a well-established framework for continuous control. This paper asks how to learn a linear controller with additional structure, such as sparsity, block sparsity, or low rank. Such structure can make a policy easier to interpret, reduce its memory requirements, and support distributed use.

The authors formulate a regularized LQR problem when the system model is known. Structured Policy Iteration alternates policy evaluation with policy improvement to solve this problem efficiently. They also extend the algorithm to the model-free setting, using a smoothing procedure to estimate the gradient when direct access to the model is unavailable.

Convergence analyses cover both settings under appropriate parameter choices. This condition is part of the guarantee. Experiments vary the regularization weight to demonstrate how the method balances control performance against the degree of policy structure. The contribution gives a systematic way to pursue structured controllers while exposing that balance, rather than treating sparsity or low rank as a separate property added after optimizing control performance.
summary.tldr: Structured Policy Iteration learns sparse or low-rank LQR controllers, with conditional convergence guarantees in known-model and model-free settings.

title: Structured Policy Iteration for Linear Quadratic Regulator

abstract: Efficient exploration remains a challenging problem in reinforcement learning, especially for those tasks where rewards from environments are sparse. In this work, we introduce an exploration approach based on a novel implicit generative modeling algorithm to estimate a Bayesian uncertainty of the agent’s belief of the environment dynamics. Each random draw from our generative model is a neural network that instantiates the dynamic function, hence multiple draws would approximate the posterior, and the variance in the predictions based on this posterior is used as an intrinsic reward for exploration. We design a training algorithm for our generative model based on the amortized Stein Variational Gradient Descent. In experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this exploration algorithm in both pure exploration tasks and a downstream task, comparing with state-of-the-art intrinsic reward-based exploration approaches, including two recent approaches based on an ensemble of dynamic models. In challenging exploration tasks, our implicit generative model consistently outperforms competing approaches regarding data efficiency in exploration.

paragraphs: When rewards are sparse, a reinforcement learning agent needs another signal to guide exploration. This paper builds that signal from uncertainty about environment dynamics. Its approach uses an implicit generative model to represent a range of plausible explanations of how the environment changes in response to the agent's actions.

Each draw from the generator produces an entire neural network representing a dynamics function. Multiple draws approximate a Bayesian posterior over dynamics models. The agent compares their predictions and uses prediction variance as an intrinsic reward for exploration. The generator is trained through an algorithm based on amortized Stein Variational Gradient Descent.

The authors evaluate the method on pure exploration tasks and a downstream task, comparing it with leading intrinsic-reward approaches, including two methods using ensembles of dynamics models. On challenging exploration tasks, the proposed method consistently improves exploration data efficiency over the compared approaches. The results support using generated dynamics hypotheses to turn uncertainty into a useful guide for collecting experience.
summary.tldr: A generator of neural dynamics models supplies uncertainty-based exploration rewards that improve data efficiency in the reported tasks.

title: Implicit Generative Modeling for Efficient Exploration

abstract: Bandit learning algorithms typically involve the balance of exploration and exploitation. However, in many practical applications, worst-case scenarios needing systematic exploration are seldom encountered. In this work, we consider a smoothed setting for structured linear contextual bandits where the adversarial contexts are perturbed by Gaussian noise and the unknown parameter $\theta^*$ has structure, e.g., sparsity, group sparsity, low rank, etc. We propose simple greedy algorithms for both the single- and multi-parameter (i.e., different parameter for each context) settings and provide a unified regret analysis for $\theta^*$ with any assumed structure. The regret bounds are expressed in terms of geometric quantities such as Gaussian widths associated with the structure of $\theta^*$. We also obtain sharper regret bounds compared to earlier work for the unstructured $\theta^*$ setting as a consequence of our improved analysis. We show there is implicit exploration in the smoothed setting where a simple greedy algorithm works.

paragraphs: Bandit algorithms usually balance exploiting current knowledge against deliberately exploring alternatives. This paper studies a setting where useful exploration can arise implicitly. It assumes adversarial contexts are perturbed by Gaussian noise and that the unknown linear parameter has structure, such as sparsity, group sparsity, or low rank. The perturbation assumption is central to the analysis.

The authors propose simple greedy algorithms for both a shared-parameter setting and a setting with different parameters for different contexts. They develop a unified regret analysis that accommodates an assumed parameter structure. The bounds depend on geometric quantities, including Gaussian widths, which express how the structure enters the learning guarantee.

The improved analysis also gives sharper regret bounds for the unstructured case than earlier work. The main conclusion is that a greedy algorithm can work in this smoothed setting because the perturbed contexts supply implicit exploration. This explains why deliberate exploration need not always be essential under the stated conditions. It does not remove the role of exploration in arbitrary contexts; the result specifically depends on the analyzed smoothed model.
summary.tldr: Under Gaussian-perturbed contexts, greedy structured linear bandits benefit from implicit exploration and admit unified geometric regret bounds.

title: Structured Linear Contextual Bandits: A Sharp and Geometric Smoothed Analysis

abstract: We propose a novel variant of SGD customized for training network architectures that support anytime behavior: such networks produce a series of increasingly accurate outputs over time. Efficient architectural designs for these networks focus on re-using internal state; subnetworks must produce representations relevant for both imme- diate prediction as well as refinement by subse- quent network stages. We consider traditional branched networks as well as a new class of re- cursively nested networks. Our new optimizer, Orthogonalized SGD, dynamically re-balances task-specific gradients when training a multitask network. In the context of anytime architectures, this optimizer projects gradients from later out- puts onto a parameter subspace that does not in- terfere with those from earlier outputs. Experi- ments demonstrate that training with Orthogonal- ized SGD significantly improves generalization accuracy of anytime networks.

paragraphs: Anytime neural networks produce a sequence of predictions that become more accurate as computation continues. Efficient designs reuse internal representations across these stages. This creates a training challenge: a representation must support a useful prediction immediately while also providing information that later stages can refine into a better answer.

The paper introduces Orthogonalized SGD, an optimizer that dynamically rebalances gradients associated with different tasks or outputs. For anytime networks, it projects gradients from later outputs into a parameter subspace that does not interfere with gradients from earlier outputs. This directly addresses the relationship between early prediction and later refinement when multiple outputs depend on shared parameters.

The authors study traditional branched architectures and introduce recursively nested networks. Experiments show significant improvements in the generalization accuracy of anytime networks trained with Orthogonalized SGD. The contribution combines architectural exploration with a training rule tailored to shared computation, showing that managing interactions between output-specific gradients can improve the predictions these networks make on unseen data.
summary.tldr: Orthogonalized SGD manages gradient interference between early and later predictions to improve anytime neural networks.

title: Orthogonalized SGD and Nested Architectures for Anytime Neural Networks

abstract: This paper bridges discrete and continuous optimization approaches for decomposable submodular function minimization, in both the standard and parametric settings. We provide improved running times for this problem by reducing it to a number of calls to a maximum flow oracle. When each function in the decomposition acts on O(1) elements of the ground set V and is polynomially bounded, our running time is up to polylogarithmic factors equal to that of solving maximum flow in a sparse graph with O(|V|) vertices and polynomial integral capacities. We achieve this by providing a simple iterative method which can optimize to high precision any convex function defined on the submodular base polytope, provided we can efficiently minimize it on the base polytope corresponding to the cut function of a certain graph that we construct. We solve this minimization problem by lifting the solutions of a parametric cut problem, which we obtain via a new efficient combinatorial reduction to maximum flow. This reduction is of independent interest and implies some previously unknown bounds for the parametric minimum s,t-cut problem in multiple settings.

paragraphs: This paper studies minimizing a submodular function that is expressed as a sum of component functions. It connects discrete and continuous optimization by reducing the work to calls to a maximum flow solver. The resulting improvements cover both the standard problem and a parametric setting.

The strongest stated running-time comparison has explicit conditions: each component must involve only a constant number of ground-set elements and be polynomially bounded. Under these conditions, the runtime matches, up to polylogarithmic factors, maximum flow on a sparse graph with a number of vertices proportional to the ground-set size and polynomial integral capacities.

The construction uses an iterative method for high-precision convex optimization over a submodular base polytope, contingent on efficiently solving a related problem on a graph-cut base polytope. The authors obtain those solutions through parametric cuts and a new combinatorial reduction to maximum flow. This reduction also yields previously unknown bounds for parametric minimum cuts, giving it significance beyond the original decomposable minimization problem.
summary.tldr: New reductions to maximum flow improve decomposable submodular minimization and yield additional bounds for parametric minimum-cut problems.

title: Decomposable Submodular Function Minimization via Maximum Flow

abstract: The Stackelberg prediction game (SPG) has been extensively used to model the interactions between the learner and data provider in the training process of various machine learning algorithms. Particularly, SPGs played prominent roles in cybersecurity applications, such as intrusion detection, banking fraud detection, spam filtering, and malware detection. Often formulated as NP-hard bi-level optimization problems, it is generally computationally intractable to find global solutions to SPGs. As an interesting progress in this area, a special class of SPGs with the least squares loss (SPG-LS) have recently been shown polynomially solvable by a bisection method. However, in each iteration of this method, a semidefinite program (SDP) needs to be solved. The resulted high computational costs prevent its applications for large-scale problems. In contrast, we propose a novel approach that reformulates a SPG-LS as a single SDP of a similar form and the same dimension as those solved in the bisection method. Our SDP reformulation is, evidenced by our numerical experiments, orders of magnitude faster than the existing bisection method. We further show that the obtained SDP can be reduced to a second order cone program (SOCP). This allows us to provide real-time response to large-scale SPG-LS problems. Numerical results on both synthetic and real world datasets indicate that the proposed SOCP method is up to 20,000+ times faster than the state of the art.

paragraphs: Stackelberg prediction games model interactions between a learner and a data provider during training. These problems are often difficult bilevel optimizations, but a special class using least-squares loss admits a polynomial-time solution. The existing approach nevertheless requires solving a semidefinite program at every step of a bisection procedure, creating substantial computational overhead.

This paper reformulates the least-squares game as a single semidefinite program. Its form and dimension are similar to the programs repeatedly solved by the earlier method, but the reformulation removes the repeated sequence of solves. The authors then show that this program can be reduced further to a second-order cone program.

Experiments find the single-semidefinite-program formulation orders of magnitude faster than bisection. The second-order cone formulation produces reported speedups of up to more than 20,000 times over the state of the art on synthetic and real-world datasets, supporting real-time responses for large problems. These improvements apply to the least-squares subclass studied, rather than resolving the general difficulty of Stackelberg prediction games.
summary.tldr: New optimization reformulations greatly accelerate least-squares Stackelberg prediction games, with reported speedups exceeding 20,000 times in some experiments.

title: Fast Algorithms for Stackelberg Prediction Game with Least Squares Loss

abstract: As an important branch of weakly supervised learning, partial label learning deals with data where each instance is assigned with a set of candidate labels, whereas only one of them is true. Despite many methodology studies on learning from partial labels, there still lacks theoretical understandings of their risk consistent properties under relatively weak assumptions, especially on the link between theoretical results and the empirical choice of parameters. In this paper, we propose a family of loss functions named \textit{Leveraged Weighted} (LW) loss, which for the first time introduces the leverage parameter $\beta$ to consider the trade-off between losses on partial labels and non-partial ones. From the theoretical side, we derive a generalized result of risk consistency for the LW loss in learning from partial labels, based on which we provide guidance to the choice of the leverage parameter $\beta$. In experiments, we verify the theoretical guidance, and show the high effectiveness of our proposed LW loss on both benchmark and real datasets compared with other state-of-the-art partial label learning algorithms.
originalAbstract: As an important branch of weakly supervised learning, partial label learning deals with data where each instance is assigned with a set of candidate labels, whereas only one of them is true. In this paper, we propose a family of loss functions named \textit{Leveraged Weighted} (LW) loss, which for the first time introduces the leverage parameter $\beta$ to consider the trade-off between losses on partial labels and non-partial ones. From the theoretical side, we derive a generalized result of risk consistency for the LW loss in learning from partial labels, based on which we provide guidance to the choice of the leverage parameter $\beta$. In experiments, we verify the theoretical guidance, and show the high effectiveness of our proposed LW loss on both benchmark and real datasets compared with other state-of-the-art partial label learning algorithms.

paragraphs: In partial-label learning, each training example comes with several candidate labels, although only one is correct. Learning must therefore resolve ambiguity while building a useful classifier. This paper addresses the limited theoretical guidance for choosing losses and their parameters under relatively weak assumptions.
