This parameter balances losses associated with candidate labels against losses associated with labels outside the candidate set. They derive a generalized risk-consistency result and use it to guide the choice of β, linking the statistical analysis directly to an empirical tuning decision.

Experiments verify the proposed parameter guidance and show strong performance against existing partial-label methods on benchmark and real datasets. The contribution combines a loss design with a theoretical reason for adjusting its balance. The consistency statement belongs to the assumptions of the analysis; the abstract does not specify a universal parameter value suitable for every partial-label dataset.
summary.tldr: Leveraged Weighted loss connects a tunable balance in partial-label learning to risk-consistency theory and empirical performance.

title: Leveraged Weighted Loss for Partial Label Learning

abstract: In many machine learning problems, large-scale datasets have become the de-facto standard to train state-of-the-art deep networks at the price of heavy computation load. In this paper, we focus on condensing large training sets into significantly smaller synthetic sets which can be used to train deep neural networks from scratch with minimum drop in performance. Inspired from the recent training set synthesis methods, we propose Differentiable Siamese Augmentation that enables effective use of data augmentation to synthesize more informative synthetic images and thus achieves better performance when training networks with augmentations. Experiments on multiple image classification benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed method obtains substantial gains over the state-of-the-art, 7% improvements on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 datasets. We show with only less than 1% data that our method achieves 99.6%, 94.9%, 88.5%, 71.5% relative performance on MNIST, FashionMNIST, SVHN, CIFAR10 respectively. We also explore the use of our method in continual learning and neural architecture search, and show promising results.

paragraphs: Training deep networks on large datasets can be computationally expensive. This paper aims to replace a large training set with a much smaller collection of synthetic images that still supports training a network from scratch. The goal is to preserve as much predictive performance as possible while reducing the amount of training data.

The proposed Differentiable Siamese Augmentation makes data augmentation useful during the construction of those synthetic images. This matters because the condensed set must carry useful training information even when networks are subsequently trained with augmentations. The method therefore connects how the images are synthesized with how they will be used for learning.

Experiments report substantial gains over prior methods, including 7% improvements on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100. Using less than 1% of the data, the method achieves relative performance of 99.6% on MNIST, 94.9% on FashionMNIST, 88.5% on SVHN, and 71.5% on CIFAR10. These are relative-performance figures, not absolute accuracies. Applications to continual learning and architecture search also produce promising results.
summary.tldr: Differentiable Siamese Augmentation helps synthesize tiny training datasets that retain substantial predictive performance when used to train networks from scratch.

title: Dataset Condensation with Differentiable Siamese Augmentation

abstract: Large neural networks excel in many domains, but they are expensive to train and fine-tune. A popular approach to reduce their compute or memory requirements is to replace dense weight matrices with structured ones (e.g., sparse, low-rank, Fourier transform). These methods have not seen widespread adoption (1) in end-to-end training due to unfavorable efficiency–quality tradeoffs, and (2) in dense-to-sparse fine-tuning due to lack of tractable algorithms to approximate a given dense weight matrix. To address these issues, we propose a class of matrices (Monarch) that is hardware-efficient (they are parameterized as products of two block-diagonal matrices for better hardware utilization) and expressive (they can represent many commonly used transforms). Surprisingly, the problem of approximating a dense weight matrix with a Monarch matrix, though nonconvex, has an analytical optimal solution. These properties of Monarch matrices unlock new ways to train and fine-tune sparse and dense models. We empirically validate that Monarch can achieve favorable accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs in several end-to-end sparse training applications: speeding up ViT and GPT-2 training on ImageNet classification and Wikitext-103 language modeling by 2x with comparable model quality, and reducing the error on PDE solving and MRI reconstruction tasks by 40%. In sparse-to-dense training, with a simple technique called "reverse sparsification," Monarch matrices serve as a useful intermediate representation to speed up GPT-2 pretraining on OpenWebText by 2x without quality drop. The same technique brings 23% faster BERT pretraining than even the very optimized implementation from Nvidia that set the MLPerf 1.1 record. In dense-to-sparse fine-tuning, as a proof-of-concept, our Monarch approximation algorithm speeds up BERT fine-tuning on GLUE by 1.7x with comparable accuracy.

title: Monarch: Expressive Structured Matrices for Efficient and Accurate Training

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a powerful technique to train a model on a server with data from several clients in a privacy-preserving manner. FL incurs significant communication costs because it repeatedly transmits the model between the server and clients. Recently proposed algorithms quantize the model parameters to efficiently compress FL communication. We find that dynamic adaptations of the quantization level can boost compression without sacrificing model quality. We introduce DAdaQuant as a doubly-adaptive quantization algorithm that dynamically changes the quantization level across time and different clients. Our experiments show that DAdaQuant consistently improves client$\rightarrow$server compression, outperforming the strongest non-adaptive baselines by up to $2.8\times$.

paragraphs: Federated learning trains a shared model using data held by multiple clients, with communication between those clients and a server. Repeatedly exchanging model parameters can create a substantial communication burden. Quantization addresses this by representing parameters with fewer possible values, allowing the information sent during training to be compressed.

DAdaQuant makes the quantization level adaptive along two dimensions: it changes over the course of training and differs across clients. The central idea is that a single fixed compression setting need not be the best choice for every participant or every stage. The authors find that dynamically adjusting this setting can improve compression while preserving model quality.

In the reported experiments, DAdaQuant consistently improves compression for messages traveling from clients to the server. Its gains reach up to 2.8 times those of the strongest non-adaptive baselines. This result concerns the communication direction evaluated, and shows the practical value of treating quantization as a changing training decision rather than a fixed configuration.
summary.tldr: DAdaQuant adapts quantization across clients and training time, improving client-to-server compression by up to 2.8 times over non-adaptive baselines.

title: DAdaQuant: Doubly-adaptive quantization for communication-efficient Federated Learning

abstract: Reward signals in reinforcement learning are expensive to design and often require access to the true state which is not available in the real world. Common alternatives are usually demonstrations or goal images which can be labor-intensive to collect. On the other hand, text descriptions provide a general, natural, and low-effort way of communicating the desired task. However, prior works in learning text-conditioned policies still rely on rewards that are defined using either true state or labeled expert demonstrations. We use recent developments in building large-scale visuolanguage models like CLIP to devise a framework that generates the task reward signal just from goal text description and raw pixel observations which is then used to learn the task policy. We evaluate the proposed framework on control and robotic manipulation tasks. Finally, we distill the individual task policies into a single goal text conditioned policy that can generalize in a zero-shot manner to new tasks with unseen objects and unseen goal text descriptions.

paragraphs: Designing reinforcement-learning rewards can require access to a system’s true state, while collecting demonstrations or goal images can be labor-intensive. This paper investigates describing the desired task in ordinary text instead. Its framework uses large vision-language models such as CLIP to generate a reward signal from a goal description and raw image observations.

The generated reward is then used to train a policy for the task. This directly addresses the reward-specification stage: the task description and observed pixels provide the inputs for reward generation. The approach differs from earlier text-conditioned policy work discussed in the paper, where rewards still depended on true-state information or labeled expert demonstrations.

This combined policy can generalize without additional task-specific training to new tasks involving unseen objects and unseen goal descriptions. The work therefore connects language-based reward construction with a shared policy that supports the reported zero-shot generalization.
summary.tldr: Vision-language models turn goal text and pixels into rewards, enabling policies that can be distilled into a text-conditioned policy with zero-shot task generalization.

title: Zero-Shot Reward Specification via Grounded Natural Language

abstract: Designing protein sequences with a particular biological function is a long-lasting challenge for protein engineering. Recent advances in machine-learning-guided approaches focus on building a surrogate sequence-function model to reduce the burden of expensive in-lab experiments. In this paper, we study the exploration mechanism of model-guided sequence design. We leverage a natural property of protein fitness landscape that a concise set of mutations upon the wild-type sequence are usually sufficient to enhance the desired function. By utilizing this property, we propose Proximal Exploration (PEX) algorithm that prioritizes the evolutionary search for high-fitness mutants with low mutation counts. In addition, we develop a specialized model architecture, called Mutation Factorization Network (MuFacNet), to predict low-order mutational effects, which further improves the sample efficiency of model-guided evolution. In experiments, we extensively evaluate our method on a suite of in-silico protein sequence design tasks and demonstrate substantial improvement over baseline algorithms.

paragraphs: Model-guided protein design uses a learned relationship between sequence and function to reduce reliance on expensive laboratory experiments. This paper focuses on how to explore candidate sequences. It builds on the observation that a small set of changes to a wild-type sequence is usually sufficient to improve a desired function.

The proposed Proximal Exploration algorithm prioritizes high-fitness candidates with low mutation counts. This directs evolutionary search toward useful changes close to the starting sequence. The authors also introduce Mutation Factorization Network, a specialized prediction architecture for low-order mutational effects. Combining that predictor with the search strategy further improves the sample efficiency of model-guided evolution.

The method is evaluated across a suite of in-silico protein sequence design tasks, where it substantially improves over baseline algorithms. These results support a search strategy organized around relatively few mutations when the motivating landscape property is useful. The evidence concerns computational design tasks, and the paper’s premise is that small mutation sets are usually sufficient, rather than necessary or sufficient for every protein-design objective.
summary.tldr: PEX prioritizes high-fitness protein variants with few mutations, while MuFacNet predicts low-order mutation effects to improve sample efficiency in simulated design tasks.

title: Proximal Exploration for Model-guided Protein Sequence Design

abstract: We study the problem of $K$-armed dueling bandit for both stochastic and adversarial environments, where the goal of the learner is to aggregate information through relative preferences of pair of decision points queried in an online sequential manner. We first propose a novel reduction from any (general) dueling bandits to multi-armed bandits which allows us to improve many existing results in dueling bandits. In particular, we give the first best-of-both world result for the dueling bandits regret minimization problem —a unified framework that is guaranteed to perform optimally for both stochastic and adversarial preferences simultaneously. Moreover, our algorithm is also the first to achieve an optimal $O(\sum_{i = 1}^K \frac{\log T}{\Delta_i})$ regret bound against the Condorcet-winner benchmark, which scales optimally both in terms of the arm-size $K$ and the instance-specific suboptimality gaps $\{\Delta_i\}_{i = 1}^K$. This resolves the long standing problem of designing an instancewise gap-dependent order optimal regret algorithm for dueling bandits (with matching lower bounds up to small constant factors). We further justify the robustness of our proposed algorithm by proving its optimal regret rate under adversarially corrupted preferences—this outperforms the existing state-of-the-art corrupted dueling results by a large margin. In summary, we believe our reduction idea will find a broader scope in solving a diverse class of dueling bandits setting, which are otherwise studied separately from multi-armed bandits with often more complex solutions and worse guarantees. The efficacy of our proposed algorithms are empirically corroborated against state-of-the art dueling bandit methods.

summary.tldr: A reduction to multi-armed bandits yields optimal dueling-bandit guarantees across stochastic, adversarial, and adversarially corrupted preference settings.

title: Versatile Dueling Bandits: Best-of-both World Analyses for Learning from Relative Preferences

abstract: We showcase important features of the dynamics of the Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) in the training of neural networks. We present empirical observations that commonly used large step sizes (i) may lead the iterates to jump from one side of a valley to the other causing loss stabilization , and (ii) this stabilization induces a hidden stochastic dynamics that biases it implicitly toward simple predictors. Furthermore, we show empirically that the longer large step sizes keep SGD high in the loss landscape valleys, the better the implicit regularization can operate and find sparse representations. Notably, no explicit regularization is used: the regularization effect comes solely from the SGD dynamics influenced by the large step sizes schedule. Therefore, these observations unveil how, through the step size schedules, both gradient and noise drive together the SGD dynamics through the loss landscape of neural networks. We justify these findings theoretically through the study of simple neural network models as well as qualitative arguments inspired from stochastic processes. This analysis allows us to shed new light on some common practices and observed phenomena when training deep networks.

paragraphs: Large step sizes can make stochastic gradient descent jump repeatedly across a valley in the loss landscape. This paper investigates the learning behavior that accompanies that motion. The authors empirically observe that such jumps may stabilize the loss while an underlying stochastic process continues to influence which predictors the network learns.

Their observations suggest that this hidden dynamics biases learning toward simpler predictors and sparse representations. In the studied settings, keeping SGD high in the valley for longer allows the implicit regularization to operate more effectively. No explicit regularization term is used; the effect arises from SGD's dynamics under the large-step-size schedule.

The authors support the observations with theoretical analysis of simple neural networks and qualitative arguments drawn from stochastic processes. This combination offers an explanation for how gradients and noise jointly shape training, even during periods when the loss appears stabilized. The conclusion is qualified by its evidence: the empirical behavior and simplified theoretical models illuminate a mechanism, rather than establishing that longer large-step-size training universally produces better networks.
summary.tldr: Empirical observations and simple-model analysis suggest that prolonged large-step-size SGD can implicitly favor sparse representations.

title: SGD with Large Step Sizes Learns Sparse Features

abstract: When fitting the learning data of an individual to algorithm-like learning models, the observations are so dependent and non-stationary that one may wonder what the classical Maximum Likelihood Estimator (MLE) could do, even if it is the usual tool applied to experimental cognition. Our objective in this work is to show that the estimation of the learning rate cannot be efficient if the learning rate is constant in the classical Exp3 (Exponential weights for Exploration and Exploitation) algorithm. Secondly, we show that if the learning rate decreases polynomially with the sample size, then the prediction error and in some cases the estimation error of the MLE satisfy bounds in probability that decrease at a polynomial rate.

paragraphs: Researchers fitting learning models to an individual's behavior often use maximum likelihood estimation. However, the observations produced by a learner are dependent and non-stationary: later behavior reflects earlier experience. This paper examines what maximum likelihood can achieve when estimating the learning rate in Exp3, an algorithm that balances exploration and exploitation.

The first result identifies an obstacle when the learning rate is constant: efficient estimation of that rate is not possible in classical Exp3. This focuses attention on the data-generating learning dynamics themselves. Even a familiar estimation procedure cannot be assessed independently of how the learner's changing choices produce the observations.

The authors then consider learning rates that decrease polynomially with sample size. Under that condition, they establish probability bounds for maximum likelihood prediction error that shrink at a polynomial rate. In some cases, they also obtain decreasing bounds for parameter-estimation error. Keeping those conclusions separate matters: accurate prediction and accurate recovery of the learning rate are distinct goals, and the abstract provides the estimation guarantee only for some cases.
summary.tldr: Exp3's learning-rate schedule determines estimation behavior: constant rates resist efficient estimation, while polynomially decreasing rates permit shrinking prediction-error bounds.

title: On the convergence of the MLE as an estimator of the learning rate in the Exp3 algorithm

abstract: We consider learning in an adversarial Markov Decision Process (MDP) where the loss functions can change arbitrarily over $K$ episodes and the state space can be arbitrarily large. We assume that the Q-function of any policy is linear in some known features, that is, a linear function approximation exists. The best existing regret upper bound for this setting (Luo et al., 2021) is of order $\tilde{\mathcal O}(K^{2/3})$ (omitting all other dependencies), given access to a simulator. This paper provides two algorithms that improve the regret to $\tilde{\mathcal O}(\sqrt K)$ in the same setting. Our first algorithm makes use of a refined analysis of the Follow-the-Regularized-Leader (FTRL) algorithm with the log-barrier regularizer. This analysis allows the loss estimators to be arbitrarily negative and might be of independent interest. Our second algorithm develops a magnitude-reduced loss estimator, further removing the polynomial dependency on the number of actions in the first algorithm and leading to the optimal regret bound (up to logarithmic terms and dependency on the horizon). Moreover, we also extend the first algorithm to simulator-free linear MDPs, which achieves $\tilde{\mathcal O}(K^{8/9})$ regret and greatly improves over the best existing bound $\tilde{\mathcal O}(K^{14/15})$. This algorithm relies on a better alternative to the Matrix Geometric Resampling procedure by Neu & Olkhovskaya (2020), which could again be of independent interest.

title: Refined Regret for Adversarial MDPs with Linear Function Approximation

abstract: General function approximation is a powerful tool to handle large state and action spaces in a broad range of reinforcement learning (RL) scenarios. However, theoretical understanding of non-stationary MDPs with general function approximation is still limited. In this paper, we make the first such an attempt. We first propose a new complexity metric called dynamic Bellman Eluder (DBE) dimension for non-stationary MDPs, which subsumes majority of existing tractable RL problems in static MDPs as well as non-stationary MDPs. Based on the proposed complexity metric, we propose a novel confidence-set based model-free algorithm called SW-OPEA, which features a sliding window mechanism and a new confidence set design for non-stationary MDPs. We then establish an upper bound on the dynamic regret for the proposed algorithm, and show that SW-OPEA is provably efficient as long as the variation budget is not significantly large. We further demonstrate via examples of non-stationary linear and tabular MDPs that our algorithm performs better in small variation budget scenario than the existing UCB-type algorithms. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first dynamic regret analysis in non-stationary MDPs with general function approximation.

We further demonstrate via examples of non-stationary linear and tabular MDPs that our algorithm performs better in small variation budget scenario than the existing UCB-type algorithms. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first dynamic regret analysis in non-stationary MDPs with general function approximation.

paragraphs: Function approximation allows reinforcement learning to handle large state and action spaces, but changing environments make its theoretical analysis harder. This paper studies non-stationary Markov decision processes with general function approximation. Its goal is to characterize when learning can remain efficient as the environment evolves.

The authors introduce the dynamic Bellman Eluder dimension, a complexity measure covering a broad collection of tractable stationary and non-stationary problems. They use it to analyze SW-OPEA, a model-free algorithm built around confidence sets. The algorithm combines a sliding window with a confidence-set design tailored to non-stationarity, incorporating a mechanism for handling changing observations.

The paper derives an upper bound on dynamic regret and establishes efficiency when the variation budget is not too large. Examples involving non-stationary linear and tabular models show better performance guarantees than existing UCB-type algorithms in the small-variation regime. The central qualification is therefore how much the environment changes: the result connects efficient learning to controlled variation and the proposed complexity measure.
summary.tldr: A new complexity measure and sliding-window algorithm provide dynamic-regret guarantees for reinforcement learning with general function approximation and limited environmental change.

title: Non-stationary Reinforcement Learning under General Function Approximation

abstract: The state-action occupancy measure of a policy is the expected (discounted or undiscounted) number of times a state-action couple is visited in a trajectory. For decades, RL books have been reporting the occupancy equivalence between Markovian and non-Markovian policies in countable state-action spaces under mild conditions. This equivalence states that the occupancy of any non-Markovian policy can be equivalently obtained by a Markovian policy, i.e. a memoryless probability distribution, conditioned only on its current state. While expected, for technical reasons, the translation of this result to continuous state space has resisted until now. Our main contribution is to fill this gap and to provide a general measure-theoretic treatment of the problem, permitting, in particular, its extension to continuous MDPs. Furthermore, we show that when the occupancy is infinite, we may encounter some non-trivial cases where the result does not hold anymore.

paragraphs: A policy's occupancy measure records how often state-action pairs are expected to be visited, with or without discounting. Two policies can share this measure even if they choose actions using different information. For countable spaces, a longstanding result says that, under mild conditions, a history-dependent policy's occupancy can be reproduced by a policy that uses only the current state.

The technical challenge is to formulate and establish the result beyond countable state-action collections. The equivalence concerns expected visitation: it identifies when a memoryless randomized policy can reproduce the occupancy associated with a policy that depends on the history.

The authors also examine the boundary of the result. When occupancy is infinite, they show that nontrivial cases arise in which the equivalence fails. That qualification matters because the extension cannot be read as an unrestricted statement for every continuous decision process. The contribution both fills a theoretical gap and identifies infinite occupancy as a setting where the expected correspondence can break down.
summary.tldr: The paper extends occupancy equivalence between history-dependent and memoryless policies to continuous MDPs while identifying failures when occupancy is infinite.

title: On the Occupancy Measure of Non-Markovian Policies in Continuous MDPs

abstract: We consider the problem of multi-agent navigation and collision avoidance when observations are limited to the local neighborhood of each agent. We propose InforMARL, a novel architecture for multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) which uses local information intelligently to compute paths for all the agents in a decentralized manner. Specifically, InforMARL aggregates information about the local neighborhood of agents for both the actor and the critic using a graph neural network and can be used in conjunction with any standard MARL algorithm. We show that (1) in training, InforMARL has better sample efficiency and performance than baseline approaches, despite using less information, and (2) in testing, it scales well to environments with arbitrary numbers of agents and obstacles. We illustrate these results using four task environments, including one with predetermined goals for each agent, and one in which the agents collectively try to cover all goals.

paragraphs: Multi-agent navigation requires agents to reach goals while avoiding collisions, even when each agent sees only its local neighborhood. InforMARL addresses this setting with an architecture that uses nearby information to support decentralized path decisions. The aim is to learn effective coordination without requiring each agent to observe the entire environment.

The architecture uses a graph neural network to aggregate neighborhood information for both the actor and the critic. These components support action selection and the evaluation used during learning. InforMARL can be combined with standard multi-agent reinforcement learning algorithms, making its information-processing design usable beyond one particular training algorithm.

Across four task environments, the authors report better training performance and sample efficiency than baselines despite using less information. At test time, the architecture scales well to environments with varying numbers of agents and obstacles. The evaluated tasks include individually assigned goals and collective coverage of all goals. These results support local information aggregation as a useful basis for coordination across different team sizes and navigation objectives.
summary.tldr: InforMARL aggregates local neighborhood information with a graph neural network to improve decentralized multi-agent navigation and scaling.

title: Scalable Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning through Intelligent Information Aggregation

abstract: Sketching is one of the most fundamental tools in large-scale machine learning. It enables runtime and memory saving via randomly compressing the original large problem into lower dimensions. In this paper, we propose a novel sketching scheme for the first order method in large-scale distributed learning setting, such that the communication costs between distributed agents are saved while the convergence of the algorithms is still guaranteed. Given gradient information in a high dimension $d$, the agent passes the compressed information processed by a sketching matrix $R\in \mathbb{R}^{s\times d}$ with $s\ll d$, and the receiver de-compressed via the de-sketching matrix $R^\top$ to “recover” the information in original dimension. Using such a framework, we develop algorithms for federated learning with lower communication costs. However, such random sketching does not protect the privacy of local data directly. We show that the gradient leakage problem still exists after applying the sketching technique by presenting a specific gradient attack method. As a remedy, we prove rigorously that the algorithm will be differentially private by adding additional random noises in gradient information, which results in a both communication-efficient and differentially private first order approach for federated learning tasks. Our sketching scheme can be further generalized to other learning settings and might be of independent interest itself.

paragraphs: Distributed learning can spend substantial communication on transmitting high-dimensional gradients. This paper proposes a random sketching scheme that compresses gradient information into a much smaller vector before transmission. The receiver applies the transpose of the sketching matrix to map that information back into the original dimensional space for use in optimization.

The authors develop federated learning algorithms using this communication scheme while retaining convergence guarantees. Compression reduces the amount of information sent between participants, addressing limited communication bandwidth. However, the paper also demonstrates a gradient attack showing that the compressed messages can still leak information about local data.

To address that vulnerability, the authors add random noise to the gradient information and prove differential privacy for the resulting algorithm. This combines communication efficiency with a formal privacy guarantee in one first-order approach. The distinction between compression and privacy is central to the contribution: the sketch reduces message size, while additional noise supplies the demonstrated privacy protection.
summary.tldr: Gradient sketching reduces federated communication with convergence guarantees, while additional noise is needed for the paper’s differential-privacy guarantee.

title: Sketching for First Order Method: Efficient Algorithm for Low-Bandwidth Channel and Vulnerability

abstract: Many existing reinforcement learning (RL) methods employ stochastic gradient iteration on the back end, whose stability hinges upon a hypothesis that the data-generating process mixes exponentially fast with a rate parameter that appears in the step-size selection. Unfortunately, this assumption is violated for large state spaces or settings with sparse rewards, and the mixing time is unknown, making the step size inoperable. In this work, we propose an RL methodology attuned to the mixing time by employing a multi-level Monte Carlo estimator for the critic, the actor, and the average reward embedded within an actor-critic (AC) algorithm. This method, which we call M ulti-level A ctor- C ritic (MAC), is developed specifically for infinite-horizon average-reward settings and neither relies on oracle knowledge of the mixing time in its parameter selection nor assumes its exponential decay; it is therefore readily applicable to applications with slower mixing times. Nonetheless, it achieves a convergence rate comparable to SOTA actor-critic algorithms. We experimentally show that these alleviated restrictions on the technical conditions required for stability translate to superior performance in practice for RL problems with sparse rewards.

paragraphs: Many reinforcement-learning analyses require the data-generating process to mix exponentially fast, meaning its dependence on earlier states fades at that rate. They may also require knowing the mixing time to choose a training step size. These requirements can be problematic with large state spaces or sparse rewards, and an unknown mixing time makes the prescribed choice difficult to use.

Multi-level Actor-Critic addresses this in infinite-horizon problems that optimize average reward. It incorporates multilevel Monte Carlo estimators into the actor, critic, and average-reward calculations. Its parameter choices do not require oracle knowledge of mixing time, and its analysis does not assume exponentially decaying mixing behavior.

Despite these relaxed requirements, MAC achieves a convergence rate comparable to state-of-the-art actor-critic algorithms. Experiments on sparse-reward problems also show superior performance. The contribution links a less restrictive theoretical foundation to practical improvements in the evaluated settings, making the approach relevant to slower-mixing problems where earlier stability conditions are difficult to satisfy.
summary.tldr: MAC achieves competitive actor-critic convergence without requiring exponentially fast mixing or prior knowledge of the mixing time.

title: Beyond Exponentially Fast Mixing in Average-Reward Reinforcement Learning via Multi-Level Monte Carlo Actor-Critic

abstract: Randomized smoothing is a popular method to certify robustness of image classifiers to adversarial input perturbations. It is the only certification technique which scales directly to datasets of higher dimension such as ImageNet. However, current techniques are not able to utilize the fact that any adversarial example has to lie in the image space, that is $[0,1]^d$; otherwise, one can trivially detect it. To address this suboptimality, we derive new certification formulae which lead to significant improvements in the certified $\ell_1$-robustness without the need of adapting the classifiers or change of smoothing distributions. The code is released at https://github.com/vvoracek/L1-smoothing

The code is released at https://github.com/vvoracek/L1-smoothing

paragraphs: Randomized smoothing provides certificates that an image classifier is robust to specified adversarial changes. The paper identifies a source of unnecessary conservatism in existing certification methods: they do not use the fact that valid image inputs have every coordinate between zero and one. Perturbations producing values outside that box can be detected as outside the image space.

The authors derive new certification formulas that incorporate these coordinate constraints. Their focus is robustness measured in the l1 norm, which aggregates the absolute changes across input coordinates. Incorporating the valid input region lets the certification calculation use information already available about which adversarial examples are admissible.

The new formulas yield significant improvements in certified l1 robustness without modifying the classifiers or changing the smoothing distributions. Thus, the reported improvement comes from a stronger analysis of the existing smoothed classifier under the image-space constraints. This is useful because the robustness guarantee can improve without requiring a corresponding change to the model or its noise distribution.
summary.tldr: Using valid image-value bounds strengthens randomized-smoothing l1 robustness certificates without changing classifiers or smoothing distributions.

title: Improving l1-Certified Robustness via Randomized Smoothing by Leveraging Box Constraints

abstract: Counterfactual Risk Minimization (CRM) is a framework for dealing with the logged bandit feedback problem, where the goal is to improve a logging policy using offline data. In this paper, we explore the case where it is possible to deploy learned policies multiple times and acquire new data. We extend the CRM principle and its theory to this scenario, which we call "Sequential Counterfactual Risk Minimization (SCRM)." We introduce a novel counterfactual estimator and identify conditions that can improve the performance of CRM in terms of excess risk and regret rates, by using an analysis similar to restart strategies in accelerated optimization methods. We also provide an empirical evaluation of our method in both discrete and continuous action settings, and demonstrate the benefits of multiple deployments of CRM.

We also provide an empirical evaluation of our method in both discrete and continuous action settings, and demonstrate the benefits of multiple deployments of CRM.

paragraphs: Counterfactual risk minimization learns an improved decision policy from logged bandit feedback: records generated by a previous policy with feedback on its chosen actions. This paper considers a setting where learning need not stop after one offline update. A learned policy can be deployed, collect additional data, and support another round of improvement.

The authors extend the framework and its theory to this repeated-deployment setting, calling it sequential counterfactual risk minimization. They introduce a new counterfactual estimator and analyze how using successive deployments can improve learning. Their analysis draws on ideas resembling restart strategies in accelerated optimization, connecting repeated policy updates to improved theoretical rates.

The paper identifies conditions under which excess-risk and regret rates improve over CRM. Those conditions are part of the claim: repeated deployment is analyzed as an opportunity for improvement, rather than asserted to help unconditionally. Empirical evaluations with both discrete and continuous actions demonstrate benefits from multiple CRM deployments, supporting the value of treating data collection and policy improvement as a sequence.
summary.tldr: Sequential counterfactual risk minimization uses repeated policy deployments and fresh data to improve learning rates under identified conditions.

title: Sequential Counterfactual Risk Minimization

abstract: Research on prompting has shown excellent performance with little or even no supervised training across many tasks. However, prompting for machine translation is still under-explored in the literature. We fill this gap by offering a systematic study on prompting strategies for translation, examining various factors for prompt template and demonstration example selection. We further explore the use of monolingual data and the feasibility of cross-lingual, cross-domain, and sentence-to-document transfer learning in prompting. Extensive experiments with GLM-130B (Zeng et al., 2022) as the testbed show that 1) the number and the quality of prompt examples matter, where using suboptimal examples degenerates translation; 2) several features of prompt examples, such as semantic similarity, show significant Spearman correlation with their prompting performance; yet, none of the correlations are strong enough; 3) using pseudo parallel prompt examples constructed from monolingual data via zero-shot prompting could improve translation; and 4) improved performance is achievable by transferring knowledge from prompt examples selected in other settings. We finally provide an analysis on the model outputs and discuss several problems that prompting still suffers from.

paragraphs: This paper systematically examines how prompting affects machine translation using GLM-130B as its testbed. It studies prompt templates, the selection of demonstration examples, and ways to use monolingual text. It also explores whether examples selected for one language, domain, or sentence-level setting can help in other translation settings.

The experiments show that both the number and quality of examples matter, and poor examples can degrade translation. Features such as semantic similarity have significant rank correlations with prompting performance, but none of the examined correlations is strong enough. This makes example selection more complicated than simply relying on one promising similarity signal.

The authors also find that zero-shot prompting can turn monolingual text into pseudo-parallel examples that may improve translation. Transferring prompt examples across settings can likewise produce gains, including the explored cross-lingual, cross-domain, and sentence-to-document transfers. Their output analysis identifies continuing problems with prompting. The study supplies evidence about practical prompt-design choices for the evaluated model, showing both opportunities to reuse data and the sensitivity of translation to demonstration quality.
summary.tldr: A GLM-130B translation study shows that demonstration quality matters and that monolingual-derived examples and cross-setting transfer can improve prompting.

title: Prompting Large Language Model for Machine Translation: A Case Study

abstract: Training reinforcement learning (RL) agents directly from high-dimensional image observations continues to be a challenging problem. Recent line of work on behavioral distances proposes to learn representations that encode behavioral similarities quantified by the bisimulation metric. By learning an isometric mapping to a lower dimensional space that preserves this metric, such methods attempt to learn representations that group together functionally similar states. However, such an isometric mapping may not exist, making the learning objective ill-defined. We propose an alternative objective that allows distortions in long-range distances, while preserving local metric structure – inducing representations that highlight natural clusters in the state space. This leads to new representations, which we term Behavioral Eigenmaps (BeigeMaps), corresponding to the eigenfunctions of similarity kernels induced by behavioral distances. We empirically demonstrate that when added as a drop-in modification, BeigeMaps improve the policy performance of prior behavioral distance based RL algorithms.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning from images requires representations that capture useful differences between states. Behavioral-distance methods try to place functionally similar states close together using a bisimulation metric. Some approaches seek a lower-dimensional representation that preserves all these distances exactly. This paper points out that such a mapping may not exist, making the objective ill-defined.

Behavioral Eigenmaps, or BeigeMaps, use a different objective: preserve local metric structure while allowing distortion in distances between more widely separated states. This relaxation encourages representations that reveal natural clusters in the state space. The resulting representations correspond to eigenfunctions of similarity kernels constructed from behavioral distances.

The authors evaluate BeigeMaps as a drop-in modification to existing reinforcement learning algorithms based on behavioral distances. They report improved policy performance. The significance is both conceptual and practical: the representation objective avoids demanding a potentially nonexistent global distance-preserving map, while the experiments show that retaining local behavioral relationships can help agents learn from high-dimensional visual observations.
summary.tldr: BeigeMaps preserve local behavioral relationships instead of all distances, improving reported reinforcement learning performance from images.

title: BeigeMaps: Behavioral Eigenmaps for Reinforcement Learning from Images

abstract: Fair decision making has largely been studied with respect to a single decision. Here we investigate the notion of fairness in the context of sequential decision making where multiple stakeholders can be affected by the outcomes of decisions. We observe that fairness often depends on the history of the sequential decision-making process, and in this sense that it is inherently non-Markovian. We further observe that fairness often needs to be assessed at time points within the process, not just at the end of the process. To advance our understanding of this class of fairness problems, we explore the notion of non-Markovian fairness in the context of sequential decision making. We identify properties of non-Markovian fairness, including notions of long-term, anytime, periodic, and bounded fairness. We explore the interplay between non-Markovian fairness and memory and how memory can support construction of fair policies. Finally, we introduce the FairQCM algorithm, which can automatically augment its training data to improve sample efficiency in the synthesis of fair policies via reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Fairness in a sequence of decisions can depend on what happened earlier and on how multiple stakeholders have been affected over time. The paper argues that fairness is therefore often non-Markovian: judging the current decision requires relevant history. It also emphasizes that fairness may need to hold during a process, rather than being assessed only after the final outcome.

The authors develop this perspective through notions of long-term, anytime, periodic, and bounded fairness. These distinguish different temporal requirements for assessing a decision process. They also study the connection between fairness and memory, examining how retaining information about earlier decisions can support the construction of fair policies.

The algorithmic contribution is FairQCM, a reinforcement learning method that automatically augments its training data to improve sample efficiency when synthesizing fair policies. Together, the framework and algorithm connect the specification of fairness over time with the information and learning process needed to support it. The central shift is to treat decision history as part of the fairness problem itself.
summary.tldr: The paper formalizes history-dependent fairness and introduces FairQCM to improve sample efficiency when learning fair sequential policies.

title: Remembering to Be Fair: Non-Markovian Fairness in Sequential Decision Making

abstract: The objective to be minimized in the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) has a restricted form, which allows a specialized sequential minimal optimization (SMO) that requires only a few observations in each iteration. However, the SMO iteration is still costly due to the observation noise—one observation at a point typically requires averaging over hundreds to thousands of repeated quantum measurement shots for achieving a reasonable noise level. In this paper, we propose an adaptive cost control method, named subspace in confident region (SubsCoRe), for SMO. SubsCoRe uses the Gaussian process (GP) surrogate, and requires it to have low uncertainty over the subspace being updated, so that optimization in each iteration is performed with guaranteed accuracy. Adaptive cost control is performed by setting the required accuracy according to the progress of the optimization, and identifying the minimum number of measurement shots, as well as their distribution, satisfying the SubsCoRe requirement.

paragraphs: A variational quantum eigensolver has an objective with enough structure to support sequential minimal optimization, which needs only a few observations per iteration. Those observations can still be expensive: quantum measurement noise means that evaluating one point typically requires averaging hundreds to thousands of measurement shots. The paper addresses the measurement cost hidden inside each optimization step.

Its method, Subspace in Confident Region, or SubsCoRe, uses a Gaussian process surrogate to represent the objective and its uncertainty. Before optimizing the subspace selected for an update, the method requires sufficiently low uncertainty throughout that subspace. This requirement connects the reliability of each optimization step to the quality of the observations supporting it.

SubsCoRe adapts the required accuracy as optimization progresses, then identifies the minimum number of measurement shots and their distribution that satisfy its confidence requirement. The central contribution is thus a way to allocate measurement effort according to the current optimization need. The stated accuracy guarantee applies through the subspace uncertainty requirement, making precision and observation cost parts of the same decision.
summary.tldr: SubsCoRe adapts quantum measurement effort to the surrogate uncertainty and accuracy required for each optimization step.

title: Adaptive Observation Cost Control for Variational Quantum Eigensolvers

abstract: The distributional simplicity bias (DSB) posits that neural networks learn low-order moments of the data distribution first, before moving on to higher-order correlations. In this work, we present compelling new evidence for the DSB by showing that networks automatically learn to perform well on maximum-entropy distributions whose low-order statistics match those of the training set early in training, then lose this ability later. We also extend the DSB to discrete domains by proving an equivalence between token $n$-gram frequencies and the moments of embedding vectors, and by finding empirical evidence for the bias in LLMs. Finally we use optimal transport methods to surgically edit the low-order statistics of one class to match those of another, and show that early-training networks treat the edited samples as if they were drawn from the target class. Code is available at https://github.com/EleutherAI/features-across-time.

paragraphs: The distributional simplicity bias proposes that neural networks first learn lower-order statistics of their training data and later learn more complex correlations. This paper supplies new evidence for that progression. It examines how networks behave on maximum-entropy distributions constructed to share low-order statistics with the training set.

Early in training, networks perform well on these matched distributions, but later lose that ability. This pattern supports the idea that their initial predictions depend on simpler statistical features before shifting toward information those distributions do not preserve. The authors also extend the analysis to discrete data by proving an equivalence between token n-gram frequencies and moments of embedding vectors, and they find empirical evidence of the bias in language models.

A further experiment uses optimal transport to change one class’s low-order statistics so they match those of another class. Early-training networks then treat the edited examples as belonging to the target class. This intervention strengthens the evidence that low-order statistics influence early predictions, complementing the observed changes in generalization over training.
summary.tldr: Statistical matching and targeted data edits support the view that networks learn simpler distributional features before higher-order correlations.

title: Neural Networks Learn Statistics of Increasing Complexity

abstract: Motivated by conditional independence testing, an essential step in constraint-based causal discovery algorithms, we study the nonparametric Von Mises estimator for the entropy of multivariate distributions built on a kernel density estimator. We establish an exponential concentration inequality for this estimator. We design a test for conditional independence (CI) based on our estimator, called VM-CI, which achieves optimal parametric rates under smoothness assumptions. Leveraging the exponential concentration, we prove a tight upper bound for the overall error of VM-CI. Furthermore, we empirically show that VM-CI outperforms other popular CI tests in terms of either time, sample complexity, or both. abstract: Since the objective functions of reinforcement learning problems are typically highly nonconvex, it is desirable that policy gradient, the most popular algorithm, escapes saddle points and arrives at second-order stationary points. Existing results only consider vanilla policy gradient algorithms with unbiased gradient estimators, but practical implementations under the infinite-horizon discounted reward setting are biased due to finite-horizon sampling. Moreover, actor-critic methods, whose second-order convergence has not yet been established, are also biased due to the critic approximation of the value function. We provide a novel second-order analysis of biased policy gradient methods, including the vanilla gradient estimator computed from Monte-Carlo sampling of trajectories as well as the double-loop actor-critic algorithm, where in the inner loop the critic improves the approximation of the value function via TD(0) learning. Separately, we also establish the convergence of TD(0) on Markov chains irrespective of initial state distribution.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning objectives are typically nonconvex, so a small gradient alone does not establish that learning has avoided a saddle point. Second-order analysis addresses this stronger convergence question. Earlier results considered vanilla policy gradients with unbiased estimates, whereas practical implementations introduce bias in several ways.

This paper analyzes biased policy gradient methods in the infinite-horizon discounted setting. One source of bias is estimating an infinite-horizon objective from finite trajectories. Another is using an approximate value function in actor-critic learning. The analysis covers Monte Carlo trajectory estimates and a double-loop actor-critic algorithm whose inner loop improves the critic through TD(0) learning.

Separately, the authors establish convergence of TD(0) on Markov chains regardless of the initial state distribution. That result concerns the value-learning component itself, complementing the broader analysis of policy updates that depend on its approximation.
summary.tldr: The paper develops second-order convergence analysis for biased policy gradients and a double-loop actor-critic method.

title: On the Second-Order Convergence of Biased Policy Gradient Algorithms

abstract: This paper introduces a novel deep-learning-based approach for numerical simulation of a time-evolving Schrödinger equation inspired by stochastic mechanics and generative diffusion models. Unlike existing approaches, which exhibit computational complexity that scales exponentially in the problem dimension, our method allows us to adapt to the latent low-dimensional structure of the wave function by sampling from the Markovian diffusion. Depending on the latent dimension, our method may have far lower computational complexity in higher dimensions. Moreover, we propose novel equations for stochastic quantum mechanics, resulting in quadratic computational complexity with respect to the number of dimensions. Numerical simulations verify our theoretical findings and show a significant advantage of our method compared to other deep-learning-based approaches used for quantum mechanics.

paragraphs: Deep Stochastic Mechanics introduces a deep-learning approach to simulating the time-dependent Schrödinger equation. The computational problem becomes difficult as the number of dimensions grows: the abstract describes existing approaches whose cost increases exponentially with dimension. The proposed method draws on stochastic mechanics and generative diffusion models to seek a more economical representation of the evolving wave function.

Its main mechanism is sampling from a Markovian diffusion that can adapt to low-dimensional structure hidden within the wave function. The potential saving therefore depends on the latent dimension, rather than following automatically from a large ambient dimension. When that underlying structure is sufficiently compact, the method may have substantially lower computational cost in high-dimensional problems.

The paper also proposes new equations for stochastic quantum mechanics with quadratic computational complexity in the number of dimensions. Numerical simulations support the theoretical findings and show a significant advantage over other deep-learning approaches considered for quantum mechanics. Together, these contributions connect a structure-adaptive sampling method with a more computationally manageable mathematical formulation.
summary.tldr: Deep Stochastic Mechanics uses diffusion sampling and new stochastic quantum equations to reduce the computational burden of simulating evolving wave functions.

title: Deep Stochastic Mechanics

abstract: Sound and complete algorithms have been proposed to compute identifiable causal queries using the causal structure and data. However, most of these algorithms assume accurate estimation of the data distribution, which is impractical for high-dimensional variables such as images. On the other hand, modern deep generative architectures can be trained to sample from high-dimensional distributions. However, training these networks are typically very costly. Thus, it is desirable to leverage pre-trained models to answer causal queries using such high-dimensional data. To address this, we propose modular training of deep causal generative models that not only makes learning more efficient, but also allows us to utilize large, pre-trained conditional generative models. To the best of our knowledge, our algorithm, Modular-DCM is the first algorithm that, given the causal structure, uses adversarial training to learn the network weights, and can make use of pre-trained models to provably sample from any identifiable causal query in the presence of latent confounders. With extensive experiments on the Colored-MNIST dataset, we demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms the baselines. We also show our algorithm’s convergence on the COVIDx dataset and its utility with a causal invariant prediction problem on CelebA-HQ.

paragraphs: Causal inference algorithms can identify which causal questions are answerable from a causal structure and data. Applying them to high-dimensional variables such as images is difficult because accurately estimating the required distributions is impractical. Deep generative models can produce samples from such distributions, but training them can itself be expensive.

Modular-DCM addresses this problem through modular training that can incorporate large pretrained conditional generative models. Given the causal structure, it uses adversarial training to learn network weights. The authors establish that the method can provably sample from identifiable causal queries even when latent confounders are present. The guarantee is specifically about identifiable queries and presupposes the supplied causal structure.

Experiments on Colored-MNIST show improvements over the compared baselines. Additional results demonstrate convergence on COVIDx and usefulness for a causal invariant prediction problem on CelebA-HQ. Together, these results support modular generative modeling as a way to connect high-dimensional data generation with causal inference while reusing pretrained components to improve learning efficiency.
summary.tldr: Modular-DCM reuses pretrained generative components to support provable sampling from identifiable causal queries given a causal structure, including settings with latent confounders.

title: Modular Learning of Deep Causal Generative Models for High-dimensional Causal Inference

abstract: Ranking algorithms are fundamental to various online platforms across e-commerce sites to content streaming services. Our research addresses the challenge of adaptively ranking items from a candidate pool for heterogeneous users, a key component in personalizing user experience. We develop a user response model that considers diverse user preferences and the varying effects of item positions, aiming to optimize overall user satisfaction with the ranked list. We frame this problem within a contextual bandits framework, with each ranked list as an action. Our approach incorporates an upper confidence bound to adjust predicted user satisfaction scores and selects the ranking action that maximizes these adjusted scores, efficiently solved via maximum weight imperfect matching. We demonstrate that our algorithm achieves a cumulative regret bound of $O(d\sqrt{NKT})$ for ranking $K$ out of $N$ items in a $d$-dimensional context space over $T$ rounds, under the assumption that user responses follow a generalized linear model. This regret alleviates dependence on the ambient action space, whose cardinality grows exponentially with $N$ and $K$ (thus rendering direct application of existing adaptive learning algorithms – such as UCB or Thompson sampling – infeasible). Experiments conducted on both simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate our algorithm outperforms the baseline.

paragraphs: Personalized ranking requires choosing which items to show and where to place them. Different users prefer different items, and an item's position can affect the response it receives. This paper models both influences and treats each complete ranked list as an action in a contextual bandit problem, where the platform learns from responses while trying to improve user satisfaction.

The algorithm adjusts predicted satisfaction using an upper confidence bound, allowing uncertainty to influence its choices. It then finds the list with the highest adjusted score through a maximum weight imperfect matching problem. This formulation matters because the number of possible lists grows exponentially with the candidate pool and list length, making direct treatment of every ranking as a separate action impractical.

Assuming responses follow a generalized linear model, the authors prove cumulative regret of order d times the square root of NKT. Here, d describes context dimension, N the candidate count, K the list length, and T the number of rounds. Experiments on simulated and real data also show improvement over the evaluated baseline.
summary.tldr: A contextual bandit ranking method uses confidence bounds and matching to personalize lists efficiently, with a regret guarantee under a generalized linear response model.

title: Adaptively Learning to Select-Rank in Online Platforms

abstract: As a more challenging domain adaptation setting, universal domain adaptation (UniDA) introduces category shift on top of domain shift, which needs to identify unknown category in the target domain and avoid misclassifying target samples into source private categories. To this end, we propose a novel UniDA approach named Batch Singular value Polarization and Weighted Semantic Augmentation (BSP-WSA). Specifically, we adopt an adversarial classifier to identify the target unknown category and align feature distributions between the two domains. Then, we propose to perform SVD on the classifier’s outputs to maximize larger singular values while minimizing those smaller ones, which could prevent target samples from being wrongly assigned to source private classes. To better bridge the domain gap, we propose a weighted semantic augmentation approach for UniDA to generate data on common categories between the two domains. Extensive experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate that BSP-WSA could outperform existing state-of-the-art UniDA approaches.

paragraphs: Universal domain adaptation handles two changes at once: examples look different across domains, and the domains do not necessarily contain the same categories. A successful model must recognize unfamiliar target categories while avoiding assignments to categories that occur only in the source domain. BSP-WSA addresses both problems within one approach.

An adversarial classifier identifies unknown target categories and helps align feature distributions across domains. The method then applies singular value decomposition to the classifier’s outputs, increasing larger singular values and decreasing smaller ones. The authors propose this polarization as a way to reduce mistaken assignments of target examples to source-only categories.

A second component generates additional data for categories shared by the domains through weighted semantic augmentation. This focuses augmentation on the categories where cross-domain transfer is relevant. Experiments on three benchmarks show that BSP-WSA can outperform existing leading universal adaptation methods. The findings support combining unknown-category handling, structured classifier outputs, and shared-category augmentation when both category membership and feature distributions change.
summary.tldr: BSP-WSA combines classifier-output polarization and shared-category augmentation to improve adaptation when domains differ in both appearance and categories.

title: Batch Singular Value Polarization and Weighted Semantic Augmentation for Universal Domain Adaptation

abstract: In most real-world reinforcement learning applications, state information is only partially observable, which breaks the Markov decision process assumption and leads to inferior performance for algorithms that conflate observations with state. Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs), on the other hand, provide a general framework that allows for partial observability to be accounted for in learning, exploration and planning, but presents significant computational and statistical challenges. To address these difficulties, we develop a representation-based perspective that leads to a coherent framework and tractable algorithmic approach for practical reinforcement learning from partial observations. We provide a theoretical analysis for justifying the statistical efficiency of the proposed algorithm, and also empirically demonstrate the proposed algorithm can surpass state-of-the-art performance with partial observations across various benchmarks, advancing reliable reinforcement learning towards more practical applications.

paragraphs: In partially observable reinforcement learning, the agent sees only part of the information describing its environment. Treating those observations as complete states can undermine algorithms built around the Markov decision process assumption. Partially observable Markov decision processes account for this distinction, but introduce substantial computational and statistical challenges.

The paper develops a representation-based perspective to make learning, exploration, and planning under partial observability more tractable. Its contribution is a coherent framework together with an algorithmic approach for working from partial observations. The representation perspective is intended to address the difficulties of the partially observable problem within a unified treatment of these decision-making activities.

The authors provide theoretical analysis supporting the algorithm's statistical efficiency. They also report empirical results showing that it can surpass state-of-the-art performance across several benchmarks with partial observations. These are complementary forms of evidence: the analysis justifies data efficiency, while the experiments demonstrate performance in the evaluated tasks. Together, they support representation learning as a practical route toward reinforcement learning that explicitly accounts for incomplete state information.
summary.tldr: A representation-based framework makes partially observable reinforcement learning tractable, with statistical analysis and strong benchmark performance.

title: Provable Representation with Efficient Planning for Partially Observable Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Generalizing vision-based reinforcement learning (RL) agents to novel environments remains a difficult and open challenge. Current trends are to collect large-scale datasets or use data augmentation techniques to prevent overfitting and improve downstream generalization. However, the computational and data collection costs increase exponentially with the number of task variations and can destabilize the already difficult task of training RL agents. In this work, we take inspiration from recent advances in computational neuroscience and propose a model, Associative Latent DisentAnglement (ALDA), that builds on standard off-policy RL towards zero-shot generalization. Specifically, we revisit the role of latent disentanglement in RL and show how combining it with a model of associative memory achieves zero-shot generalization on difficult task variations without relying on data augmentation. Finally, we formally show that data augmentation techniques are a form of weak disentanglement and discuss the implications of this insight.

Collecting many task variations or augmenting training images can help, but these approaches add data and computational demands and can complicate training. This paper studies a representation-based approach to generalizing to new task variations without relying on data augmentation.

The proposed model, Associative Latent DisentAnglement, or ALDA, builds on standard off-policy reinforcement learning. Inspired by computational neuroscience, it combines latent disentanglement with a model of associative memory. The central idea is to use these two components together to support transfer, and the authors demonstrate zero-shot generalization on difficult task variations.

This links a widely used generalization technique to the representation property that motivates ALDA. The empirical and theoretical contributions serve different roles: the model demonstrates generalization without augmentation in the studied variations, while the formal analysis explains a connection between augmentation and disentanglement. Together, they motivate examining learned representations and associative memory as mechanisms for transfer.
summary.tldr: ALDA combines latent disentanglement and associative memory to demonstrate zero-shot visual reinforcement-learning generalization without data augmentation.

title: Zero Shot Generalization of Vision-Based RL Without Data Augmentation

abstract: Text watermarking aims to subtly embeds statistical signals into text by controlling the Large Language Model (LLM)’s sampling process, enabling watermark detectors to verify that the output was generated by the specified model. The robustness of these watermarking algorithms has become a key factor in evaluating their effectiveness. Current text watermarking algorithms embed watermarks in high-entropy tokens to ensure text quality. In this paper, we reveal that this seemingly benign design can be exploited by attackers, posing a significant risk to the robustness of the watermark. We introduce a generic efficient paraphrasing attack, the Self-Information Rewrite Attack (SIRA), which leverages the vulnerability by calculating the self-information of each token to identify potential pattern tokens and perform targeted attack. Our work exposes a widely prevalent vulnerability in current watermarking algorithms. The experimental results show SIRA achieves nearly 100% attack success rates on seven recent watermarking methods with only $0.88 per million tokens cost. Our approach does not require any access to the watermark algorithms or the watermarked LLM and can seamlessly transfer to any LLM as the attack model even mobile-level models. Our findings highlight the urgent need for more robust watermarking.

paragraphs: Text watermarks introduce statistical patterns during language-model generation so detectors can recognize outputs from a specified model. Many methods place these signals in high-entropy token choices to preserve text quality. This paper shows that the same design choice can expose a shared weakness in watermark robustness.

The proposed Self-Information Rewrite Attack uses token self-information to identify likely carriers of watermark patterns and directs paraphrasing toward them. The authors also report that it can transfer across language models used for rewriting, including mobile-level models.

summary.tldr: SIRA exposes a shared weakness in seven evaluated text-watermarking methods through inexpensive, targeted paraphrasing without access to the watermarking system.

title: Revealing Weaknesses in Text Watermarking Through Self-Information Rewrite Attacks

abstract: Distributional reinforcement learning improves performance by capturing environmental stochasticity, but a comprehensive theoretical understanding of its effectiveness remains elusive. In addition, the intractable element of the infinite dimensionality of distributions has been overlooked. In this paper, we present a regret analysis of distributional reinforcement learning with general value function approximation in a finite episodic Markov decision process setting. We first introduce a key notion of Bellman unbiasedness which is essential for exactly learnable and provably efficient distributional updates in an online manner. Among all types of statistical functionals for representing infinite-dimensional return distributions, our theoretical results demonstrate that only moment functionals can exactly capture the statistical information. Secondly, we propose a provably efficient algorithm, SF-LSVI, that achieves a tight regret bound of $\tilde{O}(d_E H^{\frac{3}{2}}\sqrt{K})$ where $H$ is the horizon, $K$ is the number of episodes, and $d_E$ is the eluder dimension of a function class.

paragraphs: Distributional reinforcement learning represents the variability of future returns rather than only their average. This can capture environmental randomness, but a full return distribution is infinite-dimensional. The paper examines how such information can support provably efficient learning when value functions are approximated, working in finite episodic Markov decision processes.

The authors introduce Bellman unbiasedness as a requirement for distributional updates that are exactly learnable online and provably efficient. Their theoretical analysis identifies moment functionals as the only statistical functionals that exactly capture the relevant information under this framework. This connects learning efficiency to episode length and function-class complexity, providing a concrete theoretical foundation for distributional learning in the stated setting.
summary.tldr: Bellman unbiasedness characterizes exact distributional updates and supports a reinforcement-learning algorithm with a tight regret guarantee.

title: Bellman Unbiasedness: Toward Provably Efficient Distributional Reinforcement Learning with General Value Function Approximation

abstract: The Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) is currently experiencing rapid growth, driven by the advanced capabilities of language-based LLMs. Unlike their specialist predecessors, existing MLLMs are evolving towards a Multimodal Generalist paradigm. Initially limited to understanding multiple modalities, these models have advanced to not only comprehend but also generate across modalities. Their capabilities have expanded from coarse-grained to fine-grained multimodal understanding and from supporting singular modalities to accommodating a wide array of or even arbitrary modalities. To assess the capabilities of various MLLMs, a diverse array of benchmark test sets has been proposed. This leads to a critical question: Can we simply assume that higher performance across tasks indicates a stronger MLLM capability, bringing us closer to human-level AI? We argue that the answer is not as straightforward as it seems. In this project, we introduce an evaluation framework to delineate the capabilities and behaviors of current multimodal generalists. This framework, named General-Level, establishes 5-scale levels of MLLM performance and generality, offering a methodology to compare MLLMs and gauge the progress of existing systems towards more robust multimodal generalists and, ultimately, towards AGI (Artificial General Intelligence). Central to our framework is the use of Synergy as the evaluative criterion, categorizing capabilities based on whether MLLMs preserve synergy across comprehension and generation, as well as across multimodal interactions. To evaluate the comprehensive abilities of various generalists, we present a massive multimodal benchmark, General-Bench, which encompasses a broader spectrum of skills, modalities, formats, and capabilities, including over 700 tasks and 325,800 instances. The evaluation results that involve over 100 existing state-of-the-art MLLMs uncover the capability rankings of generalists, highlighting the challenges in reaching genuine AI. We expect this project to pave the way for future research on next-generation multimodal foundation models, providing a robust infrastructure to accelerate the realization of AGI. Project Page: https://generalist.top/, Leaderboard: https://generalist.top/leaderboard/, Benchmark: https://huggingface.co/General-Level/.

It proposes evaluating how capabilities work together, giving particular attention to the interaction between comprehension, generation, and multiple modalities.
