Its central criterion is synergy: whether capabilities remain coordinated across understanding and generation and across multimodal interactions. The framework is intended to make comparisons between generalist models more informative than a collection of isolated task scores and to characterize their behaviors as well as their performance.

The accompanying General-Bench covers more than 700 tasks and 325,800 instances across skills, modalities, formats, and capabilities. Evaluations of more than 100 state-of-the-art multimodal models produce capability rankings and expose continuing challenges in developing generalists. The contribution is an evaluation framework and a broad testing resource; the authors’ ambition to support progress toward AGI is a research direction rather than an achieved result.
summary.tldr: General-Level and General-Bench assess multimodal generalists through coordinated capabilities, using five evaluation levels and more than 700 tasks.

title: On Path to Multimodal Generalist: General-Level and General-Bench

abstract: Deep learning with noisy labels presents significant challenges. In this work, we theoretically characterize the role of label noise from a feature learning perspective. Specifically, we consider a signal-noise data distribution, where each sample comprises a label-dependent signal and label-independent noise, and rigorously analyze the training dynamics of a two-layer convolutional neural network under this data setup, along with the presence of label noise. Our analysis identifies two key stages. In Stage I, the model perfectly fits all the clean samples (i.e., samples without label noise) while ignoring the noisy ones (i.e., samples with noisy labels). During this stage, the model learns the signal from the clean samples, which generalizes well on unseen data. In Stage II, as the training loss converges, the gradient in the direction of noise surpasses that of the signal, leading to overfitting on noisy samples. Eventually, the model memorizes the noise present in the noisy samples and degrades its generalization ability. Furthermore, our analysis provides a theoretical basis for two widely used techniques for tackling label noise: early stopping and sample selection. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world setups validate our theory.

paragraphs: Incorrect training labels can interfere with learning, but the resulting damage unfolds over time. This paper analyzes that process through the features a model learns. Its theoretical setting uses a two-layer convolutional network and data containing both a label-dependent signal and label-independent noise, with additional corruption of some labels.

Under this setup, the analysis identifies two stages. First, the model fits all cleanly labeled examples while ignoring those with corrupted labels. It learns the signal from the clean examples, supporting generalization to unseen data. Later, as training loss converges, gradients associated with noise become stronger than those associated with the signal.

In the second stage, the model memorizes noise in the mislabeled examples, degrading generalization. This account provides a theoretical basis for early stopping and sample selection: both address the transition from useful signal learning toward fitting corrupted examples. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data support the theory. The two-stage characterization is tied to the analyzed data and network setup, rather than asserted as a universal description of every noisy-label training run.
summary.tldr: A theoretical analysis identifies an initial signal-learning stage followed by noise memorization, explaining why early stopping and sample selection can help.

title: On the Role of Label Noise in the Feature Learning Process

abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) is crucial when online exploration is costly or unsafe but often struggles with high epistemic uncertainty due to limited data. Existing methods rely on fixed conservative policies, restricting adaptivity and generalization. To address this, we propose Reflect-then-Plan (RefPlan), a novel doubly Bayesian offline model-based (MB) planning approach. RefPlan unifies uncertainty modeling and MB planning by recasting planning as Bayesian posterior estimation. At deployment, it updates a belief over environment dynamics using real-time observations, incorporating uncertainty into MB planning via marginalization. Empirical results on standard benchmarks show that RefPlan significantly improves the performance of conservative offline RL policies. In particular, RefPlan maintains robust performance under high epistemic uncertainty and limited data, while demonstrating resilience to changing environment dynamics, improving the flexibility, generalizability, and robustness of offline-learned policies.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns from existing data when active exploration would be costly or unsafe. Limited data can leave substantial uncertainty about how the environment behaves. Reflect-then-Plan addresses the resulting tension between cautious offline policies and the need to adapt when new observations become available during deployment.

RefPlan expresses planning as Bayesian posterior estimation and maintains a belief over environment dynamics. At deployment, real-time observations update that belief. Planning then incorporates uncertainty by marginalizing over the possible dynamics, meaning it accounts for alternatives represented in the belief. This connects learning about the environment with choosing actions in a single doubly Bayesian approach.

On standard benchmarks, RefPlan significantly improves the performance of conservative offline reinforcement-learning policies. The experiments report robust behavior with limited data and high uncertainty, together with resilience when environment dynamics change. These findings support using deployment observations to revise beliefs and plans rather than relying entirely on a fixed conservative policy. The demonstrated benefits concern empirical flexibility, generalization, and robustness in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: RefPlan updates beliefs about environment dynamics during deployment and incorporates that uncertainty into planning, improving offline-policy performance on benchmarks.

title: Reflect-then-Plan: Offline Model-Based Planning through a Doubly Bayesian Lens

abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has surpassed top human players in a variety of games. In imperfect information games, these achievements have primarily been driven by Counterfactual Regret Minimization (CFR) and its variants for computing Nash equilibrium. However, most existing research has focused on maximizing payoff, while largely neglecting the importance of strategic diversity and the need for varied play styles, thereby limiting AI’s adaptability to different user preferences. To address this gap, we propose Preference-CFR (Pref-CFR), a novel method that incorporates two key parameters: preference degree and vulnerability degree. These parameters enable the AI to adjust its strategic distribution within an acceptable performance loss threshold, thereby enhancing its adaptability to a wider range of strategic demands. In our experiments with Texas Hold’em, Pref-CFR successfully trained Aggressive and Loose Passive styles that not only match original CFR-based strategies in performance but also display clearly distinct behavioral patterns. Notably, for certain hand scenarios, Pref-CFR produces strategies that diverge significantly from both conventional expert heuristics and original CFR outputs, potentially offering novel insights for professional players.

paragraphs: Strong game-playing systems often focus on payoff and equilibrium strategies, leaving less room for users to request different playing styles. This paper studies that gap in imperfect-information games. It builds on Counterfactual Regret Minimization, or CFR, to support strategic diversity alongside competitive performance.

Preference-CFR introduces two controls, preference degree and vulnerability degree. These let the system adjust its distribution over strategies within an acceptable performance-loss threshold. The resulting framework makes style preferences part of strategy construction, allowing different behavioral patterns to be pursued while accounting for the associated performance tradeoff.

In Texas Hold’em experiments, the method learns Aggressive and Loose Passive styles that match the original CFR-based strategies in performance while behaving distinctly. For some hand scenarios, its strategies differ substantially from both conventional expert heuristics and original CFR outputs. The authors suggest that these departures could offer insights to professional players. The evidence supports producing varied competitive styles in the tested setting, while the potential value of unusual decisions to experts remains a possibility.
summary.tldr: Preference-CFR adds controls for playing style and vulnerability, producing distinct poker strategies with competitive experimental performance.

title: Preference-CFR: Beyond Nash Equilibrium for Better Game Strategies

abstract: Piecewise constant functions describe a variety of real-world phenomena in domains ranging from chemistry to manufacturing. In practice, it is often required to confidently identify the locations of the abrupt changes in these functions as quickly as possible. For this, we introduce a fixed-confidence piecewise constant bandit problem. Here, we sequentially query points in the domain and receive noisy evaluations of the function under bandit feedback. We provide instance-dependent lower bounds for the complexity of change point identification in this problem. These lower bounds illustrate that an optimal method should focus its sampling efforts adjacent to each of the change points, and the number of samples around each change point should be inversely proportional to the magnitude of the change. Building on this, we devise a simple and computationally efficient variant of Track-and-Stop and prove that it is asymptotically optimal in many regimes. We support our theoretical findings with experimental results in synthetic environments demonstrating the efficiency of our method.

paragraphs: Many processes remain approximately constant over intervals and then change abruptly. This paper asks how to locate multiple such changes quickly when observations are noisy and the learner chooses which point to query next. The objective is fixed-confidence identification: gather enough evidence to locate the changes at a specified confidence level.

The authors first derive lower bounds on the sampling complexity for individual problem instances. These bounds indicate that an optimal method should concentrate observations next to the change points. They also describe how sampling effort should depend inversely on change magnitude, directing more attention toward changes that are harder to distinguish in noisy observations.

Using this guidance, the paper develops a simple, computationally efficient variant of Track-and-Stop. The authors prove asymptotic optimality in many regimes and provide synthetic experiments supporting its efficiency. The result connects an account of where information is most valuable with an algorithm that allocates queries accordingly. Its optimality claim is explicitly asymptotic and applies to the regimes covered by the analysis.
summary.tldr: A Track-and-Stop variant locates multiple noisy change points efficiently and is asymptotically optimal in many analyzed regimes.

title: Fixed-Confidence Multiple Change Point Identification under Bandit Feedback

abstract: Deep clustering, an unsupervised technique independent of labels, necessitates tailored supervision for model training. Prior methods explore supervision like similarity and pseudo labels, yet overlook individual sample training analysis. Our study correlates sample stability during unsupervised training with clustering accuracy and network memorization on a per-sample basis. Unstable representations across epochs often lead to mispredictions, indicating difficulty in memorization and atypicality. Leveraging these findings, we introduce supervision signals for the first time based on sample stability at the representation level. Our proposed strategy serves as a versatile tool to enhance various deep clustering techniques. Experiments across benchmark datasets showcase that incorporating sample stability into training can improve the performance of deep clustering. The code is available at https://github.com/LZX-001/LFSS.

paragraphs: Deep clustering learns to group examples without access to labels, so its training must obtain supervision from other signals. Common choices include similarities between examples and labels estimated by the model itself. This paper examines another source: how consistently each individual example is represented as training progresses across epochs.

The authors connect this sample-level stability with clustering accuracy and the network’s ability to memorize individual examples. Representations that change substantially across epochs often correspond to incorrect predictions, difficulty in memorization, and atypical examples. This is a relationship observed during training, making the behavior of each sample over time informative for constructing supervision.

Building on these findings, the paper introduces training signals based on stability at the representation level. The strategy is designed to enhance multiple deep clustering techniques, and benchmark experiments show that incorporating it can improve performance. The practical contribution is a way to use the training trajectory itself to guide unsupervised learning, supplementing signals based on similarities or estimated labels.
summary.tldr: Tracking how stable each example’s representation remains across training provides supervision that can improve deep clustering.

title: Learning from Sample Stability for Deep Clustering

abstract: Techniques enabling large language models (LLMs) to "think more" by generating and attending to intermediate reasoning steps have shown promise in solving complex problems. However, the standard approaches generate sequences of discrete tokens immediately before responding, and so they can incur significant latency costs and be challenging to optimize. In this work, we demonstrate that a frozen LLM can be augmented with an offline coprocessor that operates on the model’s key-value (kv) cache. This coprocessor augments the cache with a set of latent embeddings designed to improve the fidelity of subsequent decoding. We train this coprocessor using the language modeling loss from the decoder on standard pretraining data, while keeping the decoder itself frozen. This approach enables the model to learn, in an end-to-end differentiable fashion, how to distill additional computation into its kv-cache. Because the decoder remains unchanged, the coprocessor can operate offline and asynchronously, and the language model can function normally if the coprocessor is unavailable or if a given cache is deemed not to require extra computation. We show experimentally that when a cache is augmented, the decoder achieves lower perplexity on numerous subsequent tokens. Furthermore, even without any task-specific training, our experiments demonstrate that cache augmentation consistently improves performance across a range of reasoning-intensive tasks.

paragraphs: Giving a language model additional reasoning steps can improve difficult answers, but generating those steps as text can add latency and complicate optimization. This paper explores an alternative place for extra computation: the model's key-value cache, which stores internal representations used during subsequent token generation.

The method adds a coprocessor that produces latent embeddings to augment that cache. Training uses the decoder's language-modeling loss on ordinary pretraining data, while the decoder remains frozen. This makes the extra computation differentiable end to end and teaches the coprocessor to place useful information directly into the cache.

Because the decoder itself is unchanged, the coprocessor can run offline and asynchronously. The language model can also continue operating when the coprocessor is unavailable or extra computation is unnecessary. Experiments show lower perplexity across numerous tokens following augmentation and consistent improvements on several reasoning-intensive tasks without task-specific training. These findings indicate that additional internal computation can improve later decoding without expressing every intermediate step as generated text.
summary.tldr: A trained coprocessor augments a frozen language model's cache with latent embeddings that improve subsequent predictions and reasoning.

title: Deliberation in Latent Space via Differentiable Cache Augmentation

abstract: We consider the problem of length generalization in sequence prediction. We define a new metric of performance in this setting – the Asymmetric-Regret– which measures regret against a benchmark predictor with longer context length than available to the learner. We continue by studying this concept through the lens of the spectral filter-ing algorithm. We present a gradient-based learn-ing algorithm that provably achieves length generalization for linear dynamical systems. We conclude with proof-of-concept experiments which are consistent with our theory.

We present a gradient-based learn-ing algorithm that provably achieves length generalization for linear dynamical systems. We conclude with proof-of-concept experiments which are consistent with our theory.

paragraphs: Length generalization asks how sequence predictors perform when the relevant temporal context extends beyond what is available to the learner. This paper makes that comparison explicit through a new performance measure called Asymmetric-Regret. It evaluates the learner against a benchmark predictor that can use a longer context.

The asymmetry is central to the formulation: the learner and its comparator do not receive the same amount of history. The metric therefore measures performance against a predictor with a context advantage. This gives a precise way to study length generalization rather than evaluating only against a benchmark restricted to the learner’s own context length.

The authors investigate this objective using spectral filtering and present a gradient-based learning algorithm with a provable length-generalization result for linear dynamical systems. That system class is the stated scope of the theoretical guarantee. They also provide proof-of-concept experiments consistent with the theory. The contribution combines a formal comparison criterion with an algorithmic result, giving a theoretical foundation for studying prediction with unequal context lengths.
summary.tldr: A spectral-filtering algorithm provably generalizes in context length for linear dynamical systems under a new asymmetric regret measure.

title: Provable Length Generalization in Sequence Prediction via Spectral Filtering

abstract: Recent large language models (LLMs) support long contexts ranging from 128K to 1M tokens. A popular method for evaluating these capabilities is the needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH) test, which involves retrieving a "needle" (relevant information) from a "haystack" (long irrelevant context). Extensions of this approach include increasing distractors, fact chaining, and in-context reasoning. However, in these benchmarks, models can exploit existing literal matches between the needle and haystack to simplify the task. To address this, we introduce NoLiMa, a benchmark extending NIAH with a carefully designed needle set, where questions and needles have minimal lexical overlap, requiring models to infer latent associations to locate the needle within the haystack. We evaluate 13 popular LLMs that claim to support contexts of at least 128K tokens. While they perform well in short contexts ($<$1K), performance degrades significantly as context length increases. At 32K, for instance, 11 models drop below 50% of their strong short-length baselines. Even GPT-4o, one of the top-performing exceptions, experiences a reduction from an almost-perfect baseline of 99.3% to 69.7%. Our analysis suggests these declines stem from the increased difficulty the attention mechanism faces in longer contexts when literal matches are absent, making it harder to retrieve relevant information. Even models enhanced with reasoning capabilities or CoT prompting struggle to maintain performance in long contexts. We publicly release the dataset and evaluation code at https://github.com/adobe-research/NoLiMa.

paragraphs: Long-context benchmarks often ask models to find a relevant fact inside a large amount of unrelated text. However, matching words between the question and the fact can simplify that search. NoLiMa reduces this shortcut by constructing questions and relevant passages with minimal lexical overlap, requiring models to infer the association that makes a passage relevant.

At 32K tokens, 11 models fall below half of their short-context performance. GPT-4o also declines, from a 99.3% baseline to 69.7%, despite being among the stronger exceptions.

The analysis suggests that longer contexts make attention-based retrieval harder when literal matching is unavailable. Models with reasoning capabilities and chain-of-thought prompting also struggle to sustain performance. The benchmark therefore tests an aspect of long-context use that ordinary word-overlap retrieval can obscure: finding relevant information through its meaning and associations.
summary.tldr: NoLiMa reveals substantial long-context performance declines when models must retrieve information through associations instead of literal word matches.

title: NoLiMa: Long-Context Evaluation Beyond Literal Matching

abstract: Federated learning (FL) is a popular collaborative learning paradigm, whereby agents with individual datasets can jointly train an ML model. While higher data sharing improves model accuracy and leads to higher payoffs, it also raises costs associated with data acquisition or loss of privacy, causing agents to be strategic about their data contribution. This leads to undesirable behavior at a Nash equilibrium (NE) such as free-riding, resulting in sub-optimal fairness, data sharing, and welfare. To address this, we design $\mathcal{M}^{Shap}$, a budget-balanced payment mechanism for FL, that admits Nash equilibria under mild conditions, and achieves reciprocal fairness: where each agent’s payoff equals her contribution to the collaboration, as measured by the Shapley share. In addition to fairness, we show that the NE under $\mathcal{M}^{Shap}$ has desirable guarantees in terms of accuracy, welfare, and total data collected. We validate our theoretical results through experiments, demonstrating that $\mathcal{M}^{Shap}$ outperforms baselines in terms of fairness and efficiency.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets participants train a model together, but contributing more data can involve acquisition costs or privacy loss. Participants may therefore contribute strategically even when additional data would improve the shared model. The paper examines how this can produce free-riding and poor collective outcomes at a Nash equilibrium.

The authors design a budget-balanced payment mechanism called MShap. Under mild conditions, it admits Nash equilibria and achieves reciprocal fairness: each participant’s payoff equals their contribution as measured by the Shapley share. This provides an explicit rule linking what a participant receives to the value they contribute to the collaboration.

The analysis also establishes desirable equilibrium guarantees for accuracy, welfare, and total data collected. Experiments support the theoretical results and show improvements over baselines in fairness and efficiency. The mechanism’s significance is that it addresses incentives alongside model training: rewarding contributions can alter the strategic conditions under which participants share data. The equilibrium existence claim remains conditional on the paper’s mild conditions, and reciprocal fairness has the specific Shapley-based meaning used in the analysis.
summary.tldr: A budget-balanced payment mechanism ties federated learning payoffs to Shapley contributions, with fairness and efficiency guarantees under stated conditions.

title: You Get What You Give: Reciprocally Fair Federated Learning

abstract: Plasticity, or the ability of an agent to adapt to new tasks, environments, or distributions, is crucial for continual learning. In this paper, we study the loss of plasticity in deep continual RL from the lens of churn: network output variability induced by the data in each training batch. We demonstrate that (1) the loss of plasticity is accompanied by the exacerbation of churn due to the gradual rank decrease of the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) matrix; (2) reducing churn helps prevent rank collapse and adjusts the step size of regular RL gradients adaptively. Moreover, we introduce Continual Churn Approximated Reduction (C-CHAIN) and demonstrate it improves learning performance and outperforms baselines in a diverse range of continual learning environments on OpenAI Gym Control, ProcGen, DeepMind Control Suite, and MinAtar benchmarks.

We demonstrate that (1) the loss of plasticity is accompanied by the exacerbation of churn due to the gradual rank decrease of the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) matrix; (2) reducing churn helps prevent rank collapse and adjusts the step size of regular RL gradients adaptively. paragraphs: Continual reinforcement learning requires an agent to remain able to adapt as tasks, environments, or data distributions change. That adaptability is called plasticity. This paper studies its deterioration through churn: changes in network outputs induced by the examples in each training batch. The investigation connects increasing output variability with the loss of continued learning ability.

The authors show that plasticity loss is accompanied by worsening churn as the Neural Tangent Kernel matrix gradually loses rank. They also show that reducing churn helps prevent rank collapse and adaptively adjusts the step size of ordinary reinforcement-learning gradients. This provides both a structural connection to the network's learning dynamics and a mechanism for influencing its updates.

The proposed method, Continual Churn Approximated Reduction, or C-CHAIN, puts this perspective into an algorithm. Experiments report better learning performance than baselines across continual-learning environments from OpenAI Gym Control, ProcGen, DeepMind Control Suite, and MinAtar. The findings support churn reduction as a practical way to mitigate plasticity loss across the tested environments.
summary.tldr: C-CHAIN reduces training-induced output churn to help preserve plasticity and improve continual reinforcement learning.

title: Mitigating Plasticity Loss in Continual Reinforcement Learning by Reducing Churn

abstract: Continual learning (CL) is crucial for advancing human-level intelligence, but its theoretical understanding, especially regarding factors influencing forgetting, is still relatively limited. This work aims to build a unified theoretical framework for understanding CL using feature learning theory. Different from most existing studies that analyze forgetting under linear regression model or lazy training, we focus on a more practical two-layer convolutional neural network (CNN) with polynomial ReLU activation for sequential tasks within a signal-noise data model. Specifically, we theoretically reveal how the angle between task signal vectors influences forgetting that: acute or small obtuse angles lead to benign forgetting, whereas larger obtuse angles result in harmful forgetting. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the replay method alleviates forgetting by expanding the range of angles corresponding to benign forgetting. Our theoretical results suggest that mid-angle sampling, which selects examples with moderate angles to the prototype, can enhance the replay method’s ability to mitigate forgetting. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets confirm our theoretical results and highlight the effectiveness of our mid-angle sampling strategy.

paragraphs: Continual learning requires learning new tasks while retaining earlier knowledge. This paper studies forgetting through feature learning, asking how relationships between task signals affect that process. Its theoretical setting uses sequential tasks from a signal-noise data model and a two-layer convolutional network with polynomial ReLU activation.

Within this setting, the angle between task signal vectors separates different forgetting behaviors. Acute angles and small obtuse angles lead to benign forgetting, whereas larger obtuse angles lead to harmful forgetting. The analysis also shows that replaying earlier examples expands the range of angles associated with benign forgetting. Replay therefore changes which task relationships the learner can accommodate favorably.

These results motivate mid-angle sampling, which chooses replay examples whose angles to a prototype are moderate. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support the theoretical findings and show the effectiveness of this sampling strategy. The contribution connects a geometric account of task interaction with a concrete replay-selection method, while the formal angle-based conclusions are established in the specified network and data model.
summary.tldr: A feature-learning analysis links forgetting to task-signal angles and motivates selecting moderate-angle examples for replay.

title: Understanding the Forgetting of (Replay-based) Continual Learning via Feature Learning: Angle Matters

abstract: Training large language models (LLMs) on heterogeneous data requires selecting minibatches that balance convergence speed with coverage across domains. Existing methods either select samples independently within each domain or rely on computationally expensive proxy models to learn continuous domain weights. We propose PartitionSel, a cross-domain minibatch selection approach that maximizes a validation-guided gradient-matching utility under per-domain budgets encoded as a partition-matroid constraint. By coupling the per-domain budgets through a single utility, PartitionSel is designed to reduce redundancy in selections across domains. The proposed objective is weakly submodular and admits an orthogonal matching pursuit algorithm with provable approximation guarantees. Empirically, we evaluate PartitionSel for minibatch selection during the fine-tuning of Qwen2.5 and Llama-3 on MetaMathQA and Mol-Instructions. PartitionSel achieves robust gains over per-domain and domain-agnostic baselines on both benchmarks. It also reduces the number of conflicting gradient pairs within each batch, indicating that the cross-domain coupling translates into more compatible training updates.

It also reduces the number of conflicting gradient pairs within batches, indicating more compatible training updates. title: Minibatch selection for Language Models via Partition Matroid Constrained Gradient Matching

abstract: We study code-to-metric regression: predicting numeric outcomes of code executions, a challenging task due to the open-ended nature of programming languages. While prior methods have resorted to heavy and domain-specific feature engineering, we show that a single unified Regression Language Model (RLM) using a frozen LLM encoder can simultaneously predict directly from text, (i) the memory footprint of code across multiple high-level languages such as Python and C++, (ii) the latency of Triton GPU kernels, and (iii) the accuracy and speed of trained neural networks represented in ONNX. In particular, a relatively small 300M parameter RLM based on T5Gemma, obtains $>$0.9 Spearman-rank on competitive programming submissions from APPS, and a single unified model achieves $>$0.5 average Spearman-rank across 24 different programming languages from CodeNet. Furthermore, the RLM can obtain the highest average Kendall-Tau of 0.46 on five classic NAS design spaces previously dominated by graph neural networks, and simultaneously predict architecture latencies on numerous hardware platforms.

These findings support code text as a common basis for predicting several kinds of execution-related numerical outcomes.
summary.tldr: A unified regression model with a frozen language encoder predicts code memory use, kernel latency, and neural-network performance directly from text.

title: Regression Language Models for Code

abstract: Autoregressive models (ARMs) currently constitute the dominant paradigm for large language models (LLMs). Energy-based models (EBMs) represent another class of models, which have historically been less prevalent in LLM development, yet naturally characterize the optimal policy in post-training alignment. In this paper, we present a unified view of these two model classes. Taking the chain rule of probability as a starting point, we establish an explicit bijection between ARMs and EBMs in function space, which we show to correspond to a special case of the soft Bellman equation in maximum entropy reinforcement learning. Building upon this bijection, we derive the equivalence between supervised learning of ARMs and EBMs. Furthermore, we analyze the distillation of EBMs into ARMs by providing theoretical error bounds. Our results provide insights into the ability of ARMs to plan ahead, despite being based on the next-token prediction paradigm.

paragraphs: Predicting one token at a time can seem disconnected from evaluating where an entire sequence is going. This paper connects autoregressive models with energy-based models, which also naturally describe optimal policies in post-training alignment. Its aim is to explain how these two perspectives can represent the same underlying functions.

Starting from the probability chain rule, the authors establish a one-to-one correspondence between autoregressive and energy-based models in function space. They show that this correspondence is a special case of the soft Bellman equation from maximum entropy reinforcement learning. This provides a mathematical connection between sequential token probabilities and a formulation associated with planning.

Using that connection, the paper derives an equivalence between supervised learning in the two model classes and gives theoretical error bounds for distilling energy-based models into autoregressive ones. These results clarify how next-token prediction can accommodate lookahead. They concern a relationship between model functions and learning objectives, rather than an empirical claim that every language model reliably plans.
summary.tldr: A mathematical correspondence between autoregressive and energy-based models explains how next-token prediction can support lookahead.

title: Autoregressive Language Models are Secretly Energy-Based Models: Insights into the Lookahead Capabilities of Next-Token Prediction

abstract: Bayesian Last Layers (BLLs) provide a convenient and computationally efficient way to estimate uncertainty in neural networks. However, they underestimate epistemic uncertainty because they apply a Bayesian treatment only to the final layer, ignoring uncertainty induced by earlier layers. We propose a method that improves BLLs by leveraging a projection of Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) features onto the space spanned by the last-layer features. This enables posterior inference that accounts for variability of the full network while retaining the low computational cost of inference of a standard BLL. We show that our method yields posterior variances that are provably greater or equal to those of a standard BLL, correcting its tendency to underestimate epistemic uncertainty. To further reduce computational cost, we introduce a uniform subsampling scheme for estimating the projection matrix and for posterior inference. We derive approximation bounds for both types of subsampling. Empirical evaluations on UCI regression, contextual bandits, image classification, and out-of-distribution detection tasks in image and tabular datasets, demonstrate improved calibration and uncertainty estimates compared to standard BLLs and competitive baselines, while reducing computational cost.

paragraphs: Bayesian last layers offer inexpensive neural-network uncertainty estimates by applying Bayesian inference only to the final layer. This leaves uncertainty from earlier layers unaccounted for and can underestimate epistemic uncertainty. The paper aims to include variability from the full network while retaining the low inference cost of this restricted Bayesian treatment.

The authors prove that its posterior variances are at least as large as those of a standard Bayesian last layer. The authors report improved calibration and uncertainty estimates relative to standard Bayesian last layers and competitive baselines while reducing computational cost. The larger-variance guarantee addresses the identified underestimation tendency, with the empirical tests supporting the usefulness of the resulting uncertainty estimates.
summary.tldr: Projected and subsampled NTK features enrich Bayesian last-layer uncertainty estimates while preserving inexpensive inference.

title: Richer Bayesian Last Layers with Subsampled NTK Features

abstract: Can we determine someone’s geographic location solely from the sounds they hear? Are acoustic signals enough to localize within a country, state, or even city? In this work, we tackle the challenge of global-scale audio geolocation, with a particular focus on wildlife and natural sounds. We posit that bioacoustic signals contain informative geolocation cues because of well-defined geographic ranges of species. To test this hypothesis, we benchmark image geolocation and soundscape mapping methods, design oracles and species-centric baselines, and propose a hybrid approach that combines species range prediction with retrieval-based geolocation. We further ask whether geolocation improves with species-diverse recordings and spatiotemporal aggregation across neighboring samples. Finally, we extend our study to multimodal geolocation with case studies from movies that combine both audio and visual content. Our results highlight the potential of incorporating bioacoustic signals into geospatial tasks, motivating future work on species recognition and audio geolocation.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether wildlife and other natural sounds can reveal where a recording was made. Its central hypothesis connects sound recognition to geography: species occupy particular geographic ranges, so hearing them could provide clues about location. The study considers this problem globally, asking how much geographic information audio can supply.

The researchers benchmark approaches from image geolocation and soundscape mapping, alongside species-focused baselines and oracle comparisons. They also propose a hybrid method that combines predictions about species ranges with retrieval-based geolocation. This brings together geographic information associated with species and a retrieval approach to identifying plausible recording locations.

The study additionally examines whether recordings containing more species, or combinations of nearby samples across space and time, improve localization. Movie case studies extend the investigation to audio and visual information together. The reported conclusion is that bioacoustic signals have potential for geospatial tasks; the abstract does not claim that sound reliably identifies every country, state, or city. The work motivates further development of species recognition and audio geolocation.
summary.tldr: The study explores how species sounds and geographic ranges can support audio geolocation, including a hybrid range-prediction and retrieval approach.

title: Bioacoustic Geolocation: Species Sounds as Geographic Signals

abstract: Due to limited resources and public safety concerns, deep reinforcement learning (RL) agents for many cyber-physical systems (e.g., autonomous vehicles) are first trained in simulators. However, when deployed in real world environments, they often suffer from performance degradation or safety violations because of the inevitable Sim2Real gap. Existing zero-shot approaches, such as robust safe RL and domain randomization, mitigate this issue but typically at the cost of degraded performance or residual safety risks when experiencing unmodeled system dynamics. To address these limitations, we propose a novel reinforcement learning framework that enables safe and efficient policy transfer via probabilistic latent embeddings and dynamic policy adaptation. We consider a family of Constrained Markov Decision Processes (CMDPs) under different environment contexts. By leveraging latent context variable in meta-RL, the proposed framework infers the latent representation of the environment from simulated experiences. Furthermore, it incorporates a distributional RL formulation, which allows risk levels of the deployed policy to be adjusted dynamically, based on the estimation accuracy of the latent context variable. This strategy promotes safety at the early deployment stage and improves efficiency through fast policy adaptation under the Sim2Real gap.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning agents for physical systems are often trained in simulation because real-world training is costly or raises safety concerns. Deployment can then expose differences in system dynamics that reduce performance or cause safety violations. This paper proposes a transfer framework that combines inference about the environment with dynamic adjustment of policy risk.

The formulation considers a family of constrained Markov decision processes representing different environmental contexts. A latent context variable within meta-reinforcement learning captures an inferred representation of the environment from simulated experiences. Probabilistic latent embeddings allow the framework to account for uncertainty in that context representation as part of adaptation.

The framework also uses distributional reinforcement learning so that the deployed policy's risk level can change according to how accurately the latent context is estimated. This links uncertainty about the environment to the policy's behavior during transfer. The stated strategy promotes safety early in deployment and improves efficiency through rapid adaptation as the agent deals with the simulation-to-reality gap, rather than relying on a fixed risk setting throughout.
summary.tldr: The framework couples probabilistic environment-context inference with adaptive policy risk to support safer, more efficient simulation-to-real transfer.

title: Transferable Reinforcement Learning via Probabilistic Latent Embeddings and Dynamic Policy Adaptation for Sim-to-Real Deployment

abstract: We find that current emotion-oriented Omni-MLLMs still lack reliable omni-modal perception: they (i) underutilize multimodal cues in their reasoning trajectories and (ii) exhibit unfaithful behavior, often hallucinating modality-specific statements from other modalities. Building on these insights, we propose OPPO (Omni-Perception Policy Optimization), a reinforcement learning framework that explicitly optimizes multimodal perception. First, an Omni-Perception Reward decomposes ground-truth reasoning into fine-grained visual, acoustic, and emotion cues and rewards trajectories that semantically recover these cues. Second, an Omni-Perception Loss compares the policy under full and unimodally masked inputs, applying a KL penalty only to modality-specific evidence tokens to suppress cross-modal hallucination. We further introduce MEP-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark that quantifies utilization and faithfulness. Experiments show that OPPO achieves state-of-the-art performance on MER-UniBench and substantially improves utilization and faithfulness scores on MEP-Bench, highlighting the importance of sufficient and faithful omni perception for multimodal emotion reasoning.

First, an Omni-Perception Reward decomposes ground-truth reasoning into fine-grained visual, acoustic, and emotion cues and rewards trajectories that semantically recover these cues. paragraphs: Multimodal emotion models can fail in two connected ways: they may overlook useful evidence, or they may claim that one modality contains information actually inferred from another. This paper treats using available cues and attributing them faithfully as explicit training goals. OPPO applies reinforcement learning to improve both aspects of multimodal perception.

Its reward breaks ground-truth reasoning into fine-grained visual, acoustic, and emotion cues, then rewards generated reasoning that recovers their meaning. A separate loss compares the policy with all inputs present against the policy with individual modalities masked. It applies a KL penalty specifically to modality-related evidence tokens to suppress unsupported cross-modal statements.

The authors also introduce MEP-Bench, which measures evidence utilization and faithfulness as separate diagnostic dimensions. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on MER-UniBench and substantial improvements on both MEP-Bench measures. These results support training perception directly alongside emotion reasoning. They also make the intended improvement more specific: a model should draw on relevant multimodal evidence while keeping its statements faithful to the modality supplying that evidence.
summary.tldr: OPPO trains multimodal emotion models to use more relevant evidence and reduce unsupported claims about individual modalities.

title: Omni-Perception Policy Optimization for Multimodal Emotion Reasoning

abstract: We present a black-box model-stealing attack that recovers private vision-tokenizer configurations of deployed vision-language models (VLMs), including the visual patch size and input preprocessing pipeline. The key idea is a task-level side channel induced by ViT-style patchification: when a synthetic grid image is aligned with the hidden patch grid, boundary cues are erased at tokenization, causing periodic accuracy drop. By sweeping the grid cell size and measuring these collapses, we infer the patch size; by introducing padding and a consistency-check test, we further identify whether preprocessing is dynamic- or fixed-resolution and recover the target resize resolution. Across open-source Qwen-VL variants and proprietary models including GPT and Claude, we reliably recover tokenizer-related parameters. Finally, we show that such leakage enables preprocessing-aware transfer attacks and model-targeted adversarial manipulation.

paragraphs: This paper shows that a deployed vision-language model’s observable task behavior can reveal private details of its visual tokenizer. The recovered information includes image patch size and preprocessing configuration. The attack is black-box: the leakage comes from responses to visual inputs rather than access to the model’s internal implementation.

The underlying side channel arises when synthetic image boundaries align with the tokenizer’s hidden patch grid. Tokenization can erase boundary cues, producing periodic drops in task accuracy that expose the patch structure. The authors also use padding and consistency checks to distinguish dynamic-resolution from fixed-resolution preprocessing and identify the target resize resolution.

Across open-source Qwen-VL variants and proprietary GPT and Claude models, the method reliably recovers tokenizer-related parameters. The paper further demonstrates that this information supports preprocessing-aware transfer attacks and model-targeted adversarial manipulation. Its central finding is that seemingly hidden image-processing choices can leave a measurable behavioral signature with consequences for adversarial robustness.
summary.tldr: Behavioral side channels reveal private visual-tokenizer settings and can enable more targeted adversarial manipulation of vision-language models.

title: Steal the Patch Size: Adversarially Manipulate Vision Language Models

abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) can reduce error on new and different data by updating the model on these inputs during inference. However, these updates raise the issue of privacy w.r.t. the testing data, because the model parameters now depend on all past inputs. To control this privacy risk, we cast multiple popular TTA methods (Tent, EATA, SAR, DeYO, and COME) into differential privacy (DP) forms that apply per-sample gradient clipping and Gaussian noise for all updates. On ImageNet-C, our DP-TTA methods provide adequate privacy at small cost to accuracy, and in the low-privacy regime the clipping mechanism of DP can even improve the accuracy and stability of adaptation in the continual setting. These improvements to privacy and accuracy come at only modest computational overhead. These first results on private TTA raise awareness of the issue, inform the development of more private test-time updates, and identify per-sample clipping as an effective technique for improving the accuracy and stability of adaptation.

paragraphs: Test-time adaptation updates a model using inputs encountered during inference, helping it handle data that differs from training. Those updates also make model parameters depend on previous test inputs, creating a privacy concern. This paper studies how to control that dependence while preserving the benefits of adaptation.

The authors convert Tent, EATA, SAR, DeYO, and COME into differentially private variants. Every update clips each sample's gradient and adds Gaussian noise. Clipping limits how strongly an individual input can affect an update, while the noise is part of the privacy mechanism. Applying these changes across several methods examines private adaptation as a broader approach rather than a modification to only one algorithm.

On ImageNet-C, the resulting methods provide privacy with a small accuracy cost and modest computational overhead. In the low-privacy regime, clipping can additionally improve accuracy and stability during continual adaptation. That improvement is conditional on the reported regime, not a claim that stronger privacy always improves accuracy. The findings also identify per-sample clipping as a useful stabilizing component in its own right.
summary.tldr: Differentially private test-time updates protect inference data with small reported accuracy costs, while clipping can also stabilize continual adaptation.

title: Private and Stable Test-time Adaptation with Differential Privacy

abstract: Online Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) is a prominent framework for efficient agent coordination. Crucially, enhancing policy expressiveness is pivotal for achieving superior performance. Diffusion-based generative models are well-positioned to meet this demand, having demonstrated remarkable expressiveness and multimodal representation in image generation and offline settings. Yet, their potential in online MARL remains largely under-explored. A major obstacle is that the intractable likelihoods of diffusion models impede entropy-based exploration and coordination. To tackle this challenge, we propose among the first Online off-policy MARL framework using Diffusion policies (OMAD) to orchestrate coordination. Our key innovation is a relaxed policy objective that maximizes scaled joint entropy, facilitating effective exploration without relying on tractable likelihood. Complementing this, within the centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE) paradigm, we employ a joint distributional value function to optimize decentralized diffusion policies. It leverages tractable entropy-augmented targets to guide the simultaneous updates of diffusion policies, thereby ensuring stable coordination. Extensive evaluations on MPE and MAMuJoCo establish our method as the new state-of-the-art across $10$ diverse tasks, demonstrating a remarkable $2.5\times$ to $5\times$ improvement in sample efficiency.

paragraphs: Coordinating multiple learning agents requires policies expressive enough to represent different useful actions. Diffusion models offer that flexibility, but their action likelihoods are difficult to compute. This creates a problem for online reinforcement learning methods that use entropy to encourage exploration and coordinate agents' behavior.

OMAD is an online, off-policy framework that uses diffusion policies for multiple agents. Its central change is a relaxed objective that maximizes scaled joint entropy without requiring tractable policy likelihoods. During centralized training, a joint distributional value function guides the decentralized policies using computable entropy-augmented targets. The policies are updated together to support stable coordination.

This design follows centralized training with decentralized execution: learning can use joint information while execution remains distributed across agents. Evaluations on ten tasks from MPE and MAMuJoCo report state-of-the-art performance and improvements of 2.5 to 5 times in sample efficiency. These findings support the framework's ability to make expressive diffusion policies practical for the evaluated online coordination problems, where learning efficiently from interaction is central.
summary.tldr: OMAD enables entropy-guided online learning with decentralized diffusion policies, reporting 2.5–5 times better sample efficiency across ten coordination tasks.

title: Diffusing to Coordinate: Efficient Online Multi-Agent Diffusion Policies

abstract: Example-based guidance is widely used to improve mathematical reasoning at inference time, yet its effectiveness is highly unstable across problems and models—even when the guidance is correct and problem-relevant. We show that this instability arises from a previously underexplored gap between strategy usage—whether a reasoning strategy appears in successful solutions—and strategy executability—whether the strategy remains effective when instantiated as guidance for a target model. Through a controlled analysis of paired human-written and model-generated solutions, we identify a systematic dissociation between usage and executability: human- and model-derived strategies differ in structured, domain-dependent ways, leading to complementary strengths and consistent source-dependent reversals under guidance. Building on this diagnosis, we propose Selective Strategy Retrieval (SSR), a test-time framework that explicitly models executability by selectively retrieving and combining strategies using empirical, multi-route, source-aware signals. Across multiple mathematical reasoning benchmarks, SSR yields reliable and consistent improvements over direct solving, in-context learning, and single-source guidance, improving accuracy by up to $+13$ points on AIME25 and $+5$ points on Apex for compact reasoning models. Code and benchmark are publicly available at: https://github.com/lwd17/strategy-execute-pipeline.

Through a controlled analysis of paired human-written and model-generated solutions, we identify a systematic dissociation between usage and executability: human- and model-derived strategies differ in structured, domain-dependent ways, leading to complementary strengths and consistent source-dependent reversals under guidance. Building on this diagnosis, we propose Selective Strategy Retrieval (SSR), a test-time framework that explicitly models executability by selectively retrieving and combining strategies using empirical, multi-route, source-aware signals. Across multiple mathematical reasoning benchmarks, SSR yields reliable and consistent improvements over direct solving, in-context learning, and single-source guidance, improving accuracy by up to $+13$ points on AIME25 and $+5$ points on Apex for compact reasoning models. Code and benchmark are publicly available at: https://github.com/lwd17/strategy-execute-pipeline.

paragraphs: A mathematically correct example can still provide ineffective guidance to a reasoning model. This paper distinguishes strategy usage, meaning that a strategy appears in a successful solution, from strategy executability, meaning that a target model can use that strategy effectively when given it as guidance. The distinction explains why relevant examples can produce unstable improvements.

A controlled comparison of paired human-written and model-generated solutions finds that usage and executability diverge systematically. Human and model strategies have complementary strengths that vary by domain, and which source works better can reverse when strategies become guidance. Selective Strategy Retrieval uses empirical, multi-route, source-aware signals to choose and combine strategies at inference time.

Across mathematical reasoning benchmarks, this framework consistently improves over direct solving, in-context learning, and guidance from only one source. For compact reasoning models, reported accuracy gains reach 13 points on AIME25 and five points on Apex. The findings make the target model's ability to execute a strategy central to selecting guidance, alongside the strategy's mathematical correctness and relevance.
summary.tldr: Selective Strategy Retrieval improves mathematical guidance by choosing strategies a target model can effectively execute.

title: Strategy Executability in Mathematical Reasoning: Leveraging Human–Model Differences for Effective Guidance

abstract: Many fields collect large-scale temporal data through repeated measurements (‘trials’), where each trial is labeled with a set of metadata variables spanning several categories. For example, a trial in a neuroscience study may be linked to a value from category (a): task difficulty, and category (b): animal choice. A critical challenge in time-series analysis is to understand how these labels are encoded within the multi-trial observations, and disentangle the distinct effect of each label entry across categories. Here, we present MILCCI, a novel data-driven method that i) identifies the interpretable components underlying the data, ii) captures cross-trial variability, and iii) integrates label information to understand each category’s representation within the data. MILCCI extends a sparse per-trial decomposition that leverages label similarities within each category to enable subtle, label-driven cross-trial adjustments in component compositions and to distinguish the contribution of each category. MILCCI also learns each component’s corresponding temporal trace, which evolves over time within each trial and varies flexibly across trials. We demonstrate MILCCI’s performance through both synthetic and real-world examples, including voting patterns, online page view trends, and neuronal recordings.

Together, these examples show how the method combines multiple label categories with trial-specific dynamics to support interpretation across different kinds of temporal data.
summary.tldr: MILCCI uses multiple metadata categories to disentangle interpretable components and trial-specific dynamics in repeated time-series measurements.

title: Multi-Integration of Labels Across Categories for Component Identification in Multi-trial Time Series

abstract: Predicting long-horizon trajectories of biological dynamical systems remains challenging due to substantial system heterogeneity. Most existing machine learning approaches are system-specific, requiring retraining for each new system and exhibiting limited generalization across distinct biological regimes. To address this limitation, we create a large-scale benchmark of over 1,000 ODE-based systems biology models spanning diverse organisms, biological processes, and dynamical behaviors. Building on this benchmark, we propose a regime-aware trajectory prediction framework that enables cross-system generalization and uncertainty quantification for unseen systems. Our approach introduces structured initial states derived from biological regime priors, such as growth trends and oscillatory rhythms, into conditional flow matching, replacing the standard Gaussian source distribution. We provide theoretical justification for this initialization and empirically demonstrate state-of-the-art accuracy (31% MAE reduction), well-calibrated uncertainty (17% CRPS improvement), and efficient long-horizon inference across the benchmark.

paragraphs: Biological systems can follow very different patterns over time, making it difficult to build one predictor that works across them. This paper introduces a benchmark containing more than 1,000 systems biology models expressed as ordinary differential equations. The collection spans different organisms, biological processes, and dynamical behaviors, providing a basis for evaluating prediction across systems.

The proposed framework uses biological regime information to shape how trajectory generation begins. Instead of starting conditional flow matching from a standard Gaussian distribution, it uses structured initial states informed by patterns such as growth trends and oscillations. This gives the prediction process an initial structure related to the kinds of behavior it needs to model.

The authors provide theoretical support for this initialization and evaluate both prediction accuracy and uncertainty on the benchmark. They report a 31% reduction in mean absolute error, a 17% improvement in CRPS, well-calibrated uncertainty, and efficient long-horizon inference. These findings support regime-aware initialization as a way to improve predictions and uncertainty estimates for previously unseen biological systems.
summary.tldr: Biologically structured initialization improves cross-system trajectory prediction and uncertainty estimates on a benchmark of over 1,000 biological models.

title: A Regime-Aware Trajectory Prediction Framework for 1000+ Systems Biology Models

abstract: Rubrics provide a flexible way to train LLMs on open-ended long-form answers where verifiable rewards are not applicable and human preferences provide coarse signals. Prior work shows that reinforcement learning with rubric-based rewards leads to consistent gains in LLM post-training. Most existing approaches rely on rubrics that remain static over the course of training. Such static rubrics, however, are vulnerable to reward-hacking type behaviors and fail to capture emergent desiderata that arise during training. We introduce Online Rubrics Elicitation (OnlineRubrics), a method that dynamically curates evaluation criteria in an online manner through pairwise comparisons of responses from current and reference policies. This online process enables continuous identification and mitigation of errors as training proceeds. Empirically, this approach yields consistent improvements of up to 8% over training exclusively with static rubrics across AlpacaEval, GPQA, ArenaHard as well as the validation sets of expert questions and rubrics. We qualitatively analyze the elicited criteria and identify prominent themes such as transparency, practicality, organization, and reasoning.

paragraphs: Open-ended answers are difficult to train against a single verifiable reward, while overall human preferences can provide only coarse guidance. Rubrics offer more explicit evaluation criteria, but fixed rubrics can become inadequate as a model changes. They may miss newly emerging problems or leave opportunities for reward-hacking behavior.

OnlineRubrics updates those criteria during training. It compares pairs of responses produced by the current policy and a reference policy, using those comparisons to curate evaluation criteria. This ongoing process allows the training signal to address errors that become visible as learning proceeds, rather than depending entirely on standards fixed before training began.

The authors report consistent improvements over exclusively static rubrics, with gains reaching 8% across the evaluated benchmarks and validation sets. Their qualitative analysis identifies recurring criteria involving transparency, practicality, organization, and reasoning. The findings support adapting the evaluation rubric alongside the model, so that post-training can respond to developing weaknesses in long-form answers.
summary.tldr: OnlineRubrics improves post-training by continually updating evaluation criteria from comparisons of current and reference model responses.

title: Online Rubrics Elicitation from Pairwise Comparisons

abstract: Crowdsourced fact-checking systems have been adopted by major social media companies such as X, Meta, TikTok and Google with the aim of combating misleading information at scale without relying on centralized editorial control. These systems have been developed around a common underlying concept: a bridging mechanism that identifies notes flagging misleading information when they receive support from people with different perspectives rather than simple majority support. To our knowledge the only publicly disclosed bridging algorithms deployed for fact-checking are based on matrix factorization, as deployed by both X and Meta, augmented with additional components addressing abuse, targeted manipulation, and contributor brigades. This work examines the core matrix factorization portion of these systems, presenting theoretical and empirical evaluations of the degree to which coordinated users could vote strategically by leveraging the latent representations to fabricate the appearance of synthetic consensus within the bridging mechanism. Using historic production data, we find that up to 10.7% of lower quality notes could be manipulated above consensus thresholds using less than 10 ratings. We complement these findings with a theoretical analysis, revealing counterintuitively that rating a note as “Not Helpful” can increase its helpfulness score, as well as a cost model quantifying manipulation effort. We have developed and deployed mitigations within X’s Community Notes algorithm to address synthetic consensus.

paragraphs: Crowdsourced fact-checking systems can seek agreement across different perspectives rather than relying on majority votes. Their bridging mechanisms aim to identify notes supported by people who would not ordinarily agree. This paper studies how coordinated ratings can create an artificial appearance of that cross-perspective consensus within the core matrix factorization mechanism.

The authors combine theoretical analysis with experiments on historical production data. They find that up to 10.7% of lower-quality notes could be pushed above consensus thresholds with fewer than 10 ratings. The analysis also reveals that a “Not Helpful” rating can, counterintuitively, increase a note’s helpfulness score. A cost model characterizes the effort required for manipulation.

Its findings identify weaknesses in how the core mechanism infers consensus, rather than treating deployed systems as that component alone. The authors report developing and deploying mitigations in X’s Community Notes algorithm to address this synthetic consensus.
summary.tldr: Coordinated ratings can fabricate consensus in a core fact-checking mechanism, motivating mitigations deployed in X’s Community Notes.

title: Gaming Consensus: Coordinated Manipulation in Crowdsourced Fact-Checking

abstract: Clustering-based features are widely used in machine learning, but most methods must choose a resolution—a choice that is global, fixed, and ad hoc. Recent work shows that varying the resolution parameter produces only a finite set of structurally stable partitions, known as configurations. Based on this, we introduce Configuration-Mixed Prediction (CMP), a setting where models learn to adaptively weight these configurations per sample for downstream prediction. We propose MixConfig, a plug-and-play feature augmentation module that extracts configurations from any embedding and learns energy-aware mixing weights via a novel selector that jointly reasons about sample context, cluster assignments, and stability statistics. Experiments across tabular, molecular, vision, and text domains demonstrate consistent improvements over single-resolution and static baselines across diverse predictor architectures, with gains particularly pronounced in low-data regimes.

paragraphs: Clustering can supply useful features for prediction, but choosing one clustering resolution fixes how broadly or narrowly all samples are grouped. This paper builds on the observation that changing resolution produces a finite set of structurally stable partitions, called configurations. It asks whether a predictor can learn which configurations matter for each individual sample.

The proposed Configuration-Mixed Prediction setting allows sample-dependent weighting of those partitions. MixConfig implements this idea as a feature augmentation module that extracts configurations from an embedding. Its selector combines sample context, cluster membership, and stability statistics to learn energy-aware mixing weights. The resulting features can be used with different predictor architectures.

Experiments across tabular, molecular, vision, and text tasks report consistent improvements over fixed-resolution and static baselines. Gains are particularly pronounced when training data are scarce. The findings suggest that multiple stable views of an embedding contain complementary predictive information, and that adapting their contribution per sample can be more useful than making one global resolution choice.
summary.tldr: MixConfig learns sample-specific mixtures of stable clustering configurations, improving prediction across domains, especially with limited training data.

title: Mixing Configurations for Downstream Prediction

abstract: Looped Language Models (LoopLMs) enable efficient latent reasoning through depth recurrence, yet exhibit unreliable test-time scaling behavior: performance often peaks at a certain iteration depth and then collapses with further recurrence. Through latent dynamics analysis, we find an inherent trade-off between stability and effectiveness in existing architectures and strategies. By conceptualizing reasoning as uncertainty reduction, we propose that convergence toward stable fixed points while preserving effectiveness represents a promising way. To this end, we propose STARS (STAbility-driven Recurrent Scaling), a training framework that constrains latent states to approach asymptotically stable fixed points. This is realized via efficient Jacobian Spectral Radius Regularization with random loop sampling, enabling STARS to maximize effectiveness while ensuring rigorous stability. Experiments on arithmetic tasks show that STARS achieves reliable test-time scaling, and on complex mathematical reasoning it substantially mitigates performance degradation as recurrence depth increases while also improving peak performance.

paragraphs: Looped language models reuse computation across repeated internal reasoning steps. More iterations could provide more reasoning capacity, but performance can peak and then deteriorate sharply. This paper analyzes the underlying latent dynamics and identifies a tension between keeping repeated updates stable and making them useful.

STARS trains latent states to approach asymptotically stable fixed points: states that repeated updates settle toward. The framework uses Jacobian spectral-radius regularization with random loop sampling to constrain these dynamics efficiently. Motivated by reasoning as uncertainty reduction, the approach seeks useful convergence while maintaining the stability needed for additional recurrence.

Arithmetic experiments show reliable scaling as more iterations are used at inference time. On complex mathematical reasoning, STARS substantially reduces degradation at greater recurrence depths and improves peak performance. These are distinct outcomes: the abstract reports reliable scaling for arithmetic and mitigation of degradation for harder mathematics. Together, they support shaping recurrent dynamics during training as a way to make extra internal computation more dependable, rather than assuming additional loops automatically improve reasoning.
summary.tldr: STARS stabilizes repeated latent updates, enabling reliable arithmetic scaling and reducing depth-related degradation on complex mathematical reasoning.

title: Stabilizing Recurrent Dynamics for Test-Time Scalable Latent Reasoning in Looped Language Models

abstract: In many fairness and distribution robustness problems, one has access to labeled data from multiple source distributions yet the test data may come from an arbitrary member or a mixture of them. We study the problem of constructing a conformal prediction set that is uniformly valid across multiple, heterogeneous distributions, in the sense that no matter which distribution the test point is from, the coverage of the prediction set is guaranteed to exceed a pre-specified level. We first propose a max-p aggregation scheme that delivers finite-sample, multi-distribution coverage given any conformity scores associated with each distribution. Upon studying several efficiency optimization programs subject to uniform coverage, we prove the optimality and tightness of our aggregation scheme, and propose a general algorithm to learn conformity scores that lead to efficient prediction sets after the aggregation under standard conditions. We discuss how our framework relates to group-wise distributionally robust optimization, sub-population shift, fairness, and multi-source learning. In synthetic and real-data experiments, our method delivers valid worst-case coverage across multiple distributions while greatly reducing the set size compared with naively applying max-p aggregation to single-source conformity scores, and can be comparable in size to single-source prediction sets with popular, standard conformity scores.

paragraphs: When labeled data come from several populations, a prediction set should remain reliable whichever source population supplies the next example. This paper studies coverage that holds across heterogeneous source distributions, including the setting where test data come from their mixtures. The goal is to maintain the specified coverage level without making prediction sets unnecessarily large.

The proposed max-p aggregation combines distribution-specific conformity information and provides finite-sample coverage across the sources. The authors establish optimality and tightness for this aggregation through efficiency optimization problems constrained by uniform coverage. They also introduce an algorithm that learns conformity scores to produce more efficient aggregated sets under standard conditions.

Synthetic and real-data experiments show valid worst-case coverage with substantially smaller sets than naive max-p aggregation of single-source scores. Set sizes can also approach those of single-source prediction sets using standard scores. The findings distinguish obtaining robust coverage from obtaining useful, compact uncertainty estimates: learning scores for the aggregation itself helps reduce the size cost of protecting multiple distributions.
summary.tldr: A conformal aggregation framework guarantees coverage across multiple source distributions while learning scores that make prediction sets more compact.

title: Multi-Distribution Robust Conformal Prediction

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly adapted to downstream tasks in resource-constrained scenarios, making quantization-aware fine-tuning (QAF) a common practice for practical deployment. However, we find that quantized LLMs are substantially more vulnerable to safety alignment degradation during fine-tuning than full-precision models by interpretability analyses. In this paper, we first theoretically reveal that this vulnerability is driven by quantization errors, manifesting as an initial safety shift followed by a distorted optimization path. Based on this insight, we propose Explicit-Safety Quantization-Aware Fine-tuning (ExSQF), which effectively restores model safety while preserving downstream performance. It initializes adapters by combining quantization error with a safety matrix projection to mitigate early safety shifts, followed by post-training refinement that corrects deviations in the optimization path. Extensive experimental results show that ExSQF achieves state-of-the-art safety alignment recovery, even surpassing existing full-precision safety-aware fine-tuning baseline, while effectively preserving model performance.

paragraphs: This paper examines why fine-tuning quantized language models can weaken safety alignment more severely than fine-tuning full-precision models. Quantization-aware fine-tuning supports adaptation under resource constraints, but the authors’ interpretability analyses identify an additional vulnerability. Their theoretical account links it to quantization errors that affect both the starting safety behavior and the subsequent optimization trajectory.

Explicit-Safety Quantization-Aware Fine-tuning addresses these two stages separately. At initialization, it combines quantization error with a safety matrix projection when setting up adapters, aiming to reduce the early safety shift. After training, a refinement step corrects deviations associated with the altered optimization path. The intervention therefore follows the paper’s diagnosis across both initialization and adaptation.

Experiments report state-of-the-art recovery of safety alignment while preserving downstream task performance. The method also surpasses an existing full-precision safety-aware fine-tuning baseline in the reported evaluation. These findings suggest that explicitly accounting for quantization’s effects on safety can improve the adaptation process, rather than treating quantization error solely as an issue of ordinary task accuracy.
summary.tldr: ExSQF counters quantization-related safety degradation through safety-aware adapter initialization and post-training correction while preserving reported task performance.

title: Toward Safe Quantization-Aware Fine-tuning: Understanding and Mitigating Safety Alignment Degradation

abstract: Recently, multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have been widely applied to reasoning tasks. However, they suffer from limited multi-rationale semantic modeling, insufficient logical robustness, and susceptibility to misleading cues. Therefore, we propose a Multi-rationale INtegrated Discriminative (MIND) reasoning framework, which is designed to endow MLLMs with human-like cognitive abilities of “Understand $\rightarrow$ Rethink $\rightarrow$ Correct”, and achieves a paradigm evolution from passive imitation-based reasoning to active discriminative reasoning. Specifically, we introduce a Rationale Augmentation and Discrimination (RAD) paradigm, which provides a unified and extensible data foundation. Meanwhile, we design a Progressive Two-stage Correction Learning (P2CL) strategy. The first phase enhances multi-rationale positive learning, while the second phase enables active logic discrimination and correction. In addition, to mitigate representation entanglement in the multi-rationale semantic space, we propose a Multi-rationale Contrastive Alignment (MCA) optimization strategy. Extensive experiments show that our MIND achieves SOTA performance on multiple public datasets. Our data and code are available at https://github.com/YuChuang1205/MIND.
