paragraphs: Multimodal language models can produce reasoning that is vulnerable to misleading cues or fails to distinguish between different rationales. MIND addresses these problems by organizing learning around understanding, reconsideration, and correction. The aim is to train models to discriminate between reasoning paths and repair logical problems, rather than relying only on imitation of demonstrated answers.

The framework begins with Rationale Augmentation and Discrimination, which supplies a unified, extensible data foundation. Its Progressive Two-stage Correction Learning strategy then separates two training purposes. The first phase strengthens learning from multiple positive rationales, while the second develops active logical discrimination and correction. This sequence gives reasoning acquisition and reasoning revision explicit roles in training.

MIND also uses Multi-rationale Contrastive Alignment to reduce entanglement among representations of different rationales. This component addresses how reasoning alternatives are organized internally, complementing the data and correction-learning components. Experiments achieve state-of-the-art performance on multiple public datasets. The reported results support the overall framework’s effectiveness for multimodal reasoning, while its human-like terminology describes the intended workflow rather than establishing human-equivalent cognition.
summary.tldr: MIND trains multimodal models to learn multiple rationales, distinguish logical errors, and correct their reasoning.

title: MIND: Multi-rationale INtegrated Discriminative Reasoning Framework for Multi-modal Large Models

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate syntactically valid optimization programs, yet often struggle to reliably choose an effective modeling strategy, leading to incorrect formulations and inefficient solver behavior. We propose SAGE, a strategy-aware framework that makes Modeling Strategy explicit in both data construction and post-training. SAGE builds a solver-verified multi-strategy dataset and trains a student model with supervised fine-tuning followed by Segment-Weighted GRPO using a composite reward over format compliance, correctness, and solver efficiency. Across eight benchmarks spanning synthetic and real-world settings, SAGE improves average pass@1 from 72.7 to 80.3 over the strongest open-source baseline. With multiple generations, SAGE discovers more distinct correct formulations and improves component-level diversity at pass@16 by 19-29%. At the largest scale, SAGE produces more compact constraint systems with 14.2% fewer constraints than the baseline, consistent with solver-efficient modeling. Overall, these results show that making Modeling Strategy explicit improves automated optimization modeling. The code and data are available at https://github.com/rachhhhing/SAGE.

paragraphs: Producing valid optimization code does not ensure that a language model has chosen a correct or efficient mathematical formulation. Different modeling strategies can change both correctness and solver behavior. SAGE makes strategy selection an explicit part of training so that models learn how to formulate problems as well as how to express them.

The framework constructs a solver-verified dataset containing multiple strategies. It trains a student model with supervised fine-tuning followed by Segment-Weighted GRPO. A composite reward accounts for format compliance, correctness, and solver efficiency, connecting the training objective to several requirements of useful optimization programs.

Multiple generations yield more distinct correct formulations, with component-level diversity at pass@16 improving by 19–29%. At the largest scale, generated formulations use 14.2% fewer constraints, consistent with more efficient modeling. These results support explicit strategy training as a way to improve correctness, formulation diversity, and compactness together.
summary.tldr: SAGE explicitly trains optimization-modeling strategies, improving first-attempt success, formulation diversity, and constraint compactness.

title: Strategy-Aware Optimization Modeling with Reasoning LLMs

abstract: This position paper argues that explanation stability claims are scientifically invalid without cross-method validation. Just as statistical significance requires specifying the test statistic, stability must be validated across multiple attribution paradigms or explicitly scoped to a single method’s computational objective. In controlled chest X-ray experiments, DenseNet201, ResNet50V2, and InceptionV3 achieve $>$99% AUC but exhibit reversed stability rankings across attribution methods. LayerCAM ranks InceptionV3 highest (IoU 0.777), while GradCAM++ favors DenseNet201, reducing InceptionV3’s score by 17.3%. These findings establish that explanation stability is an emergent property of the model–method pair, not an intrinsic model trait. We argue that explanation-based claims should be validated across multiple attribution methods and urge that regulatory submissions explicitly specify attribution operators to avoid illusory safety assurances.
originalAbstract: This position paper argues that explanation stability claims are scientifically invalid without cross-method validation. Just as statistical significance requires specifying the test statistic, stability must be validated across multiple attribution paradigms or explicitly scoped to a single method’s computational objective. In controlled chest X-ray experiments, DenseNet201, ResNet50V2, and InceptionV3 achieve $>$99% AUC but exhibit reversed stability rankings across attribution methods. LayerCAM ranks InceptionV3 highest (IoU 0.777), while GradCAM++ favors DenseNet201, reducing InceptionV3’s score by 17.3%. These findings establish that explanation stability is an emergent property of the model–method pair, not an intrinsic model trait. We argue that explanation-based claims should be validated across multiple attribution methods and urge that regulatory submissions explicitly specify attribution operators to avoid illusory safety assurances.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that the stability of an explanation depends on both the prediction model and the method used to explain it. A stability claim therefore needs either validation across different attribution approaches or an explicit restriction to one method's computational objective. Naming the model alone leaves the claim inadequately specified.

The authors support this argument with controlled chest X-ray experiments involving DenseNet201, ResNet50V2, and InceptionV3. All three exceed 99% AUC, yet their stability rankings change across explanation methods. LayerCAM places InceptionV3 first, with an overlap score of 0.777, while GradCAM++ favors DenseNet201 and lowers InceptionV3's score by 17.3%. Strong predictive performance does not settle which explanations appear most stable.

These reversals support the paper's central interpretation: explanation stability emerges from the model–method pairing. The authors call for explanation-based claims to be checked with multiple attribution methods and for regulatory submissions to identify the attribution operators used. This makes the scope of the evidence explicit and helps avoid safety assurances that depend on an unstated explanation choice.
summary.tldr: Chest X-ray experiments show reversed explanation-stability rankings across attribution methods, supporting evaluation of model–method pairs.

title: Position: Explanation Stability Is a Property of the Model–Method Pair, Not the Model
Learning Tactical Plans for Pilot Aiding
Reducing Real-world Failures of Approximate Explanation-based Rules
Detecting Concept Drift with Support Vector Machines

abstract: We provide a general framework for learning precise, compact, and fast representations of the Bayesian predictive distribution for a model. This framework is based on minimizing the KL divergence between the true predictive density and a suitable compact approximation. We consider various methods for doing this, both sampling based approximations, and deterministic approximations such as expectation propagation. These methods are tested on a mixture of Gaussians model for density estimation and on binary linear classification, with both synthetic data sets for visualization and several real data sets. Our results show significant reductions in prediction time and memory footprint.
originalAbstract: We provide a general framework for learning precise, compact, and fast representations of the Bayesian predictive distribution for a model. This framework is based on minimizing the KL divergence between the true predictive density and a suitable compact approximation. We consider various methods for doing this, both sampling based approximations, and deterministic approximations such as expectation propagation. These methods are tested on a mixture of Gaussians model for density estimation and on binary linear classification, with both synthetic data sets for visualization and several real data sets. paragraphs: Bayesian prediction produces a distribution over possible outcomes, and representing that distribution efficiently is the focus of this paper. The authors develop a general framework for learning a compact approximation that aims to retain predictive precision while reducing storage and prediction costs. The object being approximated is the model’s predictive distribution itself.

The framework chooses an approximation by minimizing Kullback–Leibler divergence from the true predictive density to a suitable compact representation. This gives the compression task an explicit objective: reduce the discrepancy between the predictive distribution and its approximation. The paper considers both approaches based on sampling and deterministic approaches, including expectation propagation, within this common formulation.

The methods are evaluated on Gaussian-mixture density estimation and binary linear classification. Synthetic datasets support visualization, while several real datasets provide additional tests. The reported results show significant reductions in prediction time and memory use. These findings demonstrate the practical value of learning a smaller predictive representation, with the divergence objective providing the link between compactness and fidelity.
summary.tldr: The paper learns compact Bayesian predictive approximations by minimizing KL divergence, reporting substantial savings in prediction time and memory.

title: Compact approximations to Bayesian predictive distributions

abstract: Several algorithms for learning near-optimal policies in Markov Decision Processes have been analyzed and proven efficient. Empirical results have suggested that Model-based Interval Estimation (MBIE) learns efficiently in practice, effectively balancing exploration and exploitation. This paper presents the first theoretical analysis of MBIE, proving its efficiency even under worst-case conditions. The paper also introduces a new performance metric, average loss, and relates it to its less “online” cousins from the literature.
originalAbstract: Several algorithms for learning near-optimal policies in Markov Decision Processes have been analyzed and proven efficient. Empirical results have suggested that Model-based Interval Estimation (MBIE) learns efficiently in practice, effectively balancing exploration and exploitation. This paper presents the first theoretical analysis of MBIE, proving its efficiency even under worst-case conditions. The paper also introduces a new performance metric, average loss, and relates it to its less “online” cousins from the literature.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent must choose between using what it already knows and taking actions that could teach it something useful. Model-Based Interval Estimation, or MBIE, addresses this exploration–exploitation tradeoff in Markov Decision Processes. Earlier empirical work suggested that it learned efficiently in practice. This paper asks whether that favorable behavior also has a theoretical justification.

The central contribution is the first theoretical analysis of MBIE, establishing its efficiency even in worst-case conditions. This strengthens the basis for using the algorithm: the argument extends beyond observing successful behavior in particular experiments. The result concerns efficient learning in the paper’s decision-process setting, where the objective is to obtain policies whose performance is close to optimal.

The paper also introduces average loss as a performance measure and connects it to measures from earlier work that are less directly online. This contribution brings attention to performance during ongoing interaction and learning. Together, the analysis and metric connect MBIE’s practical motivation with a formal account of learning efficiency.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes worst-case efficiency for MBIE and introduces average loss to assess performance during learning.

title: A theoretical analysis of Model-Based Interval Estimation
Efficient MAP approximation for dense energy functions
A statistical approach to rule learning

abstract: Although support vector machines (SVMs) for binary classification give rise to a decision rule that only relies on a subset of the training data points (support vectors), it will in general be based on all available features in the input space. We propose two direct, novel convex relaxations of a nonconvex sparse SVM formulation that explicitly constrains the cardinality of the vector of feature weights. One relaxation results in a quadratically-constrained quadratic program (QCQP), while the second is based on a semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxation. The QCQP formulation can be interpreted as applying an adaptive soft-threshold on the SVM hyperplane, while the SDP formulation learns a weighted inner-product (i.e. a kernel) that results in a sparse hyperplane. Experimental results show an increase in sparsity while conserving the generalization performance compared to a standard as well as a linear programming SVM.

The QCQP formulation can be interpreted as applying an adaptive soft-threshold on the SVM hyperplane, while the SDP formulation learns a weighted inner-product (i.e. a kernel) that results in a sparse hyperplane. Experimental results show an increase in sparsity while conserving the generalization performance compared to a standard as well as a linear programming SVM.

paragraphs: A support vector machine can base its prediction rule on only a subset of the training examples while still using every input feature. This paper targets feature sparsity: a decision rule with fewer nonzero feature weights. It starts from a formulation that explicitly limits how many weights can be nonzero, creating a nonconvex optimization problem.

The authors propose two convex relaxations of that formulation. One produces a quadratically constrained quadratic program and can be understood as adaptively soft-thresholding the weights of the separating hyperplane. The other uses semidefinite programming to learn a weighted inner product, or kernel, that yields a sparse hyperplane. Both formulations address the feature-count constraint through a convex optimization route.

Experiments compare the methods with a standard SVM and a linear programming SVM. The reported results show greater sparsity while preserving generalization performance in those comparisons. The contribution is therefore a pair of optimization formulations that seek more selective feature use, with empirical evidence that this selectivity need not reduce predictive performance in the tested settings.
summary.tldr: Two convex relaxations produce SVMs with fewer active features while preserving generalization performance in the reported experiments.

title: Direct convex relaxations of sparse SVM

abstract: Traditional methods for analyzing population structure, such as the Structure program, ignore the influence of mutational effects. We propose mStruct, an admixture of population-specific mixtures of inheritance models, that addresses the task of structure inference and mutation estimation jointly through a hierarchical Bayesian framework, and a variational algorithm for inference. We validated our method on synthetic data, and used it to analyze the HGDP-CEPH cell line panel of microsatellites used in (Rosenberg et al., 2002) and the HGDP SNP data used in (Conrad et al., 2006). A comparison of the structural maps of world populations estimated by mStruct and Structure is presented, and we also report potentially interesting mutation patterns in world populations estimated by mStruct, which is not possible by Structure.
originalAbstract: Traditional methods for analyzing population structure, such as the Structure program, ignore the influence of mutational effects. We propose mStruct, an admixture of population-specific mixtures of inheritance models, that addresses the task of structure inference and mutation estimation jointly through a hierarchical Bayesian framework, and a variational algorithm for inference. We validated our method on synthetic data, and used it to analyze the HGDP-CEPH cell line panel of microsatellites used in (Rosenberg et al., 2002) and the HGDP SNP data used in (Conrad et al., 2006). A comparison of the structural maps of world populations estimated by mStruct and Structure is presented, and we also report potentially interesting mutation patterns in world populations estimated by mStruct, which is not possible by Structure.

paragraphs: The paper addresses population-structure inference when genetic variation reflects both population mixing and mutations. Traditional approaches such as Structure omit mutational effects. The proposed mStruct model brings mutation estimation into the same analysis as population structure, allowing both processes to contribute to the explanation of the observed genetic data.

Its hierarchical Bayesian formulation represents admixture through population-specific mixtures of inheritance models. A variational algorithm performs inference in this framework. This construction provides a shared model for estimating population relationships and mutation patterns, making mutation-related outputs part of the analysis rather than leaving them outside the representation.

The authors validate mStruct on synthetic data and apply it to HGDP microsatellite and SNP datasets. They compare its inferred maps of world population structure with those from Structure. They also report potentially interesting mutation patterns that Structure cannot estimate. The stated findings demonstrate the model’s additional analytical capability, while treating the biological interest of the inferred mutation patterns as provisional.
summary.tldr: mStruct jointly models population admixture and mutation, producing population-structure estimates and potentially informative mutation patterns.

title: mStruct: a new admixture model for inference of population structure in light of both genetic admixing and allele mutations

abstract: This paper introduces two new methods for label ranking based on a probabilistic model of ranking data, called the Plackett-Luce model. The idea of the first method is to use the PL model to fit locally constant probability models in the context of instance-based learning. As opposed to this, the second method estimates a global model in which the PL parameters are represented as functions of the instance. Comparing our methods with previous approaches to label ranking, we find that they offer a number of advantages. Experimentally, we moreover show that they are highly competitive to start-of-the-art methods in terms of predictive accuracy, especially in the case of training data with incomplete ranking information.
originalAbstract: This paper introduces two new methods for label ranking based on a probabilistic model of ranking data, called the Plackett-Luce model. The idea of the first method is to use the PL model to fit locally constant probability models in the context of instance-based learning. As opposed to this, the second method estimates a global model in which the PL parameters are represented as functions of the instance. Comparing our methods with previous approaches to label ranking, we find that they offer a number of advantages. Experimentally, we moreover show that they are highly competitive to start-of-the-art methods in terms of predictive accuracy, especially in the case of training data with incomplete ranking information.

paragraphs: Label ranking asks a learner to produce an ordering of labels for an input. This paper introduces two methods built around the Plackett-Luce model, a probabilistic model for ranking data. Both methods connect the input to a distribution over rankings, but they differ in how they make that distribution depend on the input.

The first method uses instance-based learning and fits probability models that are locally constant. The second estimates a global model in which the Plackett-Luce parameters are functions of the instance. This creates two approaches within the same probabilistic framework: local modeling around instances and a model that describes input dependence globally.

The authors compare both methods with earlier label-ranking approaches and report advantages as well as highly competitive predictive accuracy. Their experimental results are especially favorable when training examples contain incomplete ranking information. This finding makes the methods relevant to learning settings where the available supervision supplies only part of an ordering, while retaining ranking as the prediction task.
summary.tldr: Two Plackett-Luce label-ranking methods achieve competitive accuracy, particularly when training rankings are incomplete.

title: Label Ranking Methods based on the Plackett-Luce Model

abstract: We develop a semi-supervised learning method that constrains the posterior distribution of latent variables under a generative model to satisfy a rich set of feature expectation constraints estimated with labeled data. This approach encourages the generative model to discover latent structure that is relevant to a prediction task. We estimate parameters with a coordinate ascent algorithm, one step of which involves training a discriminative log-linear model with an embedded generative model. This hybrid model can be used for test time prediction. Unlike other high-performance semi-supervised methods, the proposed method converges to a local maximum of a single objective function, and affords additional flexibility, for example to use different latent and output spaces. We conduct experiments on three sequence labeling tasks, achieving the best reported results on two of them, and showing promising results on CoNLL03 NER.

This approach encourages the generative model to discover latent structure that is relevant to a prediction task. We estimate parameters with a coordinate ascent algorithm, one step of which involves training a discriminative log-linear model with an embedded generative model. This hybrid model can be used for test time prediction. Unlike other high-performance semi-supervised methods, the proposed method converges to a local maximum of a single objective function, and affords additional flexibility, for example to use different latent and output spaces. We conduct experiments on three sequence labeling tasks, achieving the best reported results on two of them, and showing promising results on CoNLL03 NER.

paragraphs: A generative model can discover hidden structure in data, but that structure may need guidance to become useful for a prediction task. This paper provides such guidance through feature-expectation constraints estimated from labeled examples. The constraints apply to the posterior distribution of latent variables, encouraging the generative model's hidden structure to support the desired predictions.

Parameters are learned with coordinate ascent. One step trains a discriminative log-linear model containing an embedded generative model, and this hybrid can also make predictions at test time. The approach optimizes a single objective and converges to a local maximum. It additionally allows the latent representation and output labels to occupy different spaces.

Experiments cover three sequence-labeling tasks. The method achieves the best reported results on two and promising results on CoNLL03 named-entity recognition. These findings support using labeled information to shape latent structure while retaining a generative component. The stated convergence result is specifically local, connecting the training procedure to one objective without claiming that it finds a global optimum.
summary.tldr: Constraints learned from labeled data guide a generative model toward prediction-relevant latent structure, yielding strong results on sequence-labeling tasks.

title: High-Performance Semi-Supervised Learning using Discriminatively Constrained Generative Models

abstract: In this paper, we apply tools from inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) to the problem of learning from (unlabeled) demonstration trajectories of behavior generated by varying ``intentions'' or objectives. We derive an EM approach that clusters observed trajectories by inferring the objectives for each cluster using any of several possible IRL methods, and then uses the constructed clusters to quickly identify the intent of a trajectory. We show that a natural approach to IRL---a gradient ascent method that modifies reward parameters to maximize the likelihood of the observed trajectories---is successful at quickly identifying unknown reward functions. We demonstrate these ideas in the context of apprenticeship learning by acquiring the preferences of a human driver in a simple highway car simulator.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we apply tools from inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) to the problem of learning from (unlabeled) demonstration trajectories of behavior generated by varying ``intentions'' or objectives. We derive an EM approach that clusters observed trajectories by inferring the objectives for each cluster using any of several possible IRL methods, and then uses the constructed clusters to quickly identify the intent of a trajectory. We show that a natural approach to IRL---a gradient ascent method that modifies reward parameters to maximize the likelihood of the observed trajectories---is successful at quickly identifying unknown reward functions. We demonstrate these ideas in the context of apprenticeship learning by acquiring the preferences of a human driver in a simple highway car simulator.

paragraphs: Learning from demonstrations becomes more complicated when the demonstrations express different objectives. This paper considers unlabeled behavior trajectories generated by varying intentions. The learner must discover which trajectories belong together and infer the objectives behind them, without receiving intention labels that would separate the demonstrations in advance.

The authors derive an expectation-maximization approach that groups trajectories while using inverse reinforcement learning to infer an objective for each group. Several inverse reinforcement learning methods can serve within this framework. Once the clusters have been constructed, they are used to identify a trajectory’s intention quickly, connecting objective discovery with subsequent recognition.

The paper also examines a likelihood-based inverse reinforcement learning method that adjusts reward parameters through gradient ascent. It reports success in quickly identifying unknown reward functions. A demonstration in a simple highway car simulator shows the approach acquiring a human driver’s preferences. This supports the proposed combination of clustering and reward inference within the stated apprenticeship-learning example.
summary.tldr: The paper combines trajectory clustering and inverse reinforcement learning to discover and recognize multiple intentions in unlabeled demonstrations.

title: Apprenticeship Learning About Multiple Intentions

abstract: We propose a method to learn simultaneously a vector-valued function and a kernel between its components. The obtained kernel can be used both to improve learning performances and to reveal structures in the output space which may be important in their own right. Our method is based on the solution of a suitable regularization problem over a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) of vector-valued functions. Although the regularized risk functional is non-convex, we show that it is invex, implying that all local minimizers are global minimizers. We derive a block-wise coordinate descent method that efficiently exploits the structure of the objective functional. Then, we empirically demonstrate that the proposed method can improve classification accuracy. Finally, we provide a visual interpretation of the learned kernel matrix for some well known datasets.
originalAbstract: We propose a method to learn simultaneously a vector-valued function and a kernel between its components. The obtained kernel can be used both to improve learning performances and to reveal structures in the output space which may be important in their own right. Our method is based on the solution of a suitable regularization problem over a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) of vector-valued functions. Although the regularized risk functional is non-convex, we show that it is invex, implying that all local minimizers are global minimizers. We derive a block-wise coordinate descent method that efficiently exploits the structure of the objective functional. Then, we empirically demonstrate that the proposed method can improve classification accuracy. Finally, we provide a visual interpretation of the learned kernel matrix for some well known datasets.

paragraphs: This paper learns a vector-valued prediction function together with a kernel describing relationships between its output components. Those learned relationships have two possible uses: helping prediction and exposing structure in the output space. The method therefore treats the organization of the outputs as something to learn alongside the predictor.

The authors formulate a regularized learning problem in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space of vector-valued functions. Although its objective is non-convex, they prove that it is invex, which implies that every local minimum is also a global minimum. This is a specific structural result about the objective, rather than a claim that it is convex.

A block coordinate descent algorithm exploits the objective's structure by working with blocks of variables. Experiments show that the method can improve classification accuracy, and visualizations provide interpretations of learned kernel matrices on established datasets. These findings illustrate the two intended benefits: predictive improvement and an inspectable representation of output relationships. The empirical claim is that improvement is possible in the evaluated settings, not that jointly learning an output kernel always improves accuracy.
summary.tldr: Jointly learning predictions and an output kernel can improve classification, with an invex objective whose local minima are global.

title: Learning Output Kernels with Block Coordinate Descent

abstract: This paper presents the first off-policy actor-critic reinforcement learning algorithm with a per-time-step complexity that scales linearly with the number of learned parameters. Previous work on actor-critic algorithms is limited to the on-policy setting and does not take advantage of the recent advances in off-policy gradient temporal-difference learning. Off-policy techniques, such as Greedy-GQ, enable a target policy to be learned while following and obtaining data from another (behavior) policy. For many problems, however, actor-critic methods are more practical than action value methods (like Greedy-GQ) because they explicitly represent the policy; consequently, the policy can be stochastic and utilize a large action space. In this paper, we illustrate how to practically combine the generality and learning potential of off-policy learning with the flexibility in action selection given by actor-critic methods. We derive an incremental, linear time and space complexity algorithm that includes eligibility traces, prove convergence under assumptions similar to previous off-policy algorithms, and empirically show better or comparable performance to existing algorithms on standard reinforcement-learning benchmark problems.

Previous work on actor-critic algorithms is limited to the on-policy setting and does not take advantage of the recent advances in off-policy gradient temporal-difference learning. We derive an incremental, linear time and space complexity algorithm that includes eligibility traces, prove convergence under assumptions similar to previous off-policy algorithms, and empirically show better or comparable performance to existing algorithms on standard reinforcement-learning benchmark problems.

paragraphs: Off-policy reinforcement learning learns a target policy from data collected while following a different behavior policy. Actor-critic methods explicitly represent the policy, making them useful when action selection should be stochastic or the action space is large. This paper combines these two capabilities in an incremental learning algorithm.

The authors build on advances in off-policy gradient temporal-difference learning to develop an actor-critic method whose per-step computation scales linearly with the number of learned parameters. Its space requirements are also linear, and it includes eligibility traces. This makes the combination computationally manageable as the parameter count grows, while preserving explicit control over the policy representation.

The paper presents the method as the first off-policy actor-critic algorithm with this per-step scaling. It proves convergence under assumptions similar to those used for previous off-policy algorithms. On standard reinforcement-learning benchmarks, it performs better than or comparably to existing methods. The contribution is the practical combination of off-policy data use, flexible policy representation, and economical incremental updates, backed by conditional theory and empirical comparisons.
summary.tldr: An incremental off-policy actor-critic algorithm combines flexible policy learning with linear time and space requirements and a conditional convergence guarantee.

title: Linear Off-Policy Actor-Critic

abstract: Retrieval tasks typically require a ranking of items given a query. Collaborative filtering tasks, on the other hand, learn models comparing users with items. In this paper we study the joint problem of recommending items to a user with respect to a given query, which is a surprisingly common task. This setup differs from the standard collaborative filtering one in that we are given a query × user × item tensor for training instead of the more traditional user × item matrix. Compared to document retrieval we do have a query, but we may or may not have content features (we will consider both cases) and we can also take account of the user’s profile. We introduce a factorized model for this new task that optimizes the top ranked items returned for the given query and user. We report empirical results where it outperforms several baselines.

In this paper we study the joint problem of recommending items to a user with respect to a given query, which is a surprisingly common task. This setup differs from the standard collaborative filtering one in that we are given a query × user × item tensor for training instead of the more traditional user × item matrix. Compared to document retrieval we do have a query, but we may or may not have content features (we will consider both cases) and we can also take account of the user’s profile. We introduce a factorized model for this new task that optimizes the top ranked items returned for the given query and user. We report empirical results where it outperforms several baselines.

paragraphs: Retrieval usually ranks items for a query, while collaborative filtering models relationships between users and items. This paper combines those tasks: recommend items to a particular user in response to a particular query. Both the user's profile and the query can therefore influence what should appear near the top.

The training data have three dimensions—query, user, and item—rather than the two-dimensional user-item matrix common in collaborative filtering. The authors introduce a factorized model for this structure and optimize the items ranked highest for each query-user combination. They consider settings both with and without content features, so the formulation accommodates different kinds of available item information.

The reported experiments show the model outperforming several baselines. This provides empirical support for modeling the joint retrieval problem directly. Its central contribution is to bring personalization and query relevance into the same ranking formulation, with attention to the top of the returned list rather than treating the user's interests and immediate query as separate tasks.
summary.tldr: A factorized query-user-item model learns personalized retrieval rankings and outperforms several baselines in the reported experiments.

title: Latent Collaborative Retrieval

abstract: As data sets grow in size, the ability of learning methods to find structure in them is increasingly hampered by the time needed to search the large spaces of possibilities and generate a score for each that takes all of the observed data into account. For instance, Bayesian networks, the model chosen in this paper, have a super-exponentially large search space for a fixed number of variables. One possible method to alleviate this problem is to use a proxy, such as a Gaussian Process regressor, in place of the true scoring function, training it on a selection of sampled networks. We prove here that the use of such a proxy is well-founded, as we can bound the smoothness of a commonly-used scoring function for Bayesian network structure learning. We show here that, compared to an identical search strategy using the network’s exact scores, our proxy-based search is able to get equivalent or better scores on a number of data sets in a fraction of the time.

For instance, Bayesian networks, the model chosen in this paper, have a super-exponentially large search space for a fixed number of variables. One possible method to alleviate this problem is to use a proxy, such as a Gaussian Process regressor, in place of the true scoring function, training it on a selection of sampled networks. We prove here that the use of such a proxy is well-founded, as we can bound the smoothness of a commonly-used scoring function for Bayesian network structure learning. We show here that, compared to an identical search strategy using the network’s exact scores, our proxy-based search is able to get equivalent or better scores on a number of data sets in a fraction of the time.

paragraphs: The paper examines a computational bottleneck in Bayesian network structure learning: searching an enormous space of possible networks while repeatedly scoring candidates against the observed data. The number of network structures grows super-exponentially with the number of variables. Even a search strategy that visits only some candidates can spend substantial time computing their exact scores.

The proposed approach uses a learned proxy, such as a Gaussian process regressor, in place of the true scoring function. The proxy is trained on a selection of sampled networks. The authors justify this strategy by proving a smoothness bound for a commonly used structure-learning score, providing a theoretical basis for approximating scores across candidate structures.

On several datasets, proxy-based search obtains equivalent or better scores in a fraction of the time required by an identical search strategy using exact scores. Holding the search strategy fixed makes the comparison directly relevant to replacing expensive scoring. The result supports proxy evaluation as an effective computational shortcut in these experiments, rather than claiming exact recovery of every network score.
summary.tldr: A smoothness bound supports proxy scoring for Bayesian network search, which achieves equivalent or better scores faster in the reported experiments.

title: Smoothness and Structure Learning by Proxy
